## **1 Decision problem, description of the technology and clinical care pathway** 

## **1.1 Decision problem** 

The objective of the current evaluation is to determine the clinical and cost effectiveness of durvalumab (IMFINZI[®] ) in combination with gemcitabine and cisplatin as neoadjuvant treatment, followed by durvalumab as monotherapy adjuvant treatment after radical cystectomy (RC), for the treatment of patients with resectable muscle invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) (1). The aforementioned regimen, hereinafter referred to as ‘perioperative durvalumab’, involves four cycles of durvalumab combined with gemcitabine and cisplatin as neoadjuvant therapy, followed by eight cycles of durvalumab as a single-agent adjuvant therapy (1). The marketing authorisation of perioperative durvalumab in MIBC is supported by the robust clinical evidence from the NIAGARA clinical trial (2). 

MIBC poses a significant clinical challenge as it is associated with rapid progression, aggressive tumours, high recurrence rates, and limited effective treatment options (3). Standard treatments like RC and neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) offer poor survival outcomes, with a five-year overall survival (OS) rate of less than 60% (4). Patients with MIBC continue to face high risk of disease recurrence and progression even after NAC and RC (58), profoundly impacting patients' quality of life (QoL) (9, 10). Although nivolumab is available as an adjuvant immuno-oncology (IO) therapy for MIBC, following NICE recommendation, it is used as a reactive intervention, only in patients at high risk of recurrence following RC with a programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression ≥1% and for whom adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy is not suitable (11). There is an unmet need in the current treatment pathway for cisplatin-eligible patients with resectable MIBC for treatment regimens that can address the following: 

- Increase long-term survival outcomes while reducing disease recurrence and progression rates. 

- Utilise the potential of IO therapies in both neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings to enhance curative intent surgery outcomes. 

- Facilitate the use of IO treatment for all patients, taking a proactive approach. 

Addressing the highlighted unmet need is crucial, as MIBC represents the last opportunity to cure the patient before the disease advances to metastatic bladder cancer (mBC). 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 13 -->

A perioperative regimen deploying the same IO therapy before and after surgery, has the potential to improve patient outcomes by priming anti-tumour immunity before surgery and sustaining immunosurveillance to eliminate micro-metastatic disease after surgery, thereby enhancing the likelihood of long-term disease control (12). 

The NIAGARA trial is the first Phase III study of perioperative IO in MIBC to demonstrate significantly improved OS for patients receiving perioperative durvalumab as compared to NAC alone (hazard ratio [HR]=0.75; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.594, 0.934; p=0.0106) (2). The NIAGARA trial also showed a statistically significant improvement in event-free survival (EFS) in favour of perioperative durvalumab, versus NAC alone without compromising the ability of patients to undergo RC (HR=0.68; 95% CI: 0.558, 0.817; p<0.0001) (2). The survival benefits demonstrated confirm that perioperative durvalumab effectively addresses the unmet need of cisplatin-eligible resectable MIBC and therefore it is poised to become the new standard of care in this population. 

The decision problem addressed in the current appraisal is broadly consistent with the final scope published by NICE, with any deviations detailed in Table 1 (13).

## **1.3 Health condition and position of the technology in the treatment pathway** 

**Summary of health condition and position of the technology in the treatment pathway** 

## **Disease overview** 

- Bladder cancer (BC) is the 9th most prevalent cancer globally; MIBC accounts for 25% of BC cases. 

- MIBC is defined by invasion of the detrusor muscle and represents the last opportunity for curative treatment. 

- **MIBC carries a high mortality risk: ~50% of patients relapse or progress to metastatic disease within five years despite standard treatment.** 

- BC has the highest lifetime cost of any cancer, due to frequent recurrence, intensive monitoring, and substantial direct and indirect costs. 

## **Standard of Care treatment in the UK** 

- **For eligible patients, European and UK guidelines recommend cisplatin-based NAC (gemcitabine and cisplatin) followed by RC** , with NAC offering only marginal survival benefits (~5% improvement). 

- Most patients do not receive treatment after radical cystectomy; adjuvant nivolumab is only offered to a restricted subset of patients. 

- Adjuvant nivolumab is positioned as a reactive intervention for high-risk, PD-L1≥1% patients who are unsuitable for adjuvant cisplatin, failing to address the unmet need of the larger MIBC patient population in the appraisal scope. 

## **Unmet need** 

- There is a critical need for therapies that reduce recurrence and progression, especially in cisplatin-eligible patients, as **current options fail to deliver durable survival or disease control.** 

- **There is a need of perioperative IO regimen** , deploying the same IO therapy before and after surgery, that can improve surgery outcomes by priming anti-tumour immunity before RC and sustain immunosurveillance to eliminate micro-metastatic disease after RC, thereby enhancing the likelihood of long-term disease control. 

## **Proposed positioning of perioperative durvalumab** 

- Perioperative durvalumab regimen involves four cycles of durvalumab combined with gemcitabine and cisplatin as neoadjuvant therapy, followed by eight cycles of durvalumab as a single-agent adjuvant therapy. 

- The addition of durvalumab to standard neoadjuvant therapy enhances the therapeutic efficacy through synergistic interaction with chemotherapy, and its continuation as adjuvant treatment maintains immunosurveillance after surgery, supporting the 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 20 -->

elimination of micro-metastatic disease 

- **The NIAGARA trial is the first and only study of a perioperative IO regimen demonstrating a statistically significant improvement in OS and EFS.** 

- Results show a 25% reduction in the risk of death and a 32% reduction in the risk of progression/recurrence or death compared to NAC followed by RC. The benefit was consistent across all patient subgroups. 

- **These unprecedented results have led the EAU to update the clinical guidelines to incorporate perioperative durvalumab, even before formal approval by the EMA.** 

- The proactive, single-decision point intervention, initiated at the start of the neoadjuvant setting, enables early and streamlined treatment planning, facilitates optimal scheduling of clinic visits, ensures clear and consistent communication with patients, and prevents the need for repeated evaluations for adjuvant therapy. 

- Perioperative durvalumab minimises uncertainty and reduces the burden of ongoing treatment decisions – ultimately enhancing both clinical outcomes and patient experience, reducing economic burden on payers, and improving overall treatment care. 

- **UK-based clinical experts consulted by the company unanimously agree that perioperative durvalumab will represent a paradigm shift and become standard of care for eligible patients.** 

- **Perioperative durvalumab represents a transformative opportunity in the treatment of cisplatin-eligible resectable MIBC patients.** 

## **1.3.1 Disease overview** 

BC is the most common malignancy of the urinary system that originates from the cells lining the urinary tract (22). It is particularly common among older adults, with risk factors including smoking, chemical exposure, and chronic bladder inflammation (23). 

## _**1.3.1.1 Disease classification, clinical presentation, diagnosis and staging of bladder cancer**_ 

## _**Classification**_ 

The classification of BC is based on the extent of tumour invasion within the bladder walls (22). Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) is confined to the inner urothelial layers and does not penetrate the detrusor muscle. In contrast, MIBC, the focus of the appraisal, refers to highgrade tumours that have infiltrated the deep detrusor muscle layers (24-26). MIBC represents the final stage at which curative treatment remains a viable option for patients, with the primary goal of preventing progression to advanced or mBC involving distant organs and tissues (4). 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 21 -->

## _**Clinical presentation**_ 

Most BC patients are symptomatic at diagnosis. Painless macroscopic haematuria is the most frequent initial symptom experienced by over 80% patients with MIBC (27, 28). Other presenting clinical signs and symptoms include microscopic haematuria, urinary urgency, dysuria, and in more advanced tumours, pelvic pain or symptoms related to urinary tract obstruction (24, 27). A small proportion of patients are asymptomatic and detected incidentally through imaging and cystoscopy (29, 30). 

## _**Diagnosis**_ 

The European Association of Urology (EAU) guidelines for MIBC diagnosis recommend a comprehensive approach incorporating clinical evaluation, imaging, and histopathological assessment (4). Cystoscopy remains the gold standard for confirming MIBC and urinary cytology can be recommended, particularly for high-grade tumours. In cases where tumour visualisation through imaging is unequivocal, patients may proceed directly to transurethral resection of the bladder tumour without the need for diagnostic cystoscopy. Bladder imaging modalities are also essential for assessing suspected bladder masses (4). Additional methods, such as photodynamic diagnosis for carcinoma _in situ_ detection and assessments of prostatic urethra involvement in male patients, are recommended to enhance diagnostic precision, ensuring a more refined and targeted clinical evaluation (4). 

The diagnostic recommendations for MIBC provided by the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) are consistent with the guidelines established by the EAU (4, 31). 

## _**Staging**_ 

MIBC is staged using the eighth edition of the Tumour-Node-Metastasis (TNM) classification systems developed by the Union for International Cancer Control and the American Joint Committee on Cancer (32). Staging is determined by the extent of the primary tumour (T), regional lymph node involvement (N), and the presence of distant metastases (M) (32). Clinical staging is based on imaging, physical examination, and biopsy results, while pathological staging is determined after surgical removal of the tumour, providing a more definitive assessment of the disease extent (33, 34). 

Clinically and pathologically, MIBC tumours are staged as T2, T3, and T4 based on their depth of invasion, ranging from muscle invasion (T2) to invasion of surrounding tissues or nearby organs (T4), while the nodal involvement is staged as N0, N1, N2, and N3 based on the number and location of regional lymph nodes affected by metastasis, ranging from no regional lymph node 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 22 -->

metastasis (N0) to metastasis in common iliac lymph node(s) (N3) (33-35). The clinical stage of MIBC and the focus of the current appraisal is represented as T2N0/1M0-T4aN0/1M0 (32). 

Accurate staging is challenging, and several studies have reported the risk of mis-staging in BC, with patients clinically staged as T2N0 often found to be >T2N0 after RC, leading to inequities in treatment access and impacting overall outcomes (36-39). 

## _**1.3.1.2 Epidemiology**_ 

## _**Prevalence**_ 

BC is the ninth most prevalent cancer globally. In the United Kingdom (UK), BC is the eleventh most common cancer, with a five-year prevalence of 79,763 per 100,000 individuals in 2022 (40). In England, BC was the seventh most common cancer, with a five-year prevalence rate of 108.22 per 100,000 individuals in 2021 (41). Malignant BC cases (International Classification of Diseases [ICD] 10 code: C67 [Malignant neoplasm of bladder]) were 41.99 per 100,000 individuals (41). 

Gender disparities in BC are evident in the UK, with men accounting for over three times higher prevalence rate than in females (41), making it the seventh most common cancer among males in the UK as of 2022 (42). The higher prevalence of BC in males is attributed to increased likelihood of males being smokers and working in industries associated with exposure to carcinogenic substances (43-45). 

## _**Incidence**_ 

In the UK, the annual incidence rate of BC is 0.04%, translating to approximately 17,544 new cases each year (41). Of these, 90% cases are diagnosed as urothelial carcinoma, the most common histological subtype, accounting for 15,790 cases (23). 

MIBC accounts for approximately 25% of BC cases (46). 

## _**1.3.1.3 Burden of disease**_ 

## **1.3.1.3.1 Clinical burden** 

## _**Mortality**_ 

In 2022, BC ranked as the thirteenth leading cause of cancer deaths globally, with 220,596 deaths recorded (47), and an age-standardised mortality rate of 2.9 per 100,000 individuals (40). A systematic literature review (SLR) found that MIBC mortality rates in the UK range from 53.9% to 60.4%, with variations influenced by the timing of outcome measurements and the scheduling of 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 23 -->

the treatment in relation to the RC, as delays or suboptimal timing may impact disease progression and long-term survival outcomes (16, 48). 

## _**Recurrence/progression**_ 

BC imposes a significant burden on patients and the National Health Service (NHS) due to high recurrence rate (34, 42). MIBC is particularly aggressive, with nearly 50% of patients undergoing curative-intent treatment eventually relapsing and developing metastatic disease, most commonly within the first five years (24, 49). 

MIBC represents the final stage before progression to mBC, and hence preventing recurrence and reducing progression rates become highly critical as treatment goals. Current data highlight an unmet need for new treatments that can reduce or prevent disease progression and improve OS in the MIBC population. 

## **1.3.1.3.2 Humanistic burden** 

Patients with BC report worse experiences than patients with any other pelvic cancers, as shown by data from the 2011/2012 English Cancer Patient Experience Survey conducted within NHS hospitals (50). Frequent urinary dysfunction, pain, fatigue and reduced mobility can severely impact patients’ daily life and routine function (27). These physical burdens are compounded by psychological distress, including heightened anxiety and depression due to the uncertainty of disease trajectory, which collectively impair emotional and social health (51). Furthermore, disease recurrence and progression in BC significantly diminish patients’ overall well-being, intensifying both the physical and emotional burdens they face. Caregivers also face considerable strain, managing complex care needs and coping with emotional challenges, particularly during advanced stages of the disease (52). 

Although the current standard of care (SoC) treatments for MIBC (NAC followed by RC) offer potential for disease control to a certain extent, they fall short in providing long-term survival benefits and are associated with high recurrence rates (4). As a result, patients and associated caregivers often continue to experience significant psychological stress (53). There is an unmet need in patients with MIBC for a novel therapy that can not only prolong survival but also reduce or prevent disease recurrence and progression, thereby alleviating their emotional burden associated with the fear of relapse. 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 24 -->

## **1.3.1.3.3 Economic burden** 

## _**Direct costs**_ 

A study conducted in 2012 estimated that the healthcare expenses of BC including primary care, outpatient and inpatient services, accident and emergency care, and medication, accounted for 59% of the total cost and represent 5% of all cancer-related healthcare expenses (54). BC has the highest lifetime treatment costs per patient among all cancers, driven by high recurrence rates and the need for ongoing invasive monitoring (55). BC management remains suboptimal, as reflected by NHS England data showing 52,437 hospital admissions and 30,679 day cases due to malignant neoplasms of the bladder (ICD-10 code: C67) between 2020 and 2021 (56). In the UK, the total direct healthcare costs of BC were estimated at €286 million in 2012, with inpatient care alone accounting for €153 million (54). Additionally, disease progression to mBC necessitates greater healthcare resource utilisation (HCRU) than earlier stages, including frequent hospitalisations, advanced imaging, and additional therapeutic interventions (34). 

## _**Indirect costs**_ 

Beyond direct medical expenditures, BC is associated with high indirect costs, including lost productivity due to illness, workplace absenteeism, disability, and premature death (57). According to a study conducted in 2012, the indirect costs comprising of productivity losses due to morbidity and mortality, as well as informal care costs amounted to approximately €257 million in the UK (54). 

A substantial economic burden is highlighted by the direct and indirect costs associated with the treatment of BC, driven by high recurrence rates and the need for long-term monitoring, resulting in the highest lifetime treatment costs among all cancers. The financial strain on healthcare systems and society underscores an urgent need for more effective and economically sustainable treatment options that can reduce recurrence rates and disease progression, thereby alleviating the economic burden of payers. 

## **1.3.2 Clinical pathway of care** 

## _**1.3.2.1 Current treatment pathway – established/recommended treatments**_ 

## **1.3.2.1.1 Standard of Care treatment in the UK** 

EAU and ESMO therapeutic guidelines emphasise the importance of a multidisciplinary approach for treating MIBC patients. In the context of the scope of this appraisal, for MIBC patients with cT2-T4a N0-1 M0 disease, clinical guidelines recommend RC with pelvic lymph node dissection Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 25 -->

as the standard treatment (4, 31). Additionally, for patients eligible for cisplatin-based chemotherapy, which is the target population of the appraisal, clinical guidelines recommend the use of cisplatin-based chemotherapy as neoadjuvant therapy prior to RC, as it has shown to improve survival outcomes compared to RC alone (4). 

External clinical validation interviews for the purpose of this appraisal were conducted with several leading urologists and oncologists who manage patients with MIBC in routine clinical practice in the UK (hereafter referred to as the UK-based clinical experts). The UK-based clinical experts corroborated the adoption of the EAU and ESMO guidelines within their practice and confirmed that gemcitabine plus cisplatin is the standard NAC regimen in the UK (14). 

Current cisplatin eligibility criteria include an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 or 1, adequate renal function (glomerular filtration rate [GFR] of 60 mL/min/1.73 m² or above), and no significant hearing loss, peripheral neuropathy, or cardiac dysfunction (4, 31). Additionally, the UK-based clinical experts have noted that a lower GFR threshold (40-<60 mL/min/1.73) may be considered in their practice when using a split-dose regimen (14). The population included in the NIAGARA trial is aligned with the cisplatin eligibility criteria (2). 

## **1.3.2.1.2 Additional therapeutic options** 

In addition to the current SoC (NAC followed by RC) treatment guidelines include adjuvant treatments, such as adjuvant nivolumab (4, 31), that are aimed at eliminating residual disease, reducing the risk of recurrence, and improving long-term outcomes by targeting micro-metastases (4). 

## _**Adjuvant nivolumab**_ 

In 2022, NICE approved adjuvant nivolumab for patients at high risk of recurrence following RC, specifically for those with PD-L1 expression ≥1% and for whom cisplatin-based adjuvant chemotherapy is not suitable (11). In the case of cis-eligible patients adjuvant nivolumab eligibility criteria includes pathological stage of the resected tumour ypT2-ypT4a or any ypN+ stage, PDL1 expression on ≥1% of tumour cells as determined by an approved and validated PD-L1 assay and adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy being unsuitable due to prior neoadjuvant chemotherapy (11). Adjuvant nivolumab serves as a reactive approach in MIBC, guided by the postoperative risk of recurrence of the patient and PD-L1 expression (11). The duration of the treatment is one year (i.e., 13 cycles every 4-weeks)

## _**1.3.2.2 Unmet need within the current treatment pathway**_ 

## _**Overview**_ 

RC is used with curative intent in resectable MIBC. However, for many patients, it is associated with high recurrence rates and does not provide long-term survival benefits. It is estimated that up to 50% of MIBC patients will progress within five years, with either local recurrence or distant progression, even after undergoing RC (4). When the disease spreads to distant organs and tissues, causing metastasis, managing the condition becomes considerably more challenging, patient outcomes are notably poorer, and the possibility of curative-intent treatment is lost. Furthermore, the associated cost of managing metastatic disease increases substantially (4). 

Among the other available treatment regimens for MIBC: 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 27 -->

- In neoadjuvant setting, clinical experts have confirmed that gemcitabine-cisplatin is the standard in the UK, which offers only a modest survival benefit and is associated with high recurrence and progression rate (4), 

- In adjuvant setting, active treatment is use as reactive approach based on high-risk of recurrence after RC and it is furthermore limited to PD-L1 ≥1% patients for whom cisplatin is not a suitable treatment option, thereby restricting its potential benefit in a wide range of MIBC patients (14). 

The limitations of the current treatments highlight an unmet need for an effective treatment option in both neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings (4). Emerging evidence from the NIAGARA trial demonstrates that IO perioperative treatment approach offers a promising solution by mitigating recurrence and progression risks, while demonstrating long-term survival benefits (2). 

## _**Standard of care – NAC followed by RC**_ 

Surgical resection remains the cornerstone of curative intent; however, its prognostic outcomes are suboptimal, with a five-year survival rate of around 50% (4). Following RC, up to 15% MIBC patients experience local pelvic recurrence, while distant recurrence affects nearly 50% (4). 

Neoadjuvant treatment with cisplatin-based chemotherapy improves survival outcomes as compared to RC alone and is, therefore, considered a SoC treatment for MIBC (58). Studies have reported an extended five-year survival of 5% in patients receiving NAC followed by RC (4). Despite the survival improvement, the overall five-year OS rate still remains below 60% (4). Furthermore, the recurrence rates for MIBC following cisplatin-based NAC and RC still remains high (exceeding 50%) (4), highlighting the limited effectiveness of the current SoC. 

The aforementioned data highlights that the current SoC, NAC followed by RC, offers limited survival benefits and is associated with high recurrence rates, necessitating the need for a more effective treatment. 

## _**Adjuvant IO therapy**_ 

Nivolumab (an adjuvant IO therapy) has demonstrated benefits in MIBC patients at high-risk of disease recurrence post-surgery, with PD-L1 expression ≥1%, as shown in the CheckMate-274 trial (59). The treatment was restricted to patients with PD-L1 expression ≥1%, due to uncertainty of benefit in PD-L1 negative, failing to address the needs of the larger MIBC patient population (11, 14). Therefore, adjuvant nivolumab represents a reactive intervention limited to a narrow patient cohort, restricting the opportunity for early, proactive treatment planning and depriving patients of the potential benefits of immune priming with neoadjuvant immunotherapy. 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 28 -->

Patients in the scope of this appraisal are not only deprived of IO treatment in the neoadjuvant setting, but a large proportion of them will also be unable to receive IO as adjuvant treatment due to the restricted use of nivolumab (4). 

The high likelihood of recurrence, combined with the substantial burden of disease progression to the metastatic stage, places a continuous clinical and economic burden on both patients and the payers. 

## _**Need for perioperative IO therapy**_ 

The limitations of the current neoadjuvant and adjuvant therapies to prevent early-stage recurrence and provide long-term survival in cisplatin-eligible resectable MIBC patients leave a critical gap in the treatment landscape – particularly in utilising the potential of IO therapies earlier in the disease course. 

A perioperative regimen, deploying the same IO therapy before and after surgery, has the potential to improve surgery outcomes by priming anti-tumour immunity before surgery (neoadjuvant setting) and sustaining immunosurveillance to eliminate micro-metastatic disease after surgery (adjuvant setting), thereby enhancing the likelihood of long-term disease control, both of which are associated with a high risk of recurrence (12). 

Adopting perioperative regimens that establish both pre- and post-surgical treatment decisions at a single, early point in the disease course provides greater certainty in treatment planning, enabling proactive management to reduce the risk of recurrence and facilitate timely interventions. 

UK-based clinical experts emphasised the importance of effective treatments for resectable MIBC, highlighting the need to minimise the risk of relapse across a broader spectrum of patients. (14). 

Preclinical and early clinical evidence support the synergistic potential of combining IOs with chemotherapy, providing a strong rationale for perioperative strategies that integrate neoadjuvant gemcitabine and cisplatin with IO therapies (60). The efficacy results of the NIAGARA trial demonstrate that perioperative durvalumab offers a meaningful advance in curative-intent strategies for cisplatin-eligible patients with resectable MIBC (1). 

## _**1.3.2.3 Proposed positioning of perioperative durvalumab**_ 

Perioperative durvalumab is the first perioperative immune checkpoint inhibitor regimen to show benefit in survival for the treatment of resectable MIBC patients who are cisplatin eligible. The proposed positioning of durvalumab as a perioperative treatment in resectable MIBC was 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168]

validated with the UK-based clinical experts, who unanimously concluded that perioperative durvalumab would become the preferred first choice treatment for eligible patients, marking a significant shift in the therapeutic paradigm toward more durable, recurrence-preventive strategies (14). The clinical experts also unanimously agreed that the eligibility criteria that will be adopted in clinical practice for perioperative durvalumab aligns with the inclusion criteria used in the NIAGARA trial (14).

The NIAGARA trial is the first and only study demonstrating a statistically significant improvement 

in OS and EFS for all resectable MIBC cisplatin-eligible patients, treated with perioperative durvalumab combined with gemcitabine and cisplatin. Preliminary results show a 25% reduction in the risk of death and a 32% reduction in the risk of progression/recurrence or death compared to NAC (2, 61). The OS and EFS benefit with perioperative durvalumab plus NAC was consistent across patient subgroups (62, 63). Importantly, the regimen did not compromise patients' ability 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 30 -->

to undergo surgery and the safety profile was consistent with the known effects of durvalumab, with no new safety concerns and no increase in discontinuation rates due to adverse events (AEs) (2). 

These unprecedented results have led the EAU to update the clinical guidelines to incorporate perioperative durvalumab, even before formal approval by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) (1, 4). The proactive action taken by EAU is reflective of the strong clinical momentum and growing appetite for integrating perioperative IO as a potential solution to the high unmet need in the management of MIBC (14). 

Perioperative durvalumab offers a streamlined and fixed-duration regimen which is associated with a predictable budget impact and cost offsets due to reduced risk of recurrence (2, 61). By delivering clinically proven survival benefits, delaying disease progression, reducing the risk of disease recurrence, and not compromising the ability of patients to undergo surgery, perioperative durvalumab offers substantial value across the entire treatment pathway. 

Perioperative durvalumab, represents a transformative opportunity in the treatment of cisplatineligible resectable MIBC patients. The proactive, single-decision point intervention, initiated at the start of the neoadjuvant setting, enables early and streamlined treatment planning, facilitates optimal scheduling of clinic visits, ensures clear and consistent communication with patients, and prevents the need for repeated evaluations for adjuvant therapy. Perioperative durvalumab can also minimise uncertainty around efficacy and duration of the treatment before and after surgery, and reduce the burden of ongoing treatment decisions – ultimately enhancing both clinical outcomes and patient experience, reducing post-recurrence clinical and economic burden on payers, and improving overall treatment care (14). 

## **1.4 Equality considerations** 

AstraZeneca do not anticipate any equality issues to arise with the introduction of the technology presented in the current appraisal within clinical practice. 

However, the bladder cancer burden is unequal, with persistent outcome gaps among different populations. 

**Women** : Although men are more likely to develop BC, women often present with more advanced disease and have worse prognosis (19). The latter is explained by a longer diagnostic delay in women and not by treatment patterns (20, 21). Women showed lower survival rates only within the first two years after diagnosis, partly due to a higher T stage at initial diagnosis (64). 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 31 -->

**People with a lower socioeconomic status:** Factors such as lifestyle and occupation contribute to higher rates of BC, and these can often be attributed to lower-paid work and socioeconomic status. For example, globally, 33.72% of deaths caused by BC could be attributed to smoking and around 10% of BC arise following occupational exposure to carcinogen in jobs such as steel, foundry, metal, engineering and transport industries (65, 66).

**2 Clinical effectiveness** 

## **Summary of direct clinical effectiveness** 

## **NIAGARA clinical trial** 

- The efficacy and safety of perioperative durvalumab was determined in the NIAGARA trial: an ongoing, **Phase III, randomised, open label, multicentre, international study.** 

- Neoadjuvant durvalumab in combination with gemcitabine and cisplatin (G+C) every three weeks for four cycles prior to RC, followed by adjuvant durvalumab monotherapy every four weeks until recurrence, unacceptable toxicity or a maximum of eight cycles after surgery (perioperative durvalumab arm) is **compared to neoadjuvant G+C followed by RC alone with no adjuvant treatment** (control arm). 

- **Baseline characteristics and control arm were considered reflective of UK** population and standard practice by UK-based clinical experts. 

## **Summary of efficacy results** 

- Perioperative durvalumab **reduced the risk of an EFS event by 32%** when compared to the SoC (HR 0.68 [95% CI: 0.558, 0.817]). 

- An approximate **10% increase in pCR rate** was observed in the perioperative durvalumab arm compared to the control arm (37.3% versus 27.5%). 

- EFS benefit translated **in statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in OS** . Perioperative durvalumab **reduced the risk of death by 25%** compared to the SoC (HR 0.75 (95% CI: 0.594, 0.934)) 

- The **certainty in the efficacy** benefit attributable to perioperative durvalumab is further strengthened by the **multidimensional assessment** . Perioperative durvalumab demonstrated a **33% reduction in the risk of metastasis and 31% reduction in the risk of death due to bladder cancer.** 

- The early and sustained separation of survival curves observed across multiple endpoints highlights the unique value of a perioperative intervention. 

- Perioperative durvalumab arm reported reported **no decrement in HRQoL** of patients as compared to the control arm; no additional burden is conferred upon patients with the addition of perioperative durvalumab to the current SoC. 

- **Subgroup analyses demonstrated consistency** between the ITT population and subgroups outcomes. Results across PD-L1 subgroups indicate that **PD-L1 level of expression is not influencing** the efficacy of perioperative durvalumab regimen. 

## **Summary of safety results** 

- Adding durvalumab to G+C **did not negatively impact achieving surgery.** No delays in surgery were observed. A higher proportion of patients in the perioperative durvalumab arm underwent RC as planned. 

- The safety data for the perioperative durvalumab demonstrated a **well-tolerated and manageable safety profile** that aligned with the individual safety profiles of durvalumab 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 33 -->

monotherapy as well as G+C components. 

## **Conclusion** 

- The **high level of certainty** in the efficacy outcomes delivered by perioperative durvalumab in the NIAGARA trial—providing **early and sustained survival benefits** without compromising patients’ quality of life—together with a well-tolerated and manageable safety profile, has led **UK-based clinical experts to conclude that perioperative durvalumab will become the future standard of care,** addressing the significant unmet need that persists for cis-eligible resectable MIBC patients under current treatment options. 

## **2.1 Identification and selection of relevant studies** 

A _de novo_ SLR was conducted to identify published clinical efficacy and safety evidence to contextualise the clinical data collected for durvalumab in the perioperative setting for the treatment of patients with MIBC (67). MEDLINE[®] , Embase[®] and Cochrane databases were searched to identify published literature relevant to the research question. Key eligibility criteria for the SLR included adult patients (≥18 years old) with MIBC, receiving neoadjuvant or adjuvant therapy (if patient previously received neoadjuvant therapy) (67). The SLR included a broader scope in terms of comparators, but the population eligibility criteria were in alignment with the NICE final scope (13, 67). 

In summary, the SLR adhered to the guidelines published by the University of York Centre for Reviews and Dissemination (CRD), the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (68-70). The SLR research question was specified using the Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome, and Study type (PICOS) framework and was aligned with the intended patient population of perioperative durvalumab (67). 

The methods used to identify the relevant clinical evidence and a full list of studies that were included and excluded during the SLR are described in Appendix B. 

## **2.2 List of relevant clinical effectiveness evidence**

## **2.3.1 Summary of trial methodology** 

NIAGARA (NCT03732677) is an ongoing, Phase III, randomised, open label, multicentre, international study to examine the efficacy and safety of neoadjuvant durvalumab in combination with gemcitabine and cisplatin every three weeks for four cycles prior to RC, followed by adjuvant durvalumab monotherapy every four weeks until recurrence, unacceptable toxicity or a maximum of eight cycles after surgery (perioperative durvalumab arm). Perioperative durvalumab is compared to neoadjuvant gemcitabine and cisplatin followed by RC alone with no adjuvant treatment (current SoC in the UK, hereafter referred to as the control arm). Perioperative durvalumab is being investigated for the treatment of adult (≥18 years) cisplatin-eligible patients with resectable MIBC (T2N0/1M0-T4aN0/1M0) including those with divergent differentiation or histologic subtypes (2). ## **2.3.2 Patient disposition** 

Patients were randomised between 16 November 2018 and 23 August 2021 (71). At the timepoint of the second interim analysis (IA) of EFS (EFS IA-2) and the first IA of OS (OS IA1) (Data Cut-Off [DCO] 29 April 2024) (Section 2.4.2.2), 1,063 patients had been randomised to the full analysis set (FAS) (intention-to-treat [ITT] population) (71). Among 1,063 patients included in the FAS (ITT population), patients were assigned to either the perioperative durvalumab arm (N=533) or the control arm (N=530) in a 1:1 ratio. Of these, all except seven patients (three in the perioperative durvalumab arm and four in the control arm) received study 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168]

treatment. Of the patients who received treatment, 417 (78.7%) patients in the perioperative durvalumab arm and 389 (74.0%) patients in the control arm completed neoadjuvant treatment. A total of 470 (88.2%) patients in the perioperative durvalumab arm and 446 (84.2%) patients in the control arm underwent cystectomy, and six of the patients in the perioperative durvalumab arm entered the non-cystectomy phase. A total of 383 (72.3%) patients in the perioperative durvalumab arm started adjuvant durvalumab monotherapy treatment, and 287 (53.8%) patients completed eight cycles. As of EFS IA-2 (DCO 29 April 2024), 379 (71.1%) patients and 333 (62.8%) patients in the perioperative durvalumab arm and control arm, respectively, were ongoing in the study in survival follow-up. There were no major imbalances in patient disposition between study arms (Table 6) (71).

## _**2.3.2.1 Patients who undergo cystectomy**_ 

In the NIAGARA trial, a higher percentage of patients in the perioperative durvalumab arm (88.0%) underwent RC, as planned, compared to the control arm (83.2%) (Table 6). Notably, there were no delays in surgery for the perioperative durvalumab arm compared to the control arm, with the median time from the last dose of neoadjuvant therapy to cystectomy being 39.0 days in the perioperative durvalumab arm and 38.0 days in the control arm (71). Among the patients who did not undergo cystectomy, patient decision was the most common reason in each group (6.0% and 6.8% patients in the perioperative durvalumab arm and the control arm, respectively) (71). Furthermore, a greater number of patients did not proceed with surgery in the control arm due to factors that can be associated with increased morbidity and mortality, such as study discontinuation (0.6% in the perioperative durvalumab arm versus 2.3% in the control arm), being unfit for surgery (0.4% in the perioperative durvalumab arm versus 1.1% in the control arm), and death (0.9% in the perioperative durvalumab arm and 1.5% in the control arm) (Table 6) (71). 

The above evidence highlights that adding durvalumab to the current neoadjuvant SoC did not preclude or delay patients from undergoing surgery.

## **2.3.3 Demographics and baseline characteristics** 

The patient demographics and baseline disease characteristics of patients in the NIAGARA trial are presented for the FAS (ITT population) at the EFS IA-2 (N=1,063) in Table 7 (71). 

The patient demographics and disease characteristics were representative of the target population of patients with resectable MIBC, focus of this appraisal, and were well-balanced between treatment arms (71). The NIAGARA trial included four sites located in the UK, and the UK-based clinical experts confirmed that the baseline patient characteristics of patients in the NIAGARA trial are reflective of the real-world patients with resectable MIBC in the UK (14). The NIAGARA trial population is representative across most demographics (median age of patients, smoking status and renal function), while UK-based clinical experts acknowledged that some minor differences in patient population characteristics of the trial can exist as compared to the clinical practice, none of the factors were considered a cause for uncertainty or bias (14).

## _**2.4.2.3. Testing for multiplicity**_ 

To control the type I error at the 5% 2-sided alpha level, a multiple testing procedure (MTP) with a gatekeeping strategy was chosen for the dual-primary endpoints (pCR and EFS) and key secondary endpoint (OS) (Figure 4) (71, 74). Initially, the 5% alpha was split into 0.1% for pCR and 4.9% for EFS in the FAS (ITT population). The study was considered positive if either of the dual-primary endpoint was met (75). Rejected hypotheses' test mass was recycled to secondary hypotheses. The alpha level for pCR and EFS was controlled at interim and final timepoints using the Lan-DeMets spending function, approximating an O’Brien-Fleming approach (74, 76).

## _**2.4.2.4. Sample size and power calculation**_ 

The trial planned to enroll and screen approximately 1,400 patients in order to randomise approximately 1,050 eligible patients in a 1:1 ratio to the NIAGARA regimen perioperative durvalumab arm or control arm (71). The trial was sized to characterise the pCR rate and EFS benefit of the perioperative durvalumab arm versus the control arm in patients with resectable MIBC who had not received prior systemic chemotherapy. Statistical assumptions were made using a pCR rate of 50% and 35% for patients enrolled on the perioperative durvalumab arm and control arm, respectively, for the FAS (ITT population) Non-uniform accrual of patients (with k=2) was assumed when estimating the analysis times (71). The statistical analysis undertaken in the NIAGARA trial is presented in Table 12.

## **2.6.1 Dual-primary endpoint: EFS and pCR** 

The NIAGARA trial evaluated EFS and pCR as dual-primary endpoints, capturing both the immediate and longer-term benefits of perioperative treatment. The aim of the neoadjuvant setting is to remove the primary tumour and reduce the risk of subsequent recurrence, while adjuvant setting aims to sustain immunosurveillance to eliminate micro-metastatic disease after surgery, thereby enhancing the likelihood of long-term disease control (31). 

In the NIAGARA trial, EFS is defined as the time from randomisation to the first recurrence of disease after RC, the time of first documented progression in patients who are medically precluded from RC, or time of expected surgery in patients who refuse to undergo RC or failure to undergo RC in patients with residual disease, or the time of death due to any cause, whichever occurs first (2). The definition implies that EFS considers the occurrence of multiple patient-relevant events, provides a direct measure of treatment efficacy across both neoadjuvant and adjuvant treatment periods with surgery as a curative intent therapeutic strategy, and is not confounded by subsequent therapy following progression or recurrence. The EFS definition in the NIAGARA trial aligns with the therapeutic goals of the perioperative setting and evaluates the success or failure of neoadjuvant followed by adjuvant therapy. 

In addition to the strength of EFS as a direct measure of efficacy, there is strong association between EFS and OS in the perioperative MIBC setting (78). The correlation between EFS and OS in NIAGARA trial has been demonstrated in the first interim analysis of OS, as will be discussed in Section 2.6.2.1. 

The inclusion of pCR as a dual-primary endpoint addresses the discordant complexities between clinical and pathologic stages, which are typical of response assessments incorporating information from both pre- and post-neoadjuvant chemotherapy. 

The objective of neoadjuvant therapy in the treatment pathway of MIBC is to decrease primary tumour burden before consolidative local therapy. Achieving pCR following neoadjuvant treatment has been associated with a marked improvement in outcomes in patients with resectable MIBC (72, 79). 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 52 -->

In the NIAGARA trial, pCR was defined as the proportion of patients whose pathological staging was T0N0M0 as assessed using specimens obtained via RC following the neoadjuvant treatment evaluated by blinded central pathology review (2). 

## _**2.6.1.1 EFS per BICR or central pathology review (FAS [ITT population], DCO 29 April 2024)**_ 

At EFS IA-2 (DCO 29 April 2024), the NIAGARA trial met the primary objective of EFS per BICR or central pathology review in the FAS (ITT population) (71). The median duration of follow-up for EFS was similar between the perioperative durvalumab arm (34.7 months) and the control arm (27.7 months). 

**There was a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in the perioperative durvalumab arm compared to control arm, with a HR of 0.68 (95% CI: 0.558, 0.817; p<0.0001), indicating a 32% reduction in the risk of an EFS event arm** (Table 15) (71). 

The KM curves for EFS began to separate in favour of the perioperative durvalumab arm at approximately two months, prior to the planned timing of the first response evaluation criteria in solid tumours (RECIST) scan after randomisation (~12 weeks) (71). Curve separation prior to the timepoint of the first RECIST scan implies a noticeable benefit of durvalumab compared to SoC within the neoadjuvant period of the perioperative durvalumab regimen where antitumour immunity is primed prior to surgery (2). 

**The clear and sustained separation of the curve thereafter, reinforces the benefits of perioperative regimen wherein deploying durvalumab as the same IO therapy before and after surgery improves the surgery outcomes by priming anti-tumour immunity before surgery (neoadjuvant setting) and supporting immunosurveillance to eliminate micro-metastatic disease after surgery (adjuvant setting), thereby enhancing the likelihood of long-term disease control** (Figure 5) (71).

## _**2.6.1.2 pCR rate based on central pathology review (FAS [ITT population], DCO 14 January 2022)**_ 

At the time of the final pCR analysis (DCO 14 January 2022), due to a programming error the DCO date was applied to the date of central assessment rather than the date of surgery. As a result, 59 evaluable samples were omitted and 28 of them were incorrectly considered nonresponders for the pCR calculation. Consequently, the final analysis for pCR at the 14 January 2022 DCO was not statistically significant, even though results indicated a numerical improvement favouring perioperative durvalumab (71). pCR was achieved in 33.8% (95% CI: 29.8, 38.0) patients in the perioperative durvalumab arm and in 25.8% (95% CI: 22.2, 29.8) patients in the control arm (risk ratio [RR]: 1.30; 95% CI: 1.09, 1.56; p=0.004) (Table 16) (2, 71). 

At the time of EFS IA-2 (DCO 29 April 2024) an updated pCR analysis (re-analysis) was conducted, which showed a nominally significant improvement in the pCR rate (per central pathology review), with approximately a 10% increase in the perioperative durvalumab arm (37.3%) compared to the control arm (27.5%) (p=0.0005) (Table 16 and Figure 6) (2, 78).

The OS IA-1 was conducted at the same timepoint as the EFS IA-2 (DCO 29 April 2024), after 305 death events had occurred (28.7% maturity for OS overall). There was a clinically meaningful improvement in EFS (per Investigator or local biopsy review) for the perioperative durvalumab arm as compared to the control arm in the FAS (ITT population) at IA-2 (DCO 29 April 2024) (71). The HR was was 0.68 (95% CI: 0.562, 0.812, 2- sided p-value <0.001) indicating a 32% overall reduction in the risk of an EFS event (Figure 8). The results are aligned with the primary analysis for EFS by BICR or central pathology assessment (71). Further information on EFS status as per local pathology review can be found in Appendix J. The KM curves for EFS (per investigator or local biopsy review) began to separate at approximately two months in favour of perioperative durvalumab compared to the control, and there was a clear and sustained separation thereafter (Figure 8) (71).

## _**2.6.2.4 Metastasis-free survival (FAS [ITT population], DCO 29 April 2024)**_ 

MFS was defined as the time from date of randomisation until the first recognition of distant metastases or death, whichever occurs first. In addition to more established endpoints, such as EFS and OS, MFS constitutes an informative endpoint, especially in early-stage cancer, when preventing metastasis can significantly improve long-term outcomes, associated costs and overall survival (81). 

MFS data also supports the development of a cost effectiveness model as it enables local recurrence and distant metastases health states to be distinguished, aligning with the health states found in clinical practice, as described in Section 3.

## _**2.6.2.5 Disease-specific survival (FAS [ITT population], DCO 29 April 2024)**_ 

In the NIAGARA trial, DSS was defined as the time from randomisation to death specifically due to bladder cancer. DSS provides a targeted assessment of survival outcomes related to MIBC by isolating mortality attributable to the disease, and thereby minimising the confounding impact of deaths unrelated to cancer that can obscure the treatment effect (90). This distinction is particularly valuable in older or comorbid populations, where non-cancer-related deaths are more frequent (91). DSS complements OS by providing disease-specific context, and the use of both endpoints together effectively reduces uncertainty in survival outcomes for patients with resectable MIBC (82). 

**In the FAS (ITT population), at EFS IA-2 (DCO 29 April 2024), perioperative durvalumab demonstrated a clinically meaningful improvement in DSS as compared to the control arm. The HR was 0.69 (95% CI: 0.516, 0.907; p=0.0081) indicating a 31% overall reduction in the risk of death due to bladder cancer** (Table 20) (71).

## _**2.6.2.7 Time from randomisation to subsequent progression or recurrence post-EFS event (PFS-2) (FAS [ITT population], DCO 29 April 2024)**_ 

PFS-2 is a particularly valuable endpoint in the perioperative setting, where treatment strategies involve multiple phases and long-term outcomes are influenced by both initial and subsequent therapies (83). PFS-2 reflects the durability of treatment benefit beyond the first event. As such, it provides a more comprehensive measure of long-term disease control and is increasingly recognised as a meaningful surrogate for OS in trials involving immune checkpoint inhibitors (83, 84). 

In the FAS (ITT population), at EFS IA-2 (DCO 29 April 2024), patients in the perioperative durvalumab arm had a clinically meaningful improvement in PFS-2 compared with those in the control arm. **The HR was 0.76 (95% CI: 0.605, 0.949); p=0.0155, indicating a 24% overall reduction in the risk of having a PFS-2 event** . Most of the PFS-2 events were

deaths (71). The PFS-2 KM curves were similar until approximately six months, after which there was a clear and sustained separation (Figure 12) (71).

## _**2.6.2.8 European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire-Core 30 (EORTC QLQ-C30) (FAS [ITT population], DCO 29 April 2024)**_ 

In the NIAGARA trial, adjusted mean change from baseline and time to deterioration (TTD) in the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire-Core 30 (EORTC QLQ-C30) scales were secondary endpoints. Prioritised subscales of the EORTC QLQ-C30 consisted of global health status (GHS)/quality of life (QoL), physical functioning, fatigue, and pain. However, separate analyses were also conducted for each subscale (71, 74). 

The HRQoL analysis was conducted using a data set that included baseline questionnaires completed prior to the initiation of study drug. Baseline questionnaires obtained at a date and 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 66 -->

time after treatment initiation were excluded. However, a number of patients were not included in the HRQoL analyses presented in the clinical study report (CSR) because their first PRO assessment, while conducted on the day of first dosing, was recorded in the database with a time stamp after treatment had started. This resulted in a programmatically-defined missing baseline assessment. AstraZeneca has become aware that there is some uncertainty in the time stamp in the database because the PRO devices were set up with an option to select a local time zone, but the time zone was not recorded in the database. In order to maximise the number of patients for analysis, the neoadjuvant baseline was re-defined as the last PRO assessment completed before or on the day of first dose of neoadjuvant treatment irrespective of the timing of the PRO assessment relative to first dose. 

The post-hoc analysis results, presented below, align with the primary trial analysis, supporting the findings of the planned analysis. Full results of the post-hoc analysis are available in the addendum to the CSR (85), while the primary analysis results are available in the CSR (71). 

In the post-hoc analysis, no differences were observed between treatment arms in the prioritised (GHS/QoL, physical functioning, fatigue, and pain) and non-prioritised EORTC QLQ-C30 scales (85). 

In the FAS (ITT population), at the EFS IA-2 (DCO 29 April 2024), baseline compliance with the EORTC QLQ-C30 was 73.1% and 71.7% in the perioperative durvalumab arm and the control arm, respectively, and baseline mean GHS/QoL, physical functioning, fatigue, and pain scores were similar between treatment arms, reflecting the mild restricted activity as shown in the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status at baseline (Table 22) (85).

## **2.6.4 Summary of clinical effectiveness results** 

NIAGARA is the first trial of a perioperative IO regimen to provide results in MIBC. Perioperative durvalumab has demonstrated a statistically significant and clinically meaningful benefit in EFS, reducing the risk of recurrence by 32% (HR 0.68 95% CI: 0.558, 0.817). These findings are further reinforced by a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in OS (the gold standard endpoint in oncology (86)) with perioperative durvalumab reducing the risk of death by 25% (HR 0.75 95% CI: 0.594, 0.934) compared to the current UK SoC (80). Correlation with additional endpoints included in the trial as part of the multidimensional assessment, further strengthens the certainty in the benefit attributable to perioperative durvalumab, with demonstrated reductions in the risk of metastasis by 33% (MFS HR 0.67 95% CI: 0.541, 0.826) and death due to bladder cancer by 31% (DSS HR was 0.69 95% CI: 0.516, 0.907).

<!-- page 69 -->

The early and sustained separation of survival curves observed across multiple endpoints highlights the unique value of a perioperative intervention. In the NIAGARA trial, EFS curves began to separate in favour of perioperative durvalumab as early as two months, with this benefit maintained over time. Similarly, OS, MFS, and DSS curves showed clear and maintained separation starting at approximately six months post-treatment, further reinforcing the sustained impact of perioperative durvalumab. This pattern reflects the underlying mechanism of action, where the same IO therapy administered both before and after surgery primes anti-tumour immunity in the neoadjuvant setting and sustains immunosurveillance in the adjuvant setting, thereby reducing early recurrence and supporting long-term disease control. Collectively, these results emphasise the value of perioperative immunotherapy in delivering early and enduring clinical benefits for patients with resectable MIBC. 

This unprecedented direct evidence versus UK standard of care, alongside with the existing unmet medical need, has led UK-based clinical experts to conclude that perioperative durvalumab is poised to become the new standard of care for cis-eligible patients with resectable MIBC.

## **2.7.3 PD-L1 subgroups** 

As outlined in the final scope published by NICE, and for completeness, the NIAGARA trial assessed the benefit of perioperative durvalumab across different levels of PD-L1 expression (13, 71). However, the UK-based clinical experts consulted by the company unanimously confirmed that the value of PD-L1 in BC is uncertain and would not guide the use of perioperative durvalumab in their clinical practice (14). 

Several studies have evaluated the marker with mixed results, which may, partially, be related to the use of different antibodies and scoring methods (4). The variability, especially given the notable number of PD-L1-negative patients who still respond to immune checkpoint blockade, suggests that PD-L1 does not drive treatment decisions in MIBC, or BC in general, outside of patient selection for drugs that are restricted to a specific level of PD-L1 expression in the label as evidenced by the EAU and ESMO clinical guidelines (4, 31). 

The CheckMate-274 trial reported HR values for the PD-L1 negative subgroup within the MIBC patient population for the primary endpoint of DFS, which were not statistically significant. This finding led to regulatory and reimbursement restrictions limiting use to patients with PD-L1 ≥ 1%, as reflected in the NICE recommendation for TA817, aligned with the EMA license (95, 96). 

In contrast, the NIAGARA trial demonstrated that subgroup analyses of EFS and OS endpoints by PD-L1 expression were consistent with the results observed in the FAS (ITT population) (71). The HRs for both endpoints (EFS HR 0.68, OS HR 0.75) in the FAS (ITT population) fell between those observed in the PD-L1-high (EFS HR 0.70, OS HR 0.83) and PD-L1-low (EFS HR 0.62, OS HR 0.53) subgroups, and were within the respective CIs, supporting consistency across subgroups. These results indicate that PD-L1 is not influencing the efficacy of perioperative durvalumab regimen in the NIAGARA trial (2). 

Given the consistency between PD-L1 subgroups and the FAS (ITT population) in the NIAGARA trial and the lack of evidence supporting PD-L1 as a treatment effect modifier in MIBC, PD-L1 expression holds no relevance for the UK clinical practice in the context of this appraisal. Therefore, it should focus exclusively on the FAS (ITT population), as also validated by the UK-based clinical experts who confirmed that the relevance of PD-L1 subgroup is quite 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 73 -->

minor in MIBC and affirmed that perioperative durvalumab is expected to provide benefit across all patients, independent of the PD-L1 status, providing a broad application for the regimen (14).

## **Survival Time-Adjusted ITC** 

## **Objective** 

- As standard ITC methods were not considered suitable and address key questions for decision making, an alternative **‘survival-time adjusted ITC’ approach has been proposed** 

- Survival times were estimated for the control arm of the NIAGARA trial, simulating a scenario where eligible high-risk PD-L1 ≥1% patients received adjuvant nivolumab instead of no treatment after neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by radical cystectomy. 

## **Method** 

- The analysis was performed on the endpoints of EFS and OS, using the IA-2 (DCO 29 April 2024) of the NIAGARA trial and the latest 3-year extended follow-up of CheckMate-274 trial. 

- The analysis consisted of three steps: 

   1. **Estimate the acceleration factor (AF)** – extent of survival increase associated with adjuvant nivolumab 

   2. **Create the counterfactual survival times** for EFS and OS applying the AF to the ‘adjuvant phase’ survival times of eligible patients in the NIAGARA trial control arm (G+C+N) 

   **3. Conduct the ITC by comparing perioperative durvalumab with G+C+N** 

## **- Summary of Survival Time Adjusted ITC Results** 

- **Perioperative durvalumab led to a statistically significant improvement in EFS versus G+C+N with an HR of 0.742** (0.610, 0.8990) **.** 

- **Perioperative durvalumab is associated with a statistically significant improvement in OS versus G+C+N with an HR of 0.800** (0.633, 0.994) **.** 

## **Conclusions of Survival Time-Adjusted ITC** 

- **Strengths: the analysis addresses a key decision-maker question** and provides robust comparative results by capturing all relevant outcomes arising from the decision to use perioperative durvalumab. **Comprehensive data utilisation** and the application of bootstrapping methods appropriately **captured uncertainty** and further strengthened these findings. 

- **The key limitations** of the analysis are relying of PD-L1 subgroup results with different testing assays across studies and the lack of safety and tolerability evaluation, since the ITC focused on the key efficacy endpoints of EFS and OS. 

- The Survival Time-Adjusted ITC results show that perioperative durvalumab significantly improves EFS and OS compared to a regimen of neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by either no treatment or adjuvant nivolumab in eligible patients with MIBC (G+C+N). 

- **The observed results are consistent with the mechanism of action and value of perioperative IO regimens, demonstrating how a proactive approach can improve survival and address the main unmet medical need in a broader cis-eligible resectable MIBC population. These findings answer a key decision-making question and further strengthen the position of perioperative durvalumab as the new SoC in cis-eligible resectable MIBC.**

An SLR was conducted on the 22 July 2024 and updated on 25 April 2025 to identify and summarise all published evidence from randomised clinical trials (RCTs) on the clinical efficacy and safety of treatments for adult patients with MIBC, with the aim of conducting an indirect treatment comparison (ITC) feasibility assessment. Evidence connectivity was assessed by grouping RCTs based on treatment setting and cisplatin eligibility. 

The ITC feasibility assessment aimed to determine if an ITC was suitable to compare the efficacy of perioperative durvalumab to approved neoadjuvant and adjuvant therapies. Adjuvant therapies were included to provide a broader perspective of the therapeutic landscape, acknowledging that the introduction of a perioperative regimen—with a single treatment decision point encompassing both pre- and post-surgical phases—will ultimately replace interventions prescribed at the same decision point (pre-surgery). The decision to initiate perioperative durvalumab precludes patients from receiving any adjuvant therapy other than durvalumab monotherapy, including adjuvant nivolumab. 

Feasibility was assessed by evaluating differences in trial design and in effect modifiers (EMs) between the NIAGARA trial and RCTs of neoadjuvant/perioperative (randomised before radical cystectomy) and adjuvant regimens (randomised after radical cystectomy). Potential EMs and prognostic factors were identified through targeted reviews and consultation with clinical experts. Heterogeneity in study designs, patient populations, interventions and outcome definitions and assessments was explored qualitatively. 

The evidence base summary comprised 53 RCTs reporting efficacy and/or safety endpoints of interest (52 SLR-identified studies plus the NIAGARA trial). This ITC assessment, initially conducted at a global level, was subsequently adapted to align with the final scope of this appraisal and UK clinical practice. Consequently, none of the neoadjuvant studies and only one of the adjuvant studies was considered relevant (CheckMate-274 trial). 

The overlap between patients that are eligible for perioperative durvalumab and for adjuvant nivolumab is minimal. Adjuvant nivolumab is used for cisplatin-eligible or -ineligible patients who cannot receive adjuvant cisplatin, present PD-L1 positive tumours, and are at high risk of recurrence after RC, regardless of prior NAC (see Figure 2, Section 1.3). Of these, only cisplatin-eligible patients who receive NAC may be considered for perioperative durvalumab, regardless of PD-L1 status and risk of recurrence. As high-risk recurrence criteria for adjuvant nivolumab are assessed post-surgery, while perioperative durvalumab eligibility is determined pre-surgery, the exact overlap cannot be prospectively quantified. The expected decrease in adjuvant nivolumab use with the availability of perioperative durvalumab is primarily due to a reduction in the use of NAC alone, in favour of NAC plus durvalumab - followed by durvalumab 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 76 -->

after surgery- given the superior outcomes shown with perioperative durvalumab in the NIAGARA trial. 

## **Comparison of perioperative durvalumab to adjuvant nivolumab** 

Common ITC methods relying on either a network of evidence anchored by a shared control arm (“anchored comparisons”) or the cross-trial comparison of absolute outcomes in overlapping populations (“unanchored comparisons”) are not suitable for comparing the ITT cohorts of the CheckMate-274 and the NIAGARA. Furthermore, comparing adjuvant-only phases of NIAGARA to CheckMate-274 trials was deemed infeasible with existing ITC methods. The main reasons why these comparisons cannot be made, and an alternative methodology is proposed are: 

- **Differences in the primary endpoint used and secondary endpoints definition** - In CheckMate-274 trial, the primary endpoint was DFS measured since randomisation, which was defined at start of the adjuvant phase. Secondary endpoints included OS defined as time to death from randomisation (at the adjuvant baseline). In NIAGARA trial, the dual primary endpoint was EFS, which included outcomes in both the neoadjuvant and adjuvant phases. Secondary endpoints included DFS, which was measured post-randomisation from the baseline adjuvant visit in NIAGARA, and OS, which was measured since randomisation (at neoadjuvant baseline). 

EFS covers different aspects of disease to DFS and cannot therefore be compared across studies. Similarly, OS endpoints are measured from different points in the treatment pathway (neoadjuvant baseline in NIAGARA versus adjuvant baseline in CheckMate-274), capturing death events pre- and post-surgery in NIAGARA and only post-surgery in CheckMate-274. 

DFS endpoints are measured from an approximately consistent time point, however, the comparison of these endpoints is not considered appropriate, because of differences in inclusion criteria discussed below. 

- **Differences in the inclusion criteria** - In the CheckMate-274 trial, all patients had to be sufficiently fit and willing to undergo RC and had to achieve disease-free status within four weeks prior to randomisation. Conversely, in the NIAGARA trial, patients entered the study as medically fit to undergo radical cystectomy, however a proportion of patients became ineligible or refused surgery during the neoadjuvant phase or fail to achieve disease-free status post-surgery (59). The exclusion of patients with these unfavourable prognostic characteristics from enrolment in the CheckMate-274 trial could introduce selection bias. Other differences in the inclusion criteria include receipt 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 77 -->

of prior IO in the neoadjuvant phase of the NIAGARA trial, and risk of recurrence at adjuvant baseline. 

- **Differences in the control arms** – Placebo in CheckMate-274 trial and neoadjuvant gemcitabine-cisplatin followed by RC in NIAGARA trial

## **followed by RC with or without adjuvant nivolumab** 

To overcome traditional ITC method’s challenges, an alternative ‘survival-time adjusted ITC’ approach has been proposed. This approach allows a more appropriate comparison of outcomes between perioperative durvalumab, and NAC followed by no treatment or adjuvant nivolumab in PD-L1≥1% high-risk MIBC patients after surgery. Whilst the ITT population CheckMate-274 trial does not specify PD-L1≥1%, this is aligned to the NICE recommendation of nivolumab in this setting (TA817). 

In addition to avoiding the bias that renders typical ITC methods unfeasible, this approach: 

- Represents the treatment decision points of clinical practice in the neoadjuvant and perioperative space: patients treated with perioperative durvalumab only have one treatment decision point before surgery, that dictates treatment pre- and post-RC. 

- Aligns with current treatment landscape for patients in the scope (cis-eligible resectable MIBC) where patients will be treated with adjuvant nivolumab only if they have received NAC and therefore are ineligible for adjuvant cisplatin. 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 78 -->

- Current treatment displacement of nivolumab by durvalumab will occur only in those patients who received NAC followed by RC and would have met adjuvant nivolumab eligibility criteria, reflecting a limited overlap. 

The proposed survival-time adjusted ITC approach uses counterfactual survival time methods to estimate the outcomes of neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by no treatment or adjuvant nivolumab in high-risk patients PD-L1≥1%, where counterfactual survival time represents the survival time that would have been observed for an individual under a different treatment or condition than the one they actually experienced. The methodology uses established techniques originally developed for adjusting survival times for the impact of crossover or treatment switching (87). These existing methods have been adapted to capture the effect of including a new therapy (i.e., adjuvant nivolumab) in the pathway. In this analysis, survival times were estimated for the control arm of the NIAGARA trial, simulating a scenario where eligible high-risk PD-L1 ≥1% patients received adjuvant nivolumab instead of no treatment after NAC and RC.

Given this approach attempts to estimate the relative efficacy of NAC followed by RC with or without adjuvant nivolumab, using the prior NAC subgroup from the CheckMate-274 trial could be considered. 

The analysis was performed on the endpoints of EFS and OS, using the IA-2 (DCO 29 April 2024) of the NIAGARA trial and the 3-year extended follow-up of the CheckMate-274 trial (88) (Table 24).

## **2.9.2 Methods** 

The analysis consisted of three steps: 

1. **Estimate the acceleration factor (AF)** – the amount by which an individual’s expected survival time is increased by treatment - for adjuvant nivolumab versus placebo from the MIBC and PD-L1>1% subgroup of the CheckMate-274 trial (15). 

2. **Create the counterfactual survival times** by applying the AF from step one to the control arm of the NIAGARA trial. The AF was applied to the ‘adjuvant phase’ survival times from the control arm for patients who identified as eligible for adjuvant nivolumab. The survival times of eligible patients up to the adjuvant phase, as well as the total survival times of patients who were ineligible for adjuvant nivolumab, remained unchanged from the observed outcomes in the NIAGARA trial. 

3. **Conduct the ITC** comparing perioperative durvalumab versus the counterfactual control arm created in step two. Randomisation in the NIAGARA trial ensured comparable baseline characteristics across all arms in the ITC and population adjustment was not required. 

Following treatment switching guidelines, the counterfactual survival analysis was performed with and without re-censoring (87).

## _**Step 1: Estimate the effect (AF) of adjuvant nivolumab in the CheckMate-274 trial**_ 

The effect of nivolumab was estimated using pseudo patient-level data reconstructed from the CheckMate-274 trial KM curves for the subgroup of patients with high-risk MIBC and tumour PD-L1 ≥ 1%. Pseudo patient data were recovered from published KM plots using the Guyot _et al._ algorithm ref (89). 

The AF for nivolumab versus placebo was estimated by fitting a series of accelerated failure time (AFT) models (log-normal, Weibull, generalised gamma, log-logistic, and gamma) to a data set containing both arms of the CheckMate-274 trial with a covariate representing treatment. The treatment covariate in each model estimates the effect of nivolumab in the form of a constant AF, representing a multiplicative factor by which an individual’s expected survival time is increased by nivolumab when compared with placebo. 

Model selection was based on visual fit to the CheckMate-274 trial KM curves and goodness of fit statistics (AIC and BIC) (15). Where standard AFT models did not fit well, flexible parametric models with time-varying treatment effects, such as Royston-Parmar cubic spline models, were considered. The spline analysis used an odds link function, which is an extension of the log-logistic AFT model. To incorporate time-varying treatment effects for nivolumab, the treatment covariate was applied to all spline parameters, yielding survival outcomes equivalent to fitting independent models to each arm. Models with up to 4-knots were considered, and the model with the best AIC score was used to predict the time-varying AFs for nivolumab. 

Time-varying AFs were derived from the mathematical relationship between AF and quantile survival times. In a standard AFT model, the treatment effect (i.e., the AF) is modeled as a constant multiplicative shift in the outcome distribution across all survival quantiles (90). The time-varying AF adopts this principle but allows the ratio of quantiles (and hence AFs) to vary over quantile (and hence time). 

The time-varying AFs were calculated via a multi-step process. First, the quantile survival times (ranging from 0.01 to 0.99) for each arm were estimated using the best-fitting model and the predict function from the flexure package. In the second step, the AFs were calculated as the ratio of quantile survival times for nivolumab and placebo. To apply these AFs to the NIAGARA trial, a generalised additive model (GAM) with a cubic spline term was then fitted to the AFs, with quantile value for the placebo arm included as an independent variable. The observed survival times of each eligible patient in the NIAGARA trial was mapped to the quantile scale using KM estimates (i.e., the quantile was 1 minus the survival probability at time X). The GAM was then used to predict the AF for nivolumab based on each individual’s 

Company evidence submission for durvalumab as neoadjuvant (with gemcitabine and cisplatin) and adjuvant (as monotherapy) treatment for MIBC [ID6168] 





<!-- page 81 -->

quantile value. This approach assumes that nivolumab’s effect (multiplicative effect on survival time) is consistent for patients at corresponding quantiles in both studies.

## _**Step 2: Estimate the counterfactual control arm survival times in the NIAGARA trial for adjuvant nivolumab eligible patients**_ 

## _Identification of eligible patients for adjuvant nivolumab in the NIAGARA trial population_ 

A counterfactual control arm representing treatment with NAC and RC followed by no treatment or adjuvant nivolumab in eligible patients was created from the NIAGARA trial control arm, using the AF estimates from Step 1 to predict counterfactual survival times in those eligible for adjuvant nivolumab in the UK: 

- Patients who underwent cystectomy and were disease-free (eligible for DFS measurement in the NIAGARA and CheckMate-274 trials) and 

- are determined high-risk MIBC based on staging criteria in the CheckMate-274 trial (15) and 

- have PD-L1 tumour expression of at least 1%.

Guidelines for treatment switching analysis recommend consideration of the use of recensoring when applying counterfactual survival time methods. This helps to guard against informative censoring bias in the counterfactual data set which may occur through the adjustment of survival times of eligible ‘high-risk’ patients but not for ineligible patients in the NIAGARA trial. These include patients who did not have surgery, those who had residual disease after surgery and those considered at a low risk of recurrence.
