It is also important to note that, while post-discontinuation chemotherapy is established practice in the UK, the specific regimens and sequencing of therapy can vary internationally. Therefore, adapting the subsequent therapy data from NIAGARA to reflect UK clinical practice—through detailed consultation with UK-based clinical experts—has been an essential step in ensuring an accurate and meaningful costeffectiveness evaluation of perioperative durvalumab for the UK NHS. 

## **b. Please discuss the extent to which differences in subsequent therapies between the NIAGARA trial and NHS practice may affect the applicability of OS estimates from NIAGARA to NHS practice.** 

The proportion of patients receiving subsequent therapy in the NIAGARA trial was relatively low overall (13.7%). The use of immune-oncology (IO) agents as subsequent therapy following discontinuation in either treatment arm was 7.5% overall, with a higher use in the control arm (11.7%) compared to perioperative durvalumab arm (3.4%). This pattern supports that the observed statistically significant OS benefit can be primarily attributed to perioperative durvalumab itself rather than to differences in later lines of therapy. Given the low frequency of subsequent therapies, their potential influence on overall survival outcomes is inherently limited. 

Furthermore, as detailed in CS Section 2.6.7 and previously mentioned in Question A7, PFS-2 outcomes show that even after progression and initiation of a subsequent anticancer therapy, patients in the perioperative durvalumab arm demonstrated superior outcomes compared to the control arm, with a 24% PFS-2 improvement observed. Since this benefit cannot be explained by a greater use of innovative therapies in the perioperative arm, this indicates that the sustained separation of the Kaplan–Meier curves beyond six months underscores the durable clinical benefit of perioperative durvalumab seen in NIAGARA. 



<!-- page 213 -->

The feedback from UK clinical experts suggested that there would be a higher proportion of patients receiving subsequent therapies in clinical practice, with experts agreeing that IO-based regimens are an important post-progression treatment option to be considered in the management of MIBC (see response to Question B12 and Company submission Section 3.5.6). It is challenging to quantify the potential impact on OS resulting from increased subsequent therapy use in both arms, but we contend that the relative treatment effect observed in the NIAGARA trial would likely be preserved, and that differences in the use of subsequent therapies between the NIAGARA trial and NHS practice are unlikely to meaningfully affect the applicability of the trial’s OS estimates to NHS clinical practice.

## **A10. Section 2.9.2 of the CS, when describing Step 1 of the ITC, please provide details of the software and packages used to:** 

## **a. Reconstruct the Kaplan-Meier (KM) data;** 

WebPlotDigitizer (v5) was used to recover data from published KM curves. Pseudo patient data were recovered from published KM plots using the Guyot et al. algorithm (21, 22). 

## **b. Fit all accelerated failure time (AFT) models (including the flexible parametric** 

## **models);** 

The analysis was performed in R version 4.3.2 using the flexsurv package. 

## **c. Calculate the time-varying acceleration factor (AF) (the CS mentions the “flexure” package for estimating quantiles of the fitted survival models but does not specify the software used).** 

The analysis was performed in R version 4.3.2 using the flexsurv package. “flexure” was a typographical error. 



<!-- page 214 -->

## **A11. Section 2.9.2 of the CS, when describing Step 1 of the ITC, please clarify what quantiles were used in all analyses, and whether the AF estimates were sensitive to the choice of quantiles.** 

In a standard AFT model, the treatment effect (i.e., the AF) is modelled as a constant multiplicative shift in the outcome distribution across all survival quantiles. Standard models were used for EFS and OS base case. The time-varying AF allows the ratio of quantiles (and hence AFs) to vary over quantile (and hence time) (23). Time-varying analyses were only used in the sensitivity analysis for DFS as the standard AFT models yielded a sufficient fit to the trial data for OS, as described in the CS page 7980. 

Quantile survival times ranging from 0.01 to 0.99 for each arm were estimated using the best-fitting model and the predict function from the flexsurv package. Steps of 0.01 were considered sufficiently granular to capture time-varying changes in the AF. The range used (0.01-0.99) captures the full range of possible quantiles. The AF by quantile time for DFS was provided in Appendix B4 Figure 7. The time-varying AF (using the 3-knot spline model) followed an approximately bell-shaped curve with a single peak. These results suggest that the effect of nivolumab (compared to a null AF of 1.0) initially declines up to the 10th quantile, before increasing over time (‘delayed effect’), peaking around the median (50th) quantile, before diminishing in the long term. Across all quantiles, the constant AF based on the log-logistic model was 4.13.

**A13. To better understand the difference between results using the constant and time-varying AF for EFS (with re-censoring), please produce a KM plot for these two options, i.e. a plot that includes the data in Figure 19 of the Main submission** 



<!-- page 216 -->

## **and in Figure 10 of Appendix B. The scale of the plot can be changed if that will help distinguish the curves.** 

Figure 1 provides a comparison of the Kaplan-Meier survival probabilities for EFS with re-censoring using the constant (red dotted line) and time-varying AFs (blue dotted line). The curves are presented alongside the Kaplan-Meier survival probabilities for the original G+C arm (green line). As suggested, the plot y-axis has been re-scaled to between 40 and 100% to help distinguish the curves. 

The plot shows that any separation in the curves is observed during the initial period from approximately month 6 to month 30, with the time-varying AF analysis producing a lower (i.e. inferior) survival curve than the constant AF approach. Beyond month 30, there is little difference in survival across arms. This comparison confirms that the constant AF approach used in the base case provides the most conservative estimate of the effect of G+C+N, and that the choice of constant or time-varying AFs has a very limited impact on survival.

Appendix B Table 59 presents the Cox regression analysis comparing adjuvant nivolumab with no treatment in the PD-L1 positive (≥1%) high-risk subgroup of the NIAGARA trial and which yielded a hazard ratio of 0.38 (95% CI 0.22-0.66), indicating that adjuvant nivolumab was associated with a 62% reduction in the risk of a DFS event compared to no adjuvant treatment. This is aligned with the DFS hazard ratio in CheckMate-274 (0.44, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.63) for MIBC patients with PD-L1≥1% (7). 

The subgroup data available from CheckMate-274 is shown in Table 8. CheckMate274 includes patients with MIBC and muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma (MIUC). CheckMate274 reports efficacy data for the PD-L1≥1% and MIBC subgroup but not baseline characteristics. The PD-L1≥1% and MIBC subgroup from the CheckMate-274 trial was selected for the analysis as it corresponds closest with the population in the NICE recommendation for adjuvant nivolumab in this setting (24).

In the absence of these subgroup results, it is unclear whether prior receipt of cisplatin therapy would further modify the effect of nivolumab in the treatment of patients with PD-L1 MIBC. Furthermore, we do not know the proportion of MIBC PD-L1≥1% patients who received prior neoadjuvant cisplatin. 

The differential timing of treatment decisions in the studies and lack of reporting of patient characteristics for subgroups has precluded an extensive comparison of characteristics between trials. However, where characteristics are available in both trials, the studies can be considered similar, although a difference in the proportion that received prior neoadjuvant cisplatin remains between studies. Due to the reporting of the CheckMate-274 trial, it is not possible to adjust for prior neoadjuvant cisplatin in the analysis of the PD-L1 positive MIBC population; however, a scenario analysis has been provided in response to question A17 which considers this subgroup.

## **A18. The NIAGARA trial included** xx (xx.x%) **patients with high risk of recurrence and PD-L1≥1% patients, out of** xxx **who underwent surgery and were diseasefree at adjuvant visit.** 

## **a. Please comment on whether this proportion is reflective of NHS practice (and provide sources where appropriate).** 

The observed proportion of 21.7% of patients with high risk of recurrence after surgery and PD-L1 ≥1% in the NIAGARA trial is considered appropriate and reflective of NHS practice. It is expected that the overlap between adjuvant nivolumab and perioperative durvalumab would be very limited. Nivolumab is positioned as a rescue or escalation therapy, given only to those who, following surgery, are found to have both high risk of recurrence and PD-L1 >1%. In contrast, perioperative durvalumab is anticipated to be used proactively in all cisplatin-eligible patients from the neoadjuvant setting, meaning the relevant populations for each intervention are fundamentally distinct. This distinction is further compounded by the different timing of eligibility assessment: while adjuvant nivolumab is only considered for patients assessed as high-risk after surgery, perioperative durvalumab eligibility is established before surgery. As a result, the extent of overlap between the populations cannot be prospectively quantified. In addition, adjuvant nivolumab is used in NHS clinical practice in both cisplatin-eligible and cisplatin-ineligible patients with high risk of recurrence. Therefore, figures for adjuvant nivolumab from sources such as the SACT dataset cannot be assumed to accurately reflect use within the narrower appraisal population. 

To ensure that the two key elements for estimating the overlap—the positioning of adjuvant nivolumab in clinical practice and the patient population in the NIAGARA trial—accurately reflect NHS clinical practice, both factors were discussed with UKbased clinical experts as part of the company’s clinical validation. These experts confirmed that both the approach and the expected proportion of patients with highrisk of recurrence and PD-L1 ≥1% are consistent with what is observed in UK clinical practice. Furthermore, the company's methodology for the ITC specifically captures this full positioning of nivolumab for the relevant appraisal population—namely, patients who have received neoadjuvant chemotherapy, are high risk at the adjuvant baseline, and have PD-L1 >1%. This is considered the best available approach given existing clinical data. 



<!-- page 223 -->

Finally, both the ITC methodology and its outcomes were validated with UK-based clinical and HTA experts to ensure alignment with NHS routine practice, as described in the company’s submission. No additional factors beyond those encompassed by the positioning of adjuvant nivolumab according to the BlueTeq criteria for the population under scope, cisplatin eligibility, and radical cystectomy eligibility criteria influence the use of G+C+N in the NHS. All these factors are captured in the estimation performed. 

In conclusion, based on the differentiated positioning of each therapy, the specific eligibility criteria at different treatment stages, the clinical expert validation processes, and methodological considerations, the xx.x% observed in NIAGARA provides an appropriate and representative estimate for NHS practice. 

It is important to note that the ITC results and their integration into the cost effectiveness model (CEM) were included as a scenario to address specific questions from the NICE scope, despite having limited impact on decision making. 

- **b. The EAG considers that the ITC results presented in Tables 28 and 29 of the CS may be sensitive to assumptions about the prevalence of high-risk PD-L1≥1% patients. Please comment on the extent to which assumptions about the prevalence of high-risk PD-L1≥1% patients in the adjuvant setting may affect the ITC results, supported by sensitivity analyses as appropriate.** 

As outlined in response to question A18 a, xx.x% of patients in the NIAGARA trial were identified as being at high risk of recurrence after surgery and PD-L1 ≥1%,  which is considered representative of UK clinical practice. This proportion is fixed, as the ITC relies on the observed control arm data in the NIAGARA trial to inform the counterfactual (G+C+N) arm. Changing the proportion of nivolumab eligible patients in the control arm of NIAGARA is not possible as we have not observed the outcomes for a population with a different prevalence of high-risk PD-L1≥1% status that would be eligible for nivolumab. 

**A19. PRIORITY: Please supply the ITC analysis and results for distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS) as this outcome is used in the economic model and KM curves in the 3-year extended follow-up of the CheckMate-274 trial(27)** 



<!-- page 224 -->

## **for the MIBC population with PD-L1 expression ≥1% are available. Alternatively, please explain why DMFS was not considered in the ITC.** 

We have performed an ITC with the DMFS endpoint using the same approach as previously described for the EFS and OS ITCs. In short, the analysis involved estimating the acceleration factor (AF) for nivolumab versus placebo from pseudopatient data recovered from the DMFS curve of the PD-L1 MIBC subgroup of CheckMate-274, reported in supplementary figure 4D of Galsky et al, and applying this AF to the ‘adjuvant period’ MFS survival times of the G+C arm of NIAGARA. 

The aim of the analysis was to estimate the MFS for the control arm of NIAGARA that included the effect of adjuvant nivolumab (referred to as “counterfactual arm”). The ITC is then performed by comparing D+G+C with this counterfactual arm (representing G+C+N), and by comparing G+C+N with G+C. 

The full methodology and results are presented in Appendix - CQs. A summary of the results is presented here. 

## **Estimated AF** 

The AF for nivolumab versus placebo was estimated using parametric survival models fitted to a data set containing both arms of CheckMate-274 and including a treatment covariate. This covariate represents the effect of nivolumab in decelerating the time to an event compared to placebo. The best fitting model according to AIC and BIC was the generalised gamma. Based on visual fit, this model failed to adequately predict the trial data as it appeared to systematically underestimate survival in the nivolumab arm and overestimate survival in the placebo arm. Among the fitted models, the generalised gamma predicted the lowest AF for nivolumab versus placebo of x.xx [xx% xx x.xx – x.xx]. 

With log-normal, log-logistic and Weibull, the AF’s ranged from 2.89 to 3.37, with the log-logistic AFT yielding the most conservative (and largest) estimate of the effect of nivolumab. However, of these models, the Weibull demonstrated the poorest visual fit to the Kaplan-Meier data, with log-normal and log-logistic providing a similar level of fit to the DMFS curve. Due to time constraints, it was not possible to perform the ITC utilizing time-varying AFs for DMFS. Nevertheless, as observed in the ITCs for EFS, 



<!-- page 225 -->

implementing time-varying AFs had minimal impact on the outcomes and, when applied, generally resulted in a more conservative estimation of nivolumab's effect. 

Of the standard AFT models, the log-logistic (AF= x.xx [xx x.xx, x.xx]) was considered most suitable for the ITC as it provided the most optimistic and conservative estimate of treatment effect for nivolumab. 

## **Counterfactual Survival** 

The counterfactual arm was created using the control arm of NIAGARA and applying the AF of adjuvant nivolumab from CheckMate-274 to the ‘adjuvant period’ MFS survival times of patients eligible for treatment. As described previously in the Company Submission (Section 2.9.2), in total, xx patients (xx.x%) were considered eligible for adjuvant nivolumab having undergone cystectomy, were disease-free at the adjuvant baseline visit, tested positive for tumour PD-L1 expression >1% and considered at a high risk of recurrence. 

Figure 3 presents the ‘adjuvant period MFS’ according to high with PD-L1 and other risk MIBC in the G+C arm of NIAGARA. As expected, patients with high-risk PD-L1 1% positive MIBC had inferior DFS when compared with patients with other risk MIBC.

## **A20. In the absence of an ITC for safety outcomes, please comment on the safety profile across the three interventions of interest: perioperative durvalumab (D+G+C), adjuvant nivolumab counterfactual (G+C+N) and the control arm (G+C).** 

The ITC focused on the key efficacy endpoints of EFS and OS. The ITC did not evaluate the safety and/or tolerability of D+G+C versus G+C+N. These endpoints are typically evaluated in terms of risk (ratios or differences) and/or odds (ratios) and are reported in terms of the number of patients with an event. Without Kaplan-Meier plots, it is not possible to utilize the survival-time adjusted method to predict safety outcomes with adjuvant nivolumab in NIAGARA. The comparison of safety outcomes across adjuvant phases is at the same risks of bias as the efficacy analysis, such as the impact of prior immunotherapy, prior chemotherapy and trial population. 

To provide context to the EAG, some descriptive safety data from NIAGARA and CheckMate-274 are summarised below without any cross-trial comparison. 

In the NIAGARA trial, the reported frequencies of grade 3 and 4 events were of similar magnitude in the D+G+C arm compared to the G+C arm, and these occurred predominantly during the neoadjuvant part of the study. This suggests that chemotherapy plays a contributory role in the most commonly reported grade 3 and 4 



<!-- page 230 -->

adverse events. When comparing the overall period of the NIAGARA study to the durvalumab pan-tumour pool, a higher incidence of grade 3 and 4 adverse events is observed in NIAGARA, which is to be expected given the platinum-based backbone of the regimen and its associated toxicity (28). 

The risk of experiencing an immune-mediated adverse event (ImAE) during the overall period was 20.9% for patients receiving D+G+C, compared to 3% for those receiving G+C. For comparison, the risk of ImAEs in the Durvalumab Pan-tumour pool was 17.7%. 

Based on the CheckMate-274 trial, treatment with adjuvant nivolumab was associated with an increased risk of any grade and grade 3 or above treatment-related adverse events when compared with placebo (Grade 3+: 17.3% vs. 5.8% in nivolumab and placebo arms, respectively, in the MIBC population). The proportion of immunemediated adverse events observed was 34.5% in the nivolumab arm and 6.9% in the placebo arm. There is no safety data on G+C+N. The higher proportion of patients experiencing Grade 3+ treatment-related adverse events in the NIAGARA trial relative to the CheckMate-274 trial is consistent with the known safety profile of chemotherapy, which is already standard of care in UK clinical practice. 

**A21. Appendix B, paragraph below Figure 9 states that baseline characteristics of patients from NIAGARA eligible and non-eligible for Nivolumab are given in Table 58. However, this table just states the number of patients eligible or noneligible for Nivolumab, along with reasons and does not include details of their characteristics, e.g. age, sex, staging, levels of PG-L1 expression, renal function etc. Please provide a table displaying the summary characteristics of the** xx **patients in the NIAGARA control arm who were eligible for adjuvant nivolumab, after surgery and before adjuvant therapy. Please compare these patient characteristics with the MIBC/PD-L1 subgroup in the CheckMate-274 population, where available; or with the MIBC population of CheckMate-247 if patient characteristics for MIBC/PD-L1 subgroup are not available. (29) Please comment on any relevant differences, and provide AF estimates adjusted for those population differences with corresponding ITC results.** 

A comparison of the available patient characteristics in both trials has been included in response to question A16b. 



<!-- page 231 -->

Without access to the individual patient data for CheckMate-274, it is not possible to adjust the nivolumab acceleration factor for population differences between studies. The use of subgroup data from the MIBC and PD>L1≥1% or above subgroup of CheckMate-274 ensures that the ITC effect of adjuvant is in line with adjuvant nivolumab’s NICE recommendation. Once the relevant subgroups from NIAGARA were selected to align with this population as closely as possible, available patient characteristics were considered balanced (see response to Question A16b). 

**A22. PRIORITY: Please provide a detailed assessment of the proportional hazards assumption (consistent with the methods used in Appendix L) across the three arms, after 6 months post-randomisation (piecewise approach used in the economic model), in the ITC i.e., the perioperative durvalumab (D+G+C, active), G+C (control) and G+C+N (counterfactual) arms of the NIAGARA trial, for both constant and time-varying acceleration factors.** 

A detailed assessment of the proportional hazards assumption in the NIAGARA trial for D+G+C vs. G+C was provided in the Company Submission Section 3.3.2. The proportional hazards assumption in the Company submission was assessed over the entire trial horizon, which is appropriate for modelling D+G+C. As outlined in Company evidence submission, there was uncertainty about whether the proportional hazards assumption was valid for EFS and OS for D+G+C vs. G+C and therefore the modelling was performed using independent parametric survival models fitted to patient-level data from each arm of NIAGARA study for both endpoints. 

To support the application of a piecewise hazard ratio for G+C+N versus G+C in the economic model, the proportional hazards assumption in the post-6-month period has been evaluated using the Schoenfeld residual plot and the Grambsch-Therneau test statistic. 

In the original submission, piecewise hazard ratios were provided for the base case analysis only (constant-AF with re-censoring), as the ITC results showed consistent outcomes across scenarios with and without re-censoring, and for the analysis involving time-varying Afs for EFS. The assessment of proportional hazards beyond month 6 for EFS and OS was therefore conducted for the base case only. 

Figure 6 shows the Schoenfeld plot and test statistics for post-6-month EFS. The plot suggests some minor departure from the proportional hazards assumption after month 



<!-- page 232 -->

6 given a slight upward slope for the log-hazard ratio. Despite this, there was no significant trend to support departure from proportional hazards, p>0.05.

## **independent parametric survival curves fitted to patient-level data of the perioperative durvalumab (D+G+C, active) and G+C+N (counterfactual) arms of the NIAGARA trial.** 

Independent curves were used to model D+G+C for all endpoints, and this is justified in the Company submission. 

For G+C+N, across the three endpoints of EFS, MFS and OS, there was no strong evidence of non-proportional hazards beyond 6-months, which would otherwise warrant the use of independent models in a base case analysis. However, as there were some minor departures for EFS, a series of independent survival models were fitted to the G+C+N arm and used to explore the impact of independent extrapolations instead of hazard ratios, on results. 

Consistent with the base case selections for EFS for the D+G+C and G+C arms, the analysis was performed using flexible survival models (Royston-Parmar spline models) fitted to EFS for G+C+N. In total, 12 models were considered, including spline 



<!-- page 235 -->

models with hazard, odds and probit (normal’) link functions and 1 to 4 knots. The models were fit to EFS (with re-censoring), as measured since randomization. 

Table 13 provides a summary of the goodness of fit statistics (Akaike Information Criteria [AIC] and Bayesian Information Criteria [BIC]) for the 12 models, and Figure 9 and Figure 10 shows the accuracy of the models in predicting the Kaplan-Meier and hazard estimates. 

According to AIC and BIC, the best fitting models were the 3-knot spline normal, odds and hazards models. Among these models, there was no clear difference in goodness of fit statistics. In terms of visual fit, all of the models produced a similarly accurate fit to the Kaplan-Meier and hazard function. Beyond follow-up, the curves yield a similar hazard pattern and long-term survival probabilities, indicating that the choice of model is unlikely to materially impact on model extrapolations. 

Given this, the best-fitting model (3-knot spline normal) has been implemented in the CEM as a deterministic scenario to the scenario which includes G+C+N as a comparator. Parameters of the other two best-fitting models are provided in Table 14 for information.

As described in the Company Submission, there are challenges with conducting comparisons between the adjuvant and perioperative settings. However, the Company have provided this comparison in response to the NICE final scope using a novel methodology which is the most appropriate when comparing across treatment settings. The Company maintain that the relevance of nivolumab as a comparator for cost effectiveness decision-making in a perioperative setting is uncertain due to the limitations of this comparison and therefore, we provided the cost-effectiveness results of the comparison between D+G+C vs. G+C+N as a scenario in the NICE submission. 

In response to question A22 a, the company have provided a further extension to this scenario by independently modelling EFS for G+C+N, given that there was some evidence of a minor departure in the proportional hazards assumption for EFS. No such concern was apparent for OS or MFS. This additional scenario was performed using the base case ITC results; that is, using a constant acceleration factor and including re-censoring. This has shown that the model results are not sensitive to the use of a HR for EFS compared to the statistically best-fitting independently fit model. 

Guidelines for treatment switching analysis recommend consideration of the use of recensoring when applying counterfactual survival time methods (30). This helps to guard against informative censoring bias in the counterfactual data set which may occur through the adjustment of survival times of eligible ‘high-risk’ patients but not for ineligible patients in the NIAGARA trial. These include patients who did not have surgery, those who had residual disease after surgery and those considered at a low risk of recurrence. Without re-censoring, the survival times of the counterfactual arm extends beyond the follow-up of the NIAGARA trial, due to the effect of nivolumab in extending (by a factor of x.xx for EFS) survival times in the counterfactual arm. The application of re-censoring leads to similar follow-up across arms. The ITC results showed that there was very minimal impact between including compared to excluding re-censoring for EFS on the HR (see response to question A12).

Similarly, the submitted ITC results showed there was very minimal impact between the results using a constant AF vs. time-varying AF for EFS. The hazard ratio for EFS comparing D+G+C with G+C+N was 0.739 (95% CI: 0.595, 0.887) using the timevarying AF, which is close to the corresponding hazard ratio of 0.742 (95% CI: 0.610, 0.899) from the base case with constant AF. 

In summary, the company consider that the Company have sufficiently addressed uncertainty around the appropriateness of applying HRs in the CEM through with the scenario extension provided in response to A22a. Given this, performing the analysis with and without re-censoring for constant and time-varying models will not significantly change the conclusion that the model results are not sensitive to the use of a HR for EFS compared to the statistically best-fitting independently fit model. 

## **Section B: Clarification on cost-effectiveness data** 

## _**Model structure**_ 

**B1. PRIORITY: The company performed a systematic review to identify previous relevant economic evaluations. Although previous studies applied a state transition modelling, the company decided to apply partitioned survival modelling in their submission.** 

**a. Please provide a more comprehensive justification for the chosen modelling approach and outline the potential limitations associated with using this approach. Please ensure your response covers the following aspects: 1) the maturity of the OS data in relation to the overall extrapolation period, 2) the maturity of post-EFS and post-MFS data, and 3) potential differences in the management of patients in the trial compared to usual practice in the NHS for patients in the post-EFS and post-DMFS states (or ‘partitions’) and the inability of the partitioned survival modelling approach to formally adjust for any differences.** 

A partitioned survival model (PSM) was selected because it allows direct incorporation of key trial endpoints (EFS, OS, and MFS) using the patient-level data from NIAGARA, which represents the most robust source of evidence available for the treatment efficacy of perioperative durvalumab in MIBC patients. By fitting parametric curves to 



<!-- page 241 -->

**Error! Reference source not found.** 

the Kaplan-Meier data from NIAGARA, the PSM enables transparent extrapolation of long-term outcomes. NIAGARA has comprehensive time-to-event data which has substantial follow-up (maximum follow-up extends beyond five years) and was considered sufficiently mature for a PSM to be appropriate (see Table 17). 

It is common for CEMs, particularly those in early cancer settings, to require extrapolation beyond the follow-up period of the trial. This is a typically a requirement regardless of the modelling approach adopted. Alternative model structures, such as a semi-Markov model, were considered at the model conceptualisation stage. A semiMarkov model would still be informed by the NIAGARA trial as this would remain the best available source of evidence to inform transitions out of the LR and DM health states (i.e., no external literature was identified that would better reflect UK clinical practice, and this approach was validated in consultation with UK-based clinical experts). Given that such a model would also rely on the estimation of transition probabilities and may be less reflective of the observed survival dynamics, a PSM was ultimately preferred. 

One NICE technology appraisal in urothelial cancer was identified in the SLR of costeffectiveness studies (TA817), which evaluated adjuvant nivolumab. It is notable that this appraisal adopted a semi-Markov approach. This was necessary because analysis of OS and post-recurrence survival from the trial informing the model (CheckMate-274) were not carried out prior to the submission as insufficient OS events had occurred to trigger the analysis and the data was blinded to the Company. The Company modelled post-recurrence survival using a static transition probability sourced from the literature. Two sources were identified which reported the median post-recurrence survival, which the Company pooled and weighted assuming a 50:50 split. This is converted into a weekly transition probability of recurrence to death assuming an exponential distribution. This approach, whilst considered suitable by NICE for decision making, requires very strong assumptions which were necessary given that OS data was not available for CheckMate-274. 

Clinicians interviewed confirmed that the NIAGARA trial is representative of UK clinical practice, and when discussing survival extrapolations, consideration was given to the distribution of subsequent treatments received in UK clinical practice.

## **b. The EAG notes that in the model, patients who are in the locoregional recurrence (LR) health state cannot move back to event-free health state. Please provide additional justification to support/validate this assumption.** 

Patients enter the model in the event free (EF) state and immediately start treatment with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, either with or without perioperative durvalumab, followed by radical cystectomy, if eligible. The EF health state in the PSM represents the period during which patients have not experienced local recurrence, distant metastasis, or death, aligning with the definition of event-free survival (EFS) in the NIAGARA trial. Once a patient experiences a local recurrence, they have, by definition, had an event and are no longer event-free within the context of the model. Transitions to the local recurrence (LR) health state are therefore captured by the difference between the MFS and EFS endpoints, consistent with how the NIAGARA trial defined these events. 

The model structure reflects the typical clinical course of MIBC patients. Patients who progress to local recurrence face a different prognosis and treatment pathway. Additionally, this model structure of not allowing patients in LR health state to move back to EF health state is consistent with other technical appraisals in early-stage cancer, such as TA1030 and TA851 (31, 32). 

Therefore, the chosen structure is appropriate and grounded in both trial design and MIBC patient pathway. 

## _**Study endpoints used in the model**_ 

**B2. PRIORITY: The definition of EFS represents the pre-recurrence phase, including patients who progress before surgery or decline or are unfit for surgery. From Table 6 of the CS, the EAG notes that while 11.8% patients did** 



<!-- page 243 -->

## **not undergo cystectomy as planned, only 1.7% did not undergo cystectomy due to the disease progression.** 

- **a. For the subgroup of patients who decline surgery, please clarify if they are treated as recurrence in the definition of EFS. That is, does the locoregional recurrence health state in the model include patients who had refused surgery? If yes, please provide additional justification to support/validate this assumption and explain the impact of this assumption on the model results.** 

In the NIAGARA trial, the definition of EFS as a primary endpoint, developed in consultation with regulators (33), includes “the time of first documented progression in patients who were medically precluded from a radical cystectomy, or time of expected surgery in patients who refused to undergo a radical cystectomy or failure to undergo a radical cystectomy in participants with residual disease, or the time of death due to any cause, whichever occurred first)”. Thus, failure or refusal to undergo surgery for any reason was captured as an EFS event in the primary analysis. 

When modelling these outcomes, any patient who did not receive surgery and remained free of distant metastasis entered the locoregional recurrence health state. Patients—regardless of surgery status—who developed distant metastases were registered as an event in MFS in the NIAGARA trial and were assigned to the distant metastasis health state in the model. 

Including all patients who did not undergo surgery as planned is appropriate, as this reflects the trial’s endpoint definition and avoids the arbitrariness of censoring such patients. To further validate this approach, a post-hoc analysis was conducted in which patients who refused or failed to undergo radical cystectomy were censored for EFS in both BICR and central pathology analyses, rather than counted as events. The resulting hazard ratio (HR 0.69 [95% CI: 0.556–0.858]) were consistent with the primary analysis (HR 0.68 [95% CI: 0.558–0.817]). 

## **b. Please clarify if costs for the patients who did not undergo cystectomy as** 

## **planned were included in the model.** 

For patients who did not undergo cystectomy as planned, all neoadjuvant treatment exposure was captured in the time-on-treatment analysis. Drug costs and drug 



<!-- page 244 -->

administration costs for these patients were included in the model in the neoadjuvant phase. 

The six patients who refused cystectomy but achieved a complete clinical response entered the non-cystectomy extension phase and received durvalumab for up to eight additional cycles, following their initial four cycles of neoadjuvant durvalumab plus chemotherapy. Cycles administered during the non-cystectomy extension phase were excluded from the treatment cost calculation as the licensed indication specifies perioperative durvalumab use before and after surgery. As these six patients, representing only 1.1% (6/530) of the perioperative durvalumab arm, were technically treated off-label, their exclusion has a negligible impact on overall model results. 

Importantly, patients who did not undergo cystectomy were still included in the safety analysis, ensuring that costs for adverse event management were fully captured. As outlined in response B2.a, non-surgery patients were included in all health states within the model, meaning that resource use costs, end-of-life costs, and subsequent treatment costs were appropriately applied to these patients in respective health states. This ensures a comprehensive accounting of costs and outcomes across all relevant patient groups within the model.

## **a. Please clarify which definition for EFS and for MFS is used in the model and justify the choice.** 

As detailed in Table 4 in the CS, one of the two primary outcomes of NIAGARA is EFS, defined as the time from randomisation to the first recurrence of disease after radical cystectomy (RC), the time of first documented progression in patients who are medically precluded from a RC, or time of expected surgery in patients who refuse to undergo a RC or failure to undergo a RC in participants with residual disease, or the time of death due to any cause, whichever occurs first as evaluated by BICR or by central pathology review. Secondary outcomes include EFS per investigator and MFS, 



<!-- page 245 -->

**Error! Reference source not found.** 

per investigator assessments (or local biopsy review if a biopsy was required for a suspected new lesion). 

The model used the primary endpoint EFS per BICR and secondary endpoint MFS per Investigator assessments, both of which required a local biopsy review if a biopsy is required for a suspected new lesion.  MFS assessed by BICR was not a predefined endpoint of the study and is therefore not available for use in the model. 

EFS per BICR was selected to use in the model as it is a primary endpoint of the NIAGARA trial. BICR assessments minimise potential bias as they are conducted independently of the trial sites and are blinded to treatment assignments. For MFS, only investigator-assessed data were available from the trial, therefore it was used in the model. 

## **b. Please explain the impact of using different definitions of EFS and MFS on** 

## **the model results.** 

As detailed in CS Section 2.6.2, EFS results per investigator or local biopsy review and per BICR followed a similar trend. Both KM plots showed a separation of curves in favour of the perioperative durvalumab arm at approximately two months and the separation was clear and sustained thereafter (Figure 5 and Figure 8 in CS). The EFS hazard ratios using the two definitions are both 0.68, with minimal difference in the 95% confidence interval (EFS per BICR: 0.558, 0.817; EFS per investigator or local biopsy review: 0.562, 0.812) (FAS [ITT population], DCO 29 April 2024). EFS using the two definitions also showed the same overall 32% reduction in the risk of an EFS event compared to the control arm. 

Both EFS per BICR and per investigator demonstrated a clinically meaningful improvement in EFS in patients treated with perioperative durvalumab, consistent across assessment methodologies. This consistency demonstrates the robustness of the positive treatment effect and suggests that there is minimal variation in the modelled effectiveness for EFS due to the assessment method. Therefore, the model results are unlikely to be affected by the choice of EFS definition.

For MFS, there is only a single definition available in the NIAGARA trial. Therefore, it is not possible to evaluation the impact of alternative assessment methods on model outcomes. 

**B4. PRIORITY: The NIAGARA trial included a PFS-2 outcome, which represents the time from randomisation to subsequent progression or recurrence post EFS event or progression-free survival after second-line therapy. The EAG considers this endpoint as important in the perioperative setting to reflect the durability of treatment benefit beyond the first treatment.** 

## **a. Please clarify why this endpoint has not been used in the model to provide more granularity in the modelling of events over time.** 

Although PFS2 demonstrated the durability of perioperative durvalumab treatment effect beyond the first event, the exclusion of PFS2 data from the cost-effectiveness model was an intentional structural decision, informed by both clinical and modelling considerations. The model is based around the primary EFS endpoint and the secondary endpoints used (OS and MFS) fully captured the clinical and economic outcomes in this setting. The MFS health state in particular is widely recognised as clinically meaningful and directly relevant for tracking both disease progression and its impact on costs and patient quality of life in this disease context. The 4-state model structure and the selected endpoints used to inform the model have been validated and supported by HTA experts in an advisory board conducted by AstraZeneca. Furthermore, the approach of utilising similar primary and secondary endpoints instead of PFS-2 even though it was collected in the clinical trial is aligned with previous NICE appraisals (such as TA871, TA683 and TA816) (34-36). 

## **b. Please consider amending the existing model structure to also incorporate PFS-2 data. If this is not feasible within the proposed time frame of responses, please provide some qualitative commentary on the potential implications of excluding this data within the existing model structure.** 

Incorporating PFS2 alongside MFS would substantially complicate the model structure. To ensure health states remain mutually exclusive and exhaustive, it would be necessary to define health states in terms of both PFS2 and MFS, to capture those patients who enter MFS directly from EFS (and have no PFS2 event) and those who 



<!-- page 247 -->

**Error! Reference source not found.** 

first have a recurrence and then enter the distant metastases state (and have a PFS2 event). This would require additional, potentially non-standard state definitions and transition pathways, introducing extra complexity and uncertainty into the model for questionable analytic gain. 

The current use of MFS already robustly captures the main clinical and economic consequences of progression in this setting. MFS is a composite endpoint and is wellvalidated as a predictor of both survival and quality-adjusted life expectancy. Not including PFS2 in the cost-effectiveness analysis is unlikely to bias the results, as the key clinical and resource use inflection points are all directly modelled. While PFS2 may provide additional granularity regarding the timing and sequence of subsequent events, its omission does not neglect any major clinical or economic milestone relevant for the model, as these are already reflected in the chosen states and transitions. Furthermore, the significant improvement in PFS2 observed in NIAGARA (outlined in response to question A7) strengthens confidence that the modelled benefits of perioperative durvalumab are not a consequence of post-progression therapies but are due to a direct and persistent treatment effect. 

In summary, while it is theoretically possible to revise the model to include PFS2, doing so would reduce transparency and add complexity, without meaningfully improving decision-making accuracy in this context, and it has therefore not been provided. 

## _**Survival modelling**_ 

**B5. PRIORITY: To inform the partition survival model, the company conducted survival modelling for EFS, MFS and OS, with each curve fitted independently. As a result, applying the following structural constraints was required: OS is constrained to ≤ general population survival, MFS is constrained to values ≤ OS and EFS is constrained to values ≤ MFS. The company followed the NICE Decision Support Unit Technical Support Document (TSD) 14 and TSD 21 when conducting the survival modelling, including an assessment of the proportional hazards and accelerated failure time, generation of statistical goodness of fit, visual inspection of model fit to the trial data and an assessment of the clinical** 



<!-- page 248 -->

**Error! Reference source not found.** 

**plausibility of extrapolation. However, the survival modelling and its assessment was performed for each curve in isolation.** 

**a. For the combination of curves used in the company base-case, please evaluate whether there are any logically consistent functions that could be used across EFS, MFS and OS that would not require constraints to be imposed in the model. If applying the constraints is needed, please identify which constraints are used in the model and the time points at which these constraints need to be imposed.** 

For the combination of survival curves used in the company base-case, it was necessary to impose a constraint related to general population survival. This requirement arises due to the early-stage disease setting with a notable trend toward cure, and the lifetime horizon used in the model. The general population constraint ensures that projected survival in both arms of the model does not exceed what would be expected in the overall population, providing a logical and clinically meaningful upper limit for survival probabilities. 

In the company base-case, without any adjustments, for the G+C+D arm EFS is always positioned below OS, with the exception of month 1, where a minor inconsistency appears. EFS remains below MFS up to month 89. When general population mortality is accounted for, the difference between EFS and MFS diminishes substantially, so that only a small corrective adjustment is needed to maintain logical consistency between the endpoints. For the G+C arm, EFS stays below OS up to month 228 (excluding month 1), and remains below MFS through to month 400. As with the D+G+C arm, introducing the general population constraint shrinks the requirement for the second adjustment to OS and MFS. 

When assessing whether it is possible to identify alternative survival functions that logically align EFS, MFS, and OS without the need for such constraints, it is generally not feasible for the vast majority of parametric distributions. At minimum, the constraint to not exceed general population survival is virtually always necessary, although the specific time points at which it is applied differs between models. However, selecting a distribution solely based on this property could come at the expense of poor fit in earlier portions of the curve, which would negatively impact the overall validity of the model. 



<!-- page 249 -->

**Error! Reference source not found.** 

To ensure clinical relevance and consistency for decision making, all survival models validated with UK clinicians included the adjustment for general population survival. 

## **b. The EAG notes a setting in the model that specifies the dominant curve for extrapolation (OS=EFS after crossing or EFS=OS after crossing). Please explain these assumptions and explain why OS=EFS after crossing is chosen as the base case.** 

By definition, EFS must always be equal or less than OS, since a patient cannot be event-free if they are not alive. If, due to extrapolation, the EFS curve is modelled to exceed OS at any time point, this creates a clinically implausible scenario. In such cases, the model applies an adjustment to OS to match EFS (OS=EFS), or EFS to match OS (EFS=OS), at the point of crossing. This correction maintains a logical relationship between endpoints. 

The choice of the OS=EFS setting in the base case is based on the clinical expectation that patient achieving long-term remission in the EFS state are likely to be cured of disease and subsequently experience only background all-cause mortality. These patients remain in the EFS state until death from general population mortality. By maintaining OS = EFS in the long-term, the model ensures that patients in the EFS state face only background mortality risks over time. Conversely, if set to EFS=OS, the EFS curve could suddenly align with a lower OS curve at the point of crossing, potentially resulting in an abrupt and unrealistic decline in EFS. This would incorrectly imply a rapid increase in mortality among patients otherwise considered at minimal risk except for age- or sex-related background mortality. 

However, with the current base case extrapolations for OS and EFS in both D+G+C and G+C arms, EFS already consistently remains below OS at all time points after the constraint of general population mortality has been applied. This demonstrates that the model already adheres to the expected clinical relationship of OS being greater than or equal to EFS. As a result, switching the model setting to EFS=OS at any crossing point had no impact on the results. Therefore, the choice regarding this setting does not affect the model outcomes or the conclusions of the economic evaluation.

A systematic and comprehensive approach was used for the selection of extrapolations for all endpoints, including an assessment of the proportional hazards and accelerated failure time, statistical goodness of fit, visual inspection of model fit to the trial data and clinical plausibility of long-term extrapolation assessed by UK clinical experts and external literature where available. Curve selection was not based solely on statistical goodness-of-fit, but rather on a balanced assessment of both quantitative and qualitative factors. 

The log-logistic model was selected as the base case for the control arm OS because among all curves nominated by clinicians (log-logistic, log-normal, and Gompertz), the log-logistic model demonstrated the closest alignment with long-term OS data for MIBC patients in the best external evidence identified, as detailed in Section 3.3.2 of the CS and summarised in Table 40, supporting its selection as the most appropriate base case model. Additionally, the log-logistic model was the most preferred model by clinicians consulted, with two out of four experts identifying it as the most clinically plausible when presented with long-term OS projections adjusted for general population mortality. 

While generalised gamma provides the best statistical fits according to AIC and BIC, it was not selected as the primary model because none of the consulted clinicians considered it the most appropriate for long-term extrapolation. However, the lognormal model was preferred by one clinician and provides the second-best fit statistically, and the Gompertz model was also preferred by one clinician. The lognormal and Gompertz model were both included as scenario analyses. Importantly, these scenarios both produced ICERs that remained below the £20,000 per QALY threshold, supporting the conclusion that perioperative durvalumab is a cost-effective treatment option.

**B9. PRIORITY: The EAG notes that the OS curve for the durvalumab arm converges with and subsequently falls below the age- and gender-adjusted general population mortality rate after** x.xx **years, at which point** xx% **of the patient cohort remains alive. This can be interpreted to imply that** xx% **of patients are considered cured of cancer after** x.xx **years, also based on the decreasing and plateauing hazard rates for EFS and MFS shown in Figures 1, 6, 7, 10, 15-18 in Appendix L. Please justify whether this model estimate is** 



<!-- page 260 -->

**Error! Reference source not found.** 

## **clinically plausible and consistent with the current understanding of the longterm MIBC prognosis.** 

To address the plausibility of the model estimate regarding cure in the durvalumab arm, previous appraisals in the MIBC setting were reviewed to understand different approaches for estimating long-term outcomes in health technology assessments. In TA817 assessing adjuvant nivolumab in urothelial cancer, the Company incorporated a structural cure assumption in the CEM at five years— after five years in the initial DFS health state, patients were assumed to be cured (that is, the cancer can no longer recur) and all patients were moved to the LT DFS health state where the mortality risk was assumed to be the same as an age- and sex-matched general population mortality (24). While the appraisal committee acknowledged uncertainty regarding the most appropriate timepoint to assume cure (five or ten years), they accepted five years as appropriate for decision making. This assumption aligns with clinical practice in the NHS, where recurrence beyond five years is considered uncommon and therefore patients are typically discharged from routine follow-up, as described in the guidelines for the management of bladder cancer published by the West Midland Expert Advisory Group for Urology Cancer (37). 

Implicitly modelling cure at x.xx years can therefore be considered a conservative and clinically plausible approach. To further inform the company’s approach and in response to the concerns raised by the committee during TA817, feedback was sought from UK-based clinical experts through clinical validation interviews. Uniformly, clinical experts indicated a preference for using the term “risk of recurrence” rather than “cure assumption.” There was no consensus among experts regarding whether a five- or ten-year timepoint would be preferable should a specific point of cure need to be defined. Given the lack of consensus over the timing of cure and the prevailing clinical preference to frame long-term outcomes as risk of recurrence, the company decided not to incorporate an explicit cure assumption in the CEM. This approach is further supported by the behaviour of the survival curves themselves, which indicate a de facto ‘cure’ through declining hazard rates for EFS, MFS, and OS, together with the application of background mortality adjustments.

## **B10. PRIORITY: Please clarify how the time on treatment was estimated. Does the time on treatment in the trial include people who did and did not receive cystectomy?** 

In the CEM, the time on treatment for the neoadjuvant and adjuvant components of the D+G+C and G+C arms is modelled using the observed proportions of patients who received each scheduled cycle in each arm of the NIAGARA trial. 

Table 24 shows the number of cycles completed by number of patients. This shows that from the 530 patients that received study treatment in the D+G+C arm (see CONSORT diagram provided in Appendix B of the Company submission), 85.28% had four cycles of neoadjuvant durvalumab and 86.23% had four cycles of neoadjuvant G+C. From the 383 patients treated in the adjuvant phase, 74.67% completed the full eight cycles of adjuvant durvalumab. From the 526 patients that received study treatment in the G+C arm, 81.18% completed the four cycles in the neoadjuvant phase. 

The model starts with 100% of patients receive treatment. The proportions in Table 24 are then subtracted from each cycle as patients discontinue. For example, for neoadjuvant durvalumab, 100% are on treatment in cycle 1, 96.79% of patients are on treatment in cycle 2 (100% - 3.21%), and 93.77% of patients are on treatment in cycle 3 (96.79% - 3.02%), etc,. The full table reporting the proportion on treatment in each cycle is provide in the Company Submission Section 3.5.2 Table 49. 

As of the data cutoff date, no patient remained on neoadjuvant or adjuvant treatment in the NIAGARA trial. Therefore, the observed proportions of patients who received each neoadjuvant and adjuvant treatment cycle can be used directly, without the need for extrapolation.

Radical cystectomy was to be performed as soon as possible after completion of, and recovery from, neoadjuvant therapy and was recommended to occur within two to eight weeks after the last dose of neoadjuvant therapy (20). The initiation of adjuvant durvalumab was recommended to occur between 42 and 120 days of cystectomy, after a period of adequate recovery from radical cystectomy. 

In the model, the first dose of adjuvant durvalumab is applied at week 24 of the time horizon. This is aligned to the median times from randomization to cystectomy (16.3 weeks) and the time from cystectomy to adjuvant therapy (8.57 weeks) (20). 

As detailed in response to Question A4.c and B2.b, for patients who did not undergo cystectomy as planned, all neoadjuvant treatment exposure was captured in the timeon-treatment analysis. Drug costs and drug administration costs for these patients were included in the model in the neoadjuvant phase. The six patients who refused cystectomy but achieved a complete clinical response entered the non-cystectomy extension phase and received durvalumab for up to eight additional cycles, following their initial four cycles of neoadjuvant durvalumab plus chemotherapy. ## **B11. Please clarify what is meant with ‘non-cystectomy extension phase’ (Table 6, page 38 of the CS). Who are these patients? How are these patients included in the analysis and what are the implications for EFS, health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and resource use and costs?** 

The definition of non-cystectomy extension phase according to the protocol of NIAGARA trial can be found in Question A4.c, this phase was available exclusively to patients who refused radical cystectomy at the specified time after achieving a complete clinical response, as locally determined by multimodal assessment and without additional interventions. Only six patients (1.1%) in the perioperative durvalumab arm entered the non-cystectomy extension phase. Non-cystectomy extension phase patients were administered durvalumab 1500 mg as monotherapy every 28 days for a maximum of eight doses (corresponding to a maximum exposure of 12 months). 

The non-cystectomy extension phase patients were included as a part of the ITT population in the survival outcomes, HRQoL and safety analyses. Details regarding the inclusion of costs for these patients in the model are provided in the response to Question B2.b and B10. For these six patients, the model accounts for drug costs incurred during the neoadjuvant phase, resource use and subsequent treatment costs within the appropriate health states, as well as costs related to adverse event management. Drug costs related to the adjuvant phase are not included. 

These patients represent a very small proportion of the overall study population, and the inclusion of these patients is anticipated to have minimal impact on the overall study results.

## **clinical experts). However, the OS data used to inform the model reflect treatments received in the NIAGARA trial.** 

## **a. Please comment on how reflective of NHS practice these subsequent treatments provided are (see also question A8), and the impact of this assumption on the results.** 

A detailed list of post-discontinuation anticancer therapies administered in the NIAGARA trial can be found in the response to Question A8. As noted in Question A9.a, the NIAGARA trial was a large, global, multicentre study that included a range of post-progression treatment practices, determined by the approval and reimbursement status of therapies in each participating country, local access to clinical trials, and the availability of non-approved agents through compassionate use. Consequently, while many of the subsequent treatments provided during the NIAGARA trial align with NHS practice, both the range of therapies used and the proportion of patients receiving them do not perfectly reflect the UK setting. 

To ensure the economic analysis reflects NHS clinical practice, four UK-based clinical experts were consulted on the use and distribution of subsequent therapies. The average of these expert insights was applied in the model so that the proportion and types of post-progression treatments mirror expectations for NHS patients, making this the most robust and UK-relevant evidence available. The feedback from UK clinical experts suggested that there would be a higher proportion of patients receiving subsequent therapies in clinical practice compared with the NIAGARA trial in both arms, with experts agreeing that IO-based regimens are an important post-progression treatment option to be considered in the management of MIBC (see response to Question B12 and Company submission Section 3.5.6). 

It is important to note that the issue of additional subsequent therapies being available in NIAGARA affects both study arms. As noted in response to question A9b, it is challenging to quantify the potential impact on the results arising from increased subsequent therapy use in both arms, but we contend that the relative treatment effect observed in the NIAGARA trial would likely be preserved, and that differences in the use of subsequent therapies between the NIAGARA trial and NHS practice are unlikely to meaningfully affect the outcomes of the CEM. 



<!-- page 265 -->

**Error! Reference source not found.** 

In addition, the survival curves used in the economic model were validated by the same UK clinical experts to ensure that projected overall survival outcomes align with what would be expected for this patient population within NHS clinical practice. This expert validation provides further reassurance that the survival estimates in the model are appropriate and reflective of UK experience and the subsequent treatments receive, despite differences in the distribution of subsequent therapies between the trial and real-world NHS settings. 

Attempting to further adjust survival outcomes in the model to account for these differences would be challenging and could introduce additional uncertainties or bias, without necessarily improving the reliability of the results.

**B13 PRIORITY: Please clarify whether the subsequent treatments combine treatments for locoregional recurrence and metastatic recurrence. If this is the case, please explain whether locoregional recurrence and metastatic recurrence are treated with the same treatments in the UK clinical practice and the impact of the assumption to combine these treatments and apply to both LR and distant metastasis (DM) health states on the model results.** 

The model applies subsequent treatment costs as an aggregated one-off cost to all patients who experience any recurrence upon leaving the EFS state. In other words, subsequent treatment in the model represents a pooled combination of treatments for patients entering both the locoregional recurrence (LR) and distant metastasis (DM) health states. This approach captures the entire range of subsequent therapies a patient may receive over their lifetime, regardless of whether the recurrence is locoregional or metastatic. It is a commonly adopted assumption in cost-effectiveness modelling to apply a one-off cost upon disease progression, given the practical challenges and limited data available for modelling every possible treatment sequence following progression. 

Under the aggregated subsequent treatment assumption, all treatments received postrecurrence are reflected in the distribution of subsequent therapies, meaning that all relevant costs and resource use are captured irrespective of the location of recurrence. As a result, whether LR and DM patients receive identical or different subsequent treatments should have minimal impact on the overall model results.

## **B19. PRIORITY: Please provide comprehensive details on the methods used to estimate health state utility values, including all MMRM analyses performed, the obtained results, and model fit.** 

Section 3.4.2 of the Company Submission provides a detailed report of the methodology used to estimate health state utility values using the MMRM methodology. The MMRM methodology is routinely used to analyse repeated clinical outcome measures for regulatory and HTA submissions and is the preferred approach to analysing HRQoL data in clinical guidelines (42). The results of an MMRM analysis provides inferences that account for the within-subject correlations from longitudinal measures and is appropriate when handling data that are missing at random (43). 

Key methodological considerations will be repeated and added to here, but most of the details on the methods, results and model fit were provided in Section 3.4.2 of the Company submission. 

The MMRM analysis accounts for the following states; 

1. Pre-progression (EFS investigator), 

2. Post EFS (investigator) progression and pre-MFS (investigator) progression, 

3. Distant metastatic state (Post MFS progression), 

4. Recurrent with unknown metastatic status. 

The recurrent with unknown metastatic status is defined as scenarios where, i) MFS is censored prior to EFS event, so we are uncertain if the patient is non-metastatic or distant metastatic at EFS event time, ii) MFS is censored after EFS event. 

Where EFS (investigator) times are recorded after MFS (investigator) times, we define rules for assigning utilities as follows: 

- EFS (investigator) censoring after MFS (investigator) event All EQ-5D measures up to MFS event, set to “event-free state”; Any EQ-5D collected after MFS, set to “distant met state”. 

- EFS (investigator) event after MFS (investigator) censoring - All EQ-5D measures up to EFS (investigator) event, set to “event-free state”. 



<!-- page 270 -->

**Error! Reference source not found.** 

- EFS (investigator) event after MFS (investigator) event - All EQ-5D measures up to MFS (investigator) event, set to “event-free state”; Any EQ-5D collected after MFS(investigator), set to “distant met”. 

- Additionally, observations that occur after EFS event and MFS censoring in subjects where this MFS censoring was after the EFS event date are treated as recurrent with unknown metastatic status. 

The MMRM analysis was performed on a dataset excluding any observations recorded after the time of censoring for progression (see response to Question B18). 

The statistical relationship between EQ-5D-5L health state utility and treatment, and health status was assessed using regression analysis. Analysis was performed in R 4.3.1 using the mmrm package 0.3.14 for model fitting. The MMRM analysis was performed using the restricted maximum likelihood method (REML) with the following covariates included as fixed effects: 

- (Randomised) Treatment 

- Progression status (pre-progression, post-progression) 

- Treatment + Progression status 

- Treatment + Progression status + Treatment * Progression status (Both terms and their interaction included). 

The correlation of repeated utility measurements within subjects over time was captured via the specification of covariance structures for the MMRM.  The results from the models using the first covariance structure in the sequence that successfully converged for all models are presented here (i.e., for each of the four covariate options). If for a particular set of covariates none of the models converged, then no results are presented for that model, and the remaining model results are based on the most flexible covariance structure for which the models converged. 

The hierarchy of covariance structures tested, in order of most to least flexible, is shown below: 

1. Unstructured – each visit is allowed to have a different variance, and each combination of visits is allowed to have a different covariance. 



<!-- page 271 -->

**Error! Reference source not found.** 

2. Toeplitz with heterogeneity – each visit is allowed to have a different variance, covariances between measurements depend on how many visits apart they are. 

3. Autoregressive, order 1 (AR(1)) with heterogeneity – each visit is allowed to have a different variance, and covariances decrease based on how many visits apart they are. Covariances decrease towards zero as the number of visits between observations increases. 

4. Toeplitz – as above for number 2, but each visit shares the same variance. 

5. Autoregression, order 1 (AR(1)) – as above for number 3, but each visit shares the same variance. 

For each model, parameter estimates, and marginal (‘least square’) means are provided below including 95% confidence intervals. The marginal (‘least square’) mean provides a model-based estimate of the mean utility score by status (treatment and/or Progression status) that is averaged over observations and with adjustment for repeated measures. 

In total, 12,880 EQ-5D-5L observations were available from 986 patients. Of these, 12,130 observations were recorded in the event-free state, 150 observations were recorded in the post-EFS-pre-metastatic state, 128 observations were recorded in the distant metastatic state, 151 observations were recorded recurrent with unknown metastatic status, and 321 were recorded after censoring for MFS. 

Baseline HSU were similar across arms, with mean values of x.xx (standard deviation=x.xx) and x.xx (standard deviation=x.xx) for G+C and G+C+D, respectively. The MMRM analyses were therefore performed without adjustment for baseline HSU. 

The correlation of repeated utility measurements within subjects over time was captured via Autoregressive - order 1 with Heterogeneity as this successfully converged for all models. Table 26 shows the best fitting model in terms of AIC was the model including a term for progression status.

## **a. Present a comparison of these NIAGARA trial utility values with other published utility values for patients with MIBC in the event-free state.** 

As detailed in Section 3.4 in the CS and Appendix E, a systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted and identified 24 studies reporting HRQoL data in patients with MIBC. Only one publication evaluating the cost-effectiveness of adjuvant nivolumab by Brodtkorb et al provided relevant health state utility data, although this value is for the disease-free state rather than event-free, given the design of the CheckMate-274 trial (44). The mean disease-free health state utility applied was 0.863. This is consistent with the HSU value used for the EF health state in the NIAGARA model (0.847). It should be noted that the Brodtkorb et al utility was derived using a United States based dataset. In the NICE appraisal of adjuvant nivolumab (TA817), the Company explained that the HRQoL within disease-free (DF) from the trial exceeded age-dependent general population values, and so to address this, all patients in the DF state in the model had age-matched population values. Although the trial values were redacted and not publicly available, this indicates that trial values were used in the CheckMate-274 trial. 

Whilst an unpublished source, the Prospective Bladder Cancer Infrastructure (ProBCI) registry provides valuable insight into the HRQoL data from MIBC patients. We provided some detail of this registry in the Company submission, and feel it may be valuable to provide more context here. 

This registry collects prospective clinical and HRQoL data from patients with MIBC, non-muscle invasive and metastatic bladder cancer, recruited from 25 hospitals in the Netherlands. AstraZeneca is a partner organization to ProBCI, providing financial support for its research initiatives. As a partner, AstraZeneca can submit analysis requests to the ProBCI. To support reimbursement submissions for perioperative durvalumab, AstraZeneca requested an analysis to explore the impact of recurrence on HSU and HRQoL. This analysis was performed on a subpopulation of ProBCI that best matched the key inclusion criteria of the NIAGARA trial:

- No prior systemic chemotherapy or immunotherapy for MIBC. 

A recurrence event included local or distant recurrence of disease or progressive disease. The association between recurrence and HSU was estimated using a MMRM analysis with covariates for recurrence and the calendar date of HSU collection, measured in terms of the quarter of each year (e.g., quarter 1, 2024). The data set used in the analysis contained 257 EQ-5D-5L observations from 166 subjects.

The mean HSU for patients in the pre-event state was 0.852.

## **b. Comment on the appropriateness of using these relatively high utility values in the model, given the clinical context, and outline the potential impact of this assumption on the model results.** 

The health state utility values were based on the EQ-5D-5L data collected in the NIAGARA trial and further validated in interviews conducted with UK clinical experts. As discussed in response to Question B20 a, the value used in the EF state is appropriate and aligned with external sources of evidence in this setting. We therefore maintain that the values used in the Company submission base case are appropriate and aligned with the NICE reference case (38). 

To test the sensitivity of the model results to lower utility values, we have conducted a scenario applying an arbitrary decrement to the EF utility. In TA817, the EAG had previously suggested a 0.02 utility decrement to address concerns that the diseasefree survival health state utility, using the age- and sex-matched general population utility value, was too high. This was applied up until the timepoint in the model where patients were considered ‘cured’, as a structural cure was assumed. Here we present the same 0.02 decrement applied to the EF utility in a scenario analysis. This is considered conservative given that it is applied for the duration of the time spent in the EF state and despite the fact that TA817 used higher utility values to begin with (matching general population values). As shown in Table 30, the adjustment made negligible impact on the ICER compared to the base case, demonstrating that the model results are robust to reductions in the EF health state utility. 

It is important to highlight that in TA817, clinical and patient experts agreed that, after a period of adjustment, people with resected urothelial cancer often adapt very well to

post-surgical changes and often achieve a good quality of life with a fully functional lifestyle. Furthermore, the appraisal committee acknowledged the application of a utility decrement as arbitrary, since there is insufficient evidence to precisely quantify the appropriate value. 

Overall, these findings confirm that the model’s conclusions regarding the costeffectiveness of perioperative durvalumab remain stable, even when applying a lower utility for the event-free health state.

## **a. Please justify the choice of the duration of the acute negative impact in the analysis.** 

As detailed in Section 3.4.5 in the CS, the impact of radical cystectomy on HRQoL was modelled using HSUs from the UK Life After Bladder Cancer (LABC) study (41). The LABC study collected EQ-5D-5L questionnaires at baseline, and at 6, 9 and 12 months after diagnosis. HSUs were estimated using the Van Hout et al 5L to 3L crosswalk algorithm for the UK value set (46) and mapped to ‘baseline’ (prior to surgery), ‘post-treatment’ (first survey after surgery) and ‘recovery’ (at least 6 months since surgery) phases. Compared to the NIAGARA cohort, the cohort in LABC was older on average (39% aged >75 years old versus 11% in NIAGARA) but had a similar sex distribution (79% Male in LABC versus 82% in NIAGARA). 

In patients who received radical radiotherapy or cystectomy, there was a decline in mean EQ5D-5L HSU of approximately -x.xx from baseline to the post-treatment phase (46). At the recovery phase (6-12 months after surgery), there was no difference in general HRQoL when compared to baseline (46). These findings indicate that cystectomy may lead to an initial QALY loss of approximately x.xx-x.xx per surgery patient, calculated as the utility loss of x.xx multiplied by the x.x-xx-x.x-year recovery period. In the NIAGARA cost-effectiveness base case, the recovery period after surgery was set to 6 months. In the next question (B22.b) the negative impact is expanded to 12-month as a sensitivity analysis. The results shows that there is a minimal impact on the conclusion that perioperative durvalumab represents a cost-effective treatment option in this setting at the £20,000 WTP threshold.
