**B23. PRIORITY: Clinical advice to the EAG was that cystectomy is expected to have a life-long impact on HRQoL due to the need of a urostomy bag for the rest of patients’ life. This impact is in addition to the acute negative impact associated with the surgery.** 

## **a. Please explain why the life-long impact of using urostomy bag was not included in the analysis** 

The company acknowledges the rationale behind this question. During the submission process, careful consideration was given to whether to include a life-long utility decrement associated with the use of a urostomy bag. Ultimately, this was excluded, consistent with feedback received during the technical engagement for TA817. 

During this engagement, both clinical experts and patient advocacy groups (NCRIACP-RCP-RCR, Action Bladder Cancer, and Fight Bladder Cancer) concluded that, while many individuals experience negative impacts from permanent changes in urinary and sexual function, these impacts are generally short-lived as patients adapt over time. Importantly, the loss of function or presence of a disability does not necessarily equate to a sustained loss in quality of life, and it is entirely possible for individuals with such disabilities to experience a high quality of life. It was also noted that the quality of life for individuals with resected high-risk urothelial cancer is similar to those who are disease-free. 

Furthermore, none of the previous eight urothelial carcinoma medicines assessed by NICE included an additional disutility for the life-long impact of using a urostomy bag. This is aligned with the view that inclusion of a long-term decrement is not warranted in this context. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 282 -->

**Error! Reference source not found.** 

Given this evidence and considering that any long-term disutility associated with a urostomy bag would apply equally to both treatment arms involving cystectomy (G+C and D+G+C), thus effectively cancelling itself out in terms of incremental analysis, it was determined that including such a decrement in the cost-effectiveness model would not be informative for decision making. For these reasons, a lifelong HRQoL decrement due to urostomy was not included in the analysis. 

## **b. In the economic model, please incorporate a scenario analysis that applies a life-long health utility decrement for patients who underwent cystectomy.** 

A scenario analysis was performed as requested with the duration of utility decrement of surgery set for a lifetime horizon of 432 months (36 years). As shown in Table 33, the variation caused a negligible impact in the cost-effectiveness results, indicating the robustness of the model outcome regardless of the duration of utility decrement.

The search terms used in the search strategies were developed after examining the search strategies used in two relevant published SLRs (48, 49) and discussion with AstraZeneca medical expert. The two published SLRs used broad terms for BC instead of terms specific to MIBC. The present SLR used terms specific to MIBC to maintain balance between sensitivity and specificity of the searches. To examine the impact of using MIBC terms instead of BC terms, the recall performance of the search was assessed using a test-set of four studies for the clinical SLR and four studies for the economic SLR (50-57). All studies were successfully retrieved by the search. This decision was validated by AstraZeneca medical review. For cisplatinbased chemotherapy, the comparison is informed by the NIAGARA trial, an RCT (the gold standard evidence) which presents the direct comparison against the current standard of care in the UK. The key study informing evidence for nivolumab, CheckMate-274, is included in the SLR. 

In conclusion, the company confirms no relevant evidence was missed as a result of the population terms used in the search strategy.

<!-- page 294 -->

## **Introduction** 

The distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS) indirect treatment comparison (ITC) was performed using the same approach as described in the Company Submission for the event free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS) ITCs. The analysis involved estimating the acceleration factor (AF) for nivolumab versus placebo from pseudopatient data recovered from the DMFS curve of the PD-L1≥1% muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) subgroup of CHECKMATE-274, reported in supplementary figure 4D of Galsky et al [1]. This AF was then applied to the ‘adjuvant period’ MFS survival times of the gemcitabine in combination with cisplatin (G+C) arm of NIAGARA. 

The aim of the analysis was to estimate the MFS for the control arm of NIAGARA that included the effect of adjuvant nivolumab (referred to as “counterfactual arm”, or G+C+N). The ITC is then performed by comparing durvalumab plus gemcitabine in combination with cisplatin (D+G+C, or perioperative durvalumab) with this counterfactual arm (representing G+C+N), and by comparing G+C+N with G+C. 

## **Estimating the AF for nivolumab** 

Pseudo patient data for DMFS in the PD-L1 >1% MIBC subgroup of CHECKMATE274 were generated by digitising the Kaplan-Meier curve from Galsky et al and applying the Guyot algorithm. Figure 1 displays the Kaplan-Meier curve derived from these pseudo patient data, while Table 1 outlines the corresponding landmark probabilities, median survival times, and the hazard ratio for nivolumab versus placebo. 

The pseudo patient data produced survival estimates that were consistent with the original results reported by Galskey et al. The treatment effect estimate derived from these data closely matches the results presented in CHECKMATE-274 (HR = 0.52, 95% CI 0.35-0.78), Additionally, the recovered data closely predicts the landmark and median survival estimates from the study publication (48.4% and 42.7% for placebo at months 24 and 36, and 68.8% and 64.3% for nivolumab at months 24 and 36, respectively. Median survival was not reached for nivolumab and was reported as 17.9 months for placebo).

<!-- page 296 -->

The AF for nivolumab versus placebo was estimated using parametric survival models (Weibull, log-logistic, lognormal and generalised gamma) fitted to a data set containing both arms of CHECKMATE-274 and including a treatment covariate. This covariate represents the effect of nivolumab in decelerating the time to an event compared to placebo. 

Table 2 presents the estimated AF for nivolumab, and Figure 2 illustrates the fit of the AFT models to the Kaplan-Meier curves. An AF value of greater than one indicates that treatment would increase or improve the time to recurrence. An AF value of less than one indicates that treatment would decrease or worsen the time to recurrence.

The best fitting model according to AIC and BIC was the generalised gamma. Based on visual fit, this model failed to adequately predict the trial data as it appeared to systematically underestimate survival in the nivolumab arm and overestimate survival in the placebo arm. Among the fitted models, the generalised gamma predicted the lowest AF for nivolumab versus placebo of 2.61 [95% CI 1.60 – 4.26]. 




<!-- page 297 -->

With log-normal, log-logistic and Weibull, the AF’s ranged from XXXXXX, with the loglogistic AFT yielding the most conservative (and largest) estimate of the effect of nivolumab (AF= XXXXXXXXXXX). Of these models, the Weibull demonstrated the poorest visual fit to the Kaplan-Meier data, with log-normal and log-logistic providing a similar level of fit to the DMFS curve. During the earlier phases of follow-up, both the lognormal and log-logistic models tended to overestimate the survival of both arms. At later time points, the opposite trend was observed where the models tended to underestimate survival for both arms. Overall, these models displayed a similar pattern of overestimation and underestimation of survival in both arms, suggesting that their estimates of treatment effect (i.e., relative difference between arms) are unlikely to be systematically biased in favor of either arm. 

Due to time constraints, it was not possible to perform the ITC utilizing time-varying AFs for DMFS. Nevertheless, as observed in the ITCs for EFS and OS, implementing time-varying AFs had minimal impact on the outcomes and, when applied, generally resulted in a more conservative estimation of nivolumab's effect. 

Of the standard AFT models, the log-logistic was considered most suitable for the ITC as it provided the most optimistic and conservative estimate of treatment effect for nivolumab.

## **Counterfactual survival** 

The counterfactual arm was created using the control arm of NIAGARA and applying the AF of adjuvant nivolumab from CHECKMATE-274 to the ‘adjuvant period’ MFS survival times of patients eligible for treatment. 

- Eligibility for adjuvant nivolumab includes: 

Durvalumab with gemcitabine and cisplatin before surgery (neoadjuvant) then alone after surgery (adjuvant) for treating muscle-invasive bladder cancer [ID6168] 





<!-- page 299 -->

- underwent cystectomy and was disease-free (eligible for DFS in NIAGARA and CHECKMATE-274) 

- high risk MIBC based on staging criteria in CHECKMATE-274 

- PD-L1 tumour expression of at least 1% 

Figure 3 illustrates the proportion of patients eligible for treatment. In total, 73 patients (13.8%) were considered eligible for adjuvant nivolumab having undergone cystectomy, were disease-free at the adjuvant baseline visit, tested positive for tumour PD-L1 expression >1% and considered at a high risk of recurrence. Patients’ ineligible for adjuvant nivolumab include those who failed to undergo cystectomy, high risk patients with residual disease or with PD-L1 <1%, and patients with non-high risk MIBC (Table 3).

Figure 5 presents the Kaplan-Meier curves for adjuvant-MFS for G+C and G+C+N in the high-risk PD-L1 and other groups using the constant AF from the log-logistic model. 

As expected, the application of the AF for nivolumab to adjuvant-MFS in the eligible ‘high-risk’ PD-L1 cohort of NIAGARA led to improved outcomes, with adjuvant nivolumab increasing the time to distant metastatic disease (left panel). Patients with low risk or non-PD-L1 positive MIBC, and who are ineligible for adjuvant nivolumab, had the same outcomes across arms.

The Cox regression analysis comparing adjuvant nivolumab with no treatment in the high-risk PD-L1 subgroup yielded a hazard ratio of 0.40 (95% CI: 0.29 – 0.99), which is lower (and more favourable) than the corresponding DMFS hazard ratio in CHECKMATE-274 (0.52, 95% CI 0.35-0.78). This discrepancy may be due to several factors, including the use of a conservative estimate of the AF from the log-logistic model. The ITC may conservatively overestimate the effect of nivolumab. 

## **Indirect treatment comparison** 

Figure 6 presents the Kaplan-Meier plots of MFS for the D+G+C, G+C and G+C+N arms of NIAGARA, with and without the application of re-censoring. 

Without re-censoring, the survival times of the counterfactual arm extends beyond the follow-up of NIAGARA, due to the effect of nivolumab in extending (by a factor of 3.37) adjuvant-MFS times in the counterfactual arm. The application of re-censoring leads to similar follow-up across arms. 




<!-- page 303 -->

In both analyses, perioperative durvalumab led to improved MFS versus both control and counterfactual arms, with the curves separating and favoring perioperative durvalumab after the first 6 months of study follow-up.

<!-- page 310 -->

**==> picture [268 x 48] intentionally omitted <==**

There can be a considerable carer burden due to quality of life for the patient together with common negative side effects from existing treatments, frequency of hospital visits arising from this, resulting delays in planned surgery or uncertainty of any future treatment options and anxieties about recurrence. Our patient groups, our patient survey responses and patient support helpline enquiries all reflect these views and similar experiences for patients with this condition.  ABC UK are often asked by these patients (or a carer/family member) what else can be done – if there are other treatment options, or treatments which may have less adverse treatment effects than already undergone. **8. Is there an unmet need** There is significant, and urgent, unmet need for new treatments for those patients with MIBC.  Treatment options **for patients with this** for muscle invasive bladder cancer are limited and patient outcomes are poor. **condition?** 

Bladder cancer patients with MIBC will have high-grade tumours, these are difficult to treat and more likely to spread through the bladder wall and outside the bladder.  Immediate treatment is required, with as little delay as possible, and should be aggressive. 50% of MIIBC patients will progress to develop advanced disease. Cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by radical cystectomy is the current standard of care for MIBC, however, less than half of patients are candidates for this treatment.  Existing treatments can show high levels of lack of tolerability and adversely affect quality of life.   Patients often experience recurrence or spread of the disease. There's an urgent unmet need for treatments that demonstrate effectiveness in reducing recurrence and the current poor survival rate.  An effective treatment for MIBC, and a treatment which reduces the current high risk of recurrence, is vital as it represents the last chance for curing the patient before the disease progresses to advanced, metastatic bladder cancer. A point to note (particularly in the context of an appraisal for a potential new treatment for this patient group and any review of comparative treatments) is that a significant number of patients with MIBC will not receive definitive treatment.  Studies show that c50% of these patients will go untreated.  This may be due to tolerability of existing treatments, suitability for current treatments due to age, overall health and comorbidities etc. 

## **Planning treatment – the patient benefit** 

In the current treatment pathway for MIBC patients, there is limited scope to draw up a longer-term treatment plan to be at the point of diagnosis, which will encompass treatment before surgery, necessary major surgery, and treatment post surgery.  Treatment at the post surgery stage can be reactive. 

Therefore, an improvement in the management of MIBC is needed to improve outcomes and reduce recurrence in these patients.  There is an urgent need for alternative, effective, treatments for these patients.

## **Benefits of this treatment** 

Durvalumab may be used both before and after surgery to remove the bladder - neoadjuvantly with gemcitabine and cisplatin, and then as an adjuvant monotherapy. 

## **Benefits of earlier treatment decision:** 

The treatment decision for Durvalumab can be made upon diagnosis, pre-surgery. It is a major advantage for a patient, and improves the current uncertainty, to have a treatment plan made at an earlier stage, and before any major treatment or surgery starts.  Patients can better understand their treatment journey, and they (and their family) have an opportunity to plan their daily lives.  Currently, the patient has to endure waiting and assessing before a decision as to whether another treatment option is used or even possible.  This compares with the decision for Nivolumab treatment, which would usually be made post surgery. 

The ability to take a treatment decision to use Durvalumab at an earlier stage, has another major benefit in terms of not delaying other treatment.  If given neoadjuvant chemotherapy, the patient may suffer adverse side effects from the chemotherapy which may result in the surgery being delayed.  This consequent delay in surgery can then adversely affect the patient’s overall health, and influence any subsequent decision regarding treatment options post surgery.  Delayed surgery may result in poorer outcomes. 

There is an acute need for effective new treatments for MIBC.  The unmet need for this patient group, lack of treatments, the high percentage of patients who do not received definitive treatment, high level of recurrence and poor outcomes, and the high cost of current unsuccessful treatment are all key factors in the consideration of Durvalumab in the treatment pathway for MIBC.  The evidence for the use of Durvalumab in improving levels of recurrence and patient outcomes is compelling. 

## **Need for a new, effective, MIBC treatment** 

It is of note that in recent years a number of new drugs have been evaluated for advanced/metastatic bladder cancer.  ABC UK and bladder cancer patients now welcome this Appraisal for a treatment for Muscle Invasive

## **Other issues** 

**13. Are there any other issues that you would like the committee to consider?** 

## **Lack of effective existing treatments for bladder cancer, and supporting progress** 

There is lack of new treatments available in the UK for bladder cancer – a common cancer with poor outcomes and high recurrence rates. It is important that Durvalumab is viewed in that context.  There is concern amongst patients, patient groups and clinicians about the slow pace for new therapies to become widely available for use in treating bladder cancer in the UK, particularly in the context of the lack of effective treatment options available. 

The UK is now out of step with other countries, such as those within the EU, and has fallen behind in terms of effective treatments being made available for those with bladder cancer.  The term the ‘gold standard’ of treatment, which is sometimes used within these appraisals as a comparative terms, may no longer be an applicable term when applied to the treatment options for bladder cancer which are currently available for wide clinical use in the UK. 

Bladder cancer has been badly neglected in terms of research spend and in the development of much-needed new treatments, which is reflected in late diagnosis, high levels of recurrence, and poor outcomes – and has remained one of the most expensive cancers to treat.  Now that demonstrably effective new treatments are available for a disease with distressingly poor outcomes, it is of the utmost importance to patients that this welcome progress is not delayed, and that patients (and their clinicians) have access to these treatments to improve their outcomes.  Progress is long overdue. 

## **Quality of Life and health related benefits** 

It is of great importance to acknowledge, and for the committee to consider in depth, the direct impact on patients and patient well-being within this appraisal’s quality of life assessments. 

The effect on patients of access to new, innovative and effective treatments would be profound – with significant emotional and psychological benefits as well as the direct clinical benefit of improved survival and level of possible recurrence.  This is particularly important for MIBC patients who undergo highly impactful surgery and neoadjuvant chemotherapy treatment with uncertain outcomes regarding the likelihood of achieving a cure or reducing the risk of recurrence.

Access to such an effective, new treatment would bring hope to a group of patients where treatment options are very limited - bringing hope to patients and families, in very difficult circumstances, of a last opportunity for curative treatment, and also bringing the knowledge that a Durvalumab regimen has shown a reduction in recurrence risk. 

**Improvement in the burden of treatment** 

A new, effective treatment could have a significant impact in reducing the burden of disease for the patient and families: 

- Improving outcomes and levels of recurrence could result in a reduction in the number of hospital visits, and the negative impact on overall health and well-being due to adverse treatment side effects. 

- Having access to a new, effective, treatment will help patients and families to deal with the emotional burden of serious disease, maintaining hope, and providing a more positive emotional and mental state that could indirectly support a more positive outcome. 

- The possibility of disease progression that prevents surgery, and also of disease recurrence after surgery, are significant concerns for patients, which have a serious negative impact on subsequent prognosis and health-related quality of life. 

- Provides patients and families with the prospect of living longer, in a better state of heath, perhaps to see other developments to provide additional treatment options if required. 

## **Early treatment planning** 

- As Durvalumab supplies a perioperative treatment option currently not available, which would be considered after diagnosis, a longer term treatment plan is then able to be drawn up.  This would give patients and their families the opportunity to plan in advance, and plan their daily lives. 

- Having such a treatment plan, would alleviate some serious anxieties and uncertainties – patients and families could understand what is coming next (many patients contact ABC UK at this point as the uncertainty is the cause of much distress).

- This treatment planning at an earlier stage not only gives more clarity and information to the patient about future steps in their treatment, this approach reduces the negative emotional impact of delays and additional tests, and also receiving bad news after cystectomy surgery, which can often happens in the current treatment pathway.   Providing the potential for a direct improvement in the quality of care for those patients with MIBC. 

## **Economic Impact of current poor outcomes and recurrence levels** 

The availability of effective treatment options for this patient group facing poor outcomes is of pressing need, and has an urgency for the NHS.  Due to the high recurrence rate, and likelihood of progression, together with continuing monitoring, the lifetime treatment costs per patient of bladder cancer is very high compared to other cancers.  Bladder cancer is one of the most expensive cancers to treat.  Within the economic analysis section of this appraisal, it is imperative that due consideration and weight is given not just to the cost of this new treatment, but to the high on-going cost of continued and unsuccessful treatment for those with MIBC, and the high potential for progression to advanced disease. 

There is also a need for rapid action to consider and assimilate new advances in treatment of bladder cancer into the health system. 

**Future potential** : A point of wider interest which this appraisal should note is that, whilst the Durvalumab trial evidence being considered was concerned with those patients who had a cystectomy, c 50% of UK patients will currently have bladder preserving treatment, usually radiotherapy.  Trial results from the RAD-IO trial, show that Durvalumab can also be used in combination with radiotherapy with efficacy. Therefore, there is considerable potential for wider effective use of Durvalumab with those patients who will not receive cystectomy. 

**Guideline NG2** :  Note should be taken that Bladder cancer: diagnosis and management (2015) NICE guideline NG2 – is now over 10 years since publication in February 2015 (and reviewed evidence available to 2014). The Guideline does not adequately cover the introduction, evidence of efficacy and availability of new treatments for bladder cancer.

## **Advantages of the technology** 

|**9. What do patients or**<br>**carers think are the**<br>**advantages of the**<br>**technology?**|They are encouraged to think that there is something which could improve both survival and reduce recurrence.<br>They feel that the addition of durvalumab to give the hope of a better outcome would give them hope and relieve<br>some of the anxiety. “It would allow us to grab some of our life back, think ahead for a change”.<br>Many are encouraged to hear that durvalumab doesn’t dramatically increase harsh side-effects.<br>“Despite my husband’s post-op challenges, having immunotherapy post-surgery is something he would have<br>considered. He would have wanted clear and concise information about it before making a decision, but if he felt<br>the benefits outweighed the decision he would have said yes.<br>I would have supported him in whatever decision he made.”|
|---|---|



## **Disadvantages of the technology** 

|**10. What do patients or**<br>**carers think are the**<br>**disadvantages of the**<br>**technology?**|Their main concerns are on the burden of extra treatments, particularly the extra hospital visits before and<br>particularly after surgery. Some were concerned about the distance they had to travel, and wondering if they<br>would feel like it after surgery. “I’ve had so many procedures already, I will then have my “bag for life” and I’m<br>feeling “hospitalled out” already!”<br>Side effects and the unknown were a worry for some, they felt that less was known about what might happen, and<br>others didn’t know if the benefits would be worth it when balanced with any “risk of side-effects on top of<br>everything else”.<br>“Had chemo then RC last year, still cancer free. I was offered immunotherapy after but opted for close<br>observation. Since I was cancer free after the operation and it never made it to my lymph nodes, I felt it wasn’t<br>worth risking in case of side-effects.<br>If there would be a recurrence I would, of course, take or remove whatever is necessary to get rid of it again.”|
|---|---|

## **Patient population** 

|**11. Are there any groups of**<br>**patients who might benefit**<br>**more or less from the**<br>**technology than others? If**<br>**so, please describe them**<br>**and explain why.**|This technology would benefit patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer who are fit enough for cisplatin-based<br>chemotherapy, with people of different ages and sex having a similar benefit.<br>“After chemo I had an RC. My scan at one year showed cancer had metastasised to my lungs. I never imagined this<br>could happen in a year. I have heard of others who have been offered a course of immunotherapy after their RC as<br>a preventative measure, but this was never offered to me”<br>Those who are very elderly, or frail, or have bad kidney function may not be suitable for cisplatin, and therefore<br>wouldn’t be suitable for this, and would receive surgery without adjuvant treatments or radiotherapy as an<br>alternative|
|---|---|



## **Equality** 

|**12. Are there any potential**<br>**equality issues that should**<br>**be taken into account when**<br>**considering this condition**<br>**and the technology?**|Bladder cancer predominantly affects older people, potentially with comorbidities that mean cisplatin based<br>chemotherapy would not be suitable and so they would be excluded<br>Women with bladder cancer often have worse outcomes than men, are diagnosed later, and experience<br>differences in post-treatment issues. Both sexes have issues with sexual disfunction, but on top of the stigma<br>related to bladder cancer, men are even less likely to discuss their needs and symptoms.<br>There are socio-economic and geographical issues, people in deprived, or rural areas should be able to get the<br>treatment. These are the people who are more likely to be diagnosed later and have less options on their<br>procedures|
|---|---|

Are there any other**<br>**issues that you would like**<br>**the committee to consider?**|With the hope of new treatments improving survival rates, it is important that other supportive services are<br>improved. Currently patients report lack of help after their surgery, they need more help with their rehabilitation,<br>stoma care and continence issues. Few have counselling of any kind and most have no sexual counselling<br>before or after surgery. It is important to also consider the carers, as any treatment decision will of course affect<br>them too.<br>Understanding the treatment plan reduces anxiety, and educational resources with clear information about<br>durvalumab’s benefits and risks should be provided in patient-friendly language at the beginning of discussions<br>with patients and carers on this potential regimen<br>Patients should be told if they are also suitable for bladder sparing treatments|

|**16. In up to 5 bullet**<br>**points, please summarise**<br>**the key messages of your**<br>**submission.**|•<br>MIBC has high relapse rates, the addition of durvalumab to chemo could mean a real improvement in<br>survival and cure rates. and a relief from constant worry of a recurrence after surgery which may or may not<br>be treatable<br>•<br>With no significant increase in severe toxicity compared to chemo alone, patients hope that this could<br>lengthen their survival without imposing extra harsh side-effects<br>•<br>Patients feel that there is insufficient attention to quality of life after a radical cystectomy, and with advances<br>in treatments and the potential for a longer life, issues like mental and sexual health are often neglected<br>•<br>Patients and carers would like to know of their options, to understand the choices and have chance to<br>discuss bladder sparing treatments if they are suitable<br>•<br>All eligible patients, regardless of their location, should have access to the drug and the necessary supportive<br>care|

|**8. In your view, is there**<br>**an unmet need for**<br>**patients and healthcare**<br>**professionals in this**<br>**condition?**|Yes<br>Despite the use of neoadjuvant chemotherapy 5 year survival of patients with muscle invasive bladder cancer<br>remains on average at 50-60%. This has not changed substantially for over 20 years and there is need for better<br>treatments to reduce post radical therapy relapse and improve survival.<br>Reducing relapse would be expected to improve patient experience and HRQOl and reduce psychological<br>stress.<br>Improving responses also holds hope to change local treatment paradigms and reduce reliance on radical<br>surgery (cystectomy) and promote bladder preserving approaches.|

## **What is the expected place of the technology in current practice?** 

|**9. How is the condition**<br>**currently treated in the**<br>**NHS?**|Patients fit enough and with good renal function receive cisplatin and gemcitabine chemotherapy x 3-4 cycles<br>followed by radical cystectomy and chemo-radiotherapy.<br>Patients unable to receive initial cisplatin/gemcitabine receive local radical treatment and then considered for<br>adjuvant chemotherapy or nivolumab.<br>Patients with poor clinical response to neoadjuvant therapy who are PDL1 positive may receive adjuvant<br>nivolumab|
|---|---|
|**9a. Are any clinical**<br>**guidelines used in the**<br>**treatment of the condition,**<br>**and if so, which?**|NG2 NICE guideline (2015)<br>NICE Single technology assessment of adjuvant nivolumab.<br>ESMO and EAU guidelines are also influential.|
|**9b. Is the pathway of care**<br>**well defined? Does it vary**<br>**or are there differences of**<br>**opinion between**<br>**professionals across the**<br>**NHS? (Please state if your**<br>**experience is from outside**<br>**England.)**|Pathway is widely recommended and accepted but there is wide variation in the use of neoadjuvant and adjuvant<br>therapies with a few sites using little neoadjuvant therapy with wider use of adjuvant therapies.<br>The use of neoadjuvant therapy may vary according to patient fitness and renal function that may affect usage.|
|**9c. What impact would the**<br>**technology have on the**<br>**current pathway of care?**|The technology would replace neoadjuvant cisplatin/gemcitabine plus selective adjuvant nivolumab. It would<br>mean that most fit patients would receive immunotherapy for up to 1 year.|
|**10. Will the technology be**<br>**used (or is it already used)**<br>**in the same way as current**<br>**care in NHS clinical**<br>**practice?**|Yes with addition of weekly Durvulamab|
|**10a. How does healthcare**<br>**resource use differ**|After cystectomy/local treatment patients will receive 4 weekly Durvalumab so will require additional IV slots.<br>This is the same as if receiving adjuvant nivolumab which may have been used for a proportion of patients.|

## **Key messages** 

|**25. In up to 5 bullet**<br>**points, please summarise**<br>**the key messages of your**<br>**submission.**|•<br>Patients with locally muscle invasive bladder cancer continue to have poor (50-60%) long term survival with<br>little change over recent decades.<br>•<br>Neoadjuvant and adjuvant Durvalumab in combination with cisplatin and gemcitabine improves overall<br>survival in people with Muscle invasive bladder cancer.<br>•<br>Using neoadjuvant durvalumab improves access for people with MIBC and will allow more secure and<br>equitable access to immunotherapy which will allow a broader range of people to benefit from this<br>technology.<br>•<br>The treatment is reported to be well tolerated by people with limited increase in toxicity.<br>•<br>Oncologists are familiar with technology and can be applied with limited training.|
|---|---|

## Clinical expert statement 

Durvalumab with gemcitabine and cisplatin before surgery (neoadjuvant) then alone after surgery (adjuvant) for treating muscleinvasive bladder cancer [ID6168] 6 of 13 



<!-- page 352 -->

**==> picture [268 x 48] intentionally omitted <==**

**==> picture [298 x 382] intentionally omitted <==**

- Pathological complete responses (pCRs) were more likely among patients who received durvalumab (37.3% compared with 27.5%), but benefit with durvalumab was seen both in patients who did and did not achieve a pCR. 

- • The addition of perioperative durvalumab to neoadjuvant chemotherapy significantly improves outcomes including event-free, metastasis-free, and overall survival (OS) in patients with MIBC. (Powles, Catto, Galsky et al NEJM, 2024) 

In summary, The **NIAGARA trial** represents a pivotal advance in the management of muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC), establishing the role of perioperative immunotherapy in improving long-term outcomes. In this large, international phase III study, the addition of **durvalumab** to standard cisplatinbased neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by adjuvant durvalumab led to **transformative clinical benefits** . The trial demonstrated a **significant improvement in event-free survival** (HR 0.68), along with marked increased **overall survival** (HR 0.75). End -points of **pathological complete response rates** , **metastasis-free survival significantly improved as well favouring the experimental arm.** 

These results provide compelling evidence that early integration of immune checkpoint inhibition into the curative treatment pathway enhances both systemic disease control and local tumour eradication. The NIAGARA data redefine the standard of care for organ-confined MIBC, offering the potential to **increase cure rates, delay or prevent relapse, and extend overall survival** for a broader population of patients. The findings are both **clinically and statistically significant** , underscoring the value of durvalumab as a key component of perioperative therapy in this disease.

## **Part 2: Key messages** 

In up to 5 sentences, please summarise the key messages of your statement: 

Bringing immune check point inhibitor durvalumab in earlier disease setting as neo-adjuvant treatment in combination with 

chemotherapy improves event free survival, pathological complete response, metastases free survival and over-all survival compared to chemotherapy alone. 

These gains are transformative and by improving cure rate will reduce the burden of palliative systemic treatments. Addition of durvalumab to chemotherapy was well tolerated 

Benefit was seen across the various subgroups. The immunotherapy agent improves outcomes both in patients who do and do not achieve a pCR. 

Quality of life is well maintained with the addition of durvalumab as perioperative treatment. 

Thank you for your time. 

Professor Syed A Hussain, MBBS, MSc, MD, FRCP, Professor of Medical Oncology, University of Sheffield, & Sheffield Teaching Hospitals, Sheffield, South Yorkshire, United Kingdom. 

Past Member: NCRI Bladder and renal group 

Past Chair: NCRI Advanced Bladder cancer sub-group

What is your experience of living with muscle-**<br>**invasive bladder cancer ?**<br>**If you are a carer (for someone with muscle-invasive**<br>**bladder cancer ) please share your experience of**<br>**caring for them**|I was diagnosed with high grade Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer G3pT2 TCC in<br>May 2020 during the pandemic.<br>I had one TURBT followed by three cycles of Gemcitabine and Cisplatin<br>chemotherapy prior to my robotically assisted Radical Cystectomy (bladder<br>removal). At the same time of my bladder removal, I also had a full hysterectomy,<br>partial vaginal removal and 41 lymph nodes removed. The surgery took 6 hours.<br>I now live with a stoma and Urostomy bag. I have had regular check ups (blood<br>tests and CT scans) as one of my lymph nodes had cancer present.<br>My diagnosis had a huge impact on my well-being. As well as the shock of<br>receiving a Cancer diagnosis I also had to cope with the knowledge I was not able<br>to be accompanied by my husband at any of my hospital appointments, scans and<br>surgery due to Covid restrictions. I felt completely isolated and extremely low during<br>the 9 days I was in hospital post my Radical Cystectomy trying to recover and adapt<br>to a new way of life. I have worked hard to overcome any mental health issues I<br>had but this is still difficult to control as the date of results of checks and scans<br>approach.<br>Living with and adapting to having a stoma was daunting in the beginning. Over<br>time I have adapted and manage my daily life well, but it has taken a long time to<br>get where I am today.|

If there are disadvantages for patients of current**<br>**NHS treatments for muscle-invasive bladder cancer**<br>**(for example, how they are given or taken, side effects**<br>**of treatment, and any others) please describe these**|Side effects of chemotherapy were harsh at times. Swollen red face, fatigue,<br>stomach cramps, nausea. I have been left with Neuropathy in my left foot despite<br>my last cycle of chemotherapy being 5 years ago. Sometimes the tingling is minimal<br>and other times it feels like I am being stabbed in the foot with hot needles. It has<br>never stopped. I have learned to live with it and the benefits of having the<br>chemotherapy treatment outweighs what I now live with. I was not able to work<br>during the cycles of chemotherapy and I was very aware that I was at risk of<br>catching Covid due to my immune system being supressed. My treatment took<br>place before the vaccine was available.<br>The knowledge I underwent chemotherapy to give myself a better outcome helps<br>with my anxiety and emotional well being about a recurrence happening.|

To<br>have a good quality of life with a potentially longer life expectancy cannot be<br>underestimated. Having an additional treatment after surgery may help reduce the<br>risk of recurrence, which is one of my greatest fears.<br>Having the new treatment could provide reassurance and peace of mind that<br>something more is being done.|

## **1 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY** 

This summary provides a brief overview of the key issues identified by the external assessment group (EAG) as being potentially important for decision making. It also includes the EAG’s preferred assumptions and the resulting incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs). 

Section 1.1 provides an overview of the key issues. Section 1.2 provides an overview of key model outcomes and the modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER. Section 1.3 explains the key issues in more detail. Secondary issues and modelling errors identified by the EAG are explored in sections 1.4 and 1.5. Background information on the condition, technology and evidence, and non-key issues are presented in later sections of the EAG report. 

All issues identified represent the EAG’s view, not the opinion of NICE. 

## _**1.1 Overview of the EAG’s key issues**_ 

**Table 1 Summary of key issues** 

|**ID6168**|**Summary of issue**|**Impact on results**|**Report**<br>**sections**|
|---|---|---|---|
|1|Uncertainty in the relative effectiveness of<br>perioperative durvalumab when the<br>comparator includes adjuvant nivolumab|Unknown|3.4, 3.5|
|2|Extrapolation of immature data|Low for EFS and<br>MFS. High for OS.|3.2, 4.2.5.2|
|3|Model selection for the extrapolation of OS|High|4.2.5.2|
|4|Startingage of modelled cohort|High|3.2.4, 4.2.5.2|
|5|Increased risk of non-cancer-related death|High|4.2.5.2|



The key differences between the company’s preferred assumptions and the EAG’s preferred assumptions are: 

- The EAG considers the relevant comparator to be neoadjuvant chemotherapy and radical cystectomy (RC), followed by no treatment or adjuvant nivolumab in eligible patients. 

- The OS extrapolations are informed by the best fitting flexible spline models for each arm: for perioperative durvalumab this is the 1-knot spline odds and for the control arm this is the 1- knot spline hazard. This contrasts with the company’s standard parametric models, with the Gompertz distribution selected for the perioperative durvalumab arm and the log-logistic distribution for the control arm. 

- Subsequent treatments post-recurrence excludes nivolumab (nivolumab is not licensed as a treatment for recurrent/metastatic MIBC), which is included in the company’s base case. 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 395 -->

- The EAG includes the cost of PD-L1 testing when the comparator arm includes adjuvant nivolumab. 

The EAG identified other uncertainties, which the EAG is unable to resolve based on the data currently available. These are described further in the sections below. 

## _**1.2 Overview of key model outcomes**_ 

NICE technology appraisals compare how much a new technology improves length (overall survival) and quality of life in a quality-adjusted life year (QALY). An ICER is the ratio of the extra cost for every QALY gained. 

Overall, the technology is modelled to affect QALYs by: 

- Increasing the proportion of patients who are alive (improvement in OS), event-free and metastasis-free (which is associated with improved health-related quality of life) over time relative to neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy alone. 

Overall, the technology is modelled to affect costs by: 

- Additional drug acquisition and administration costs associated with durvalumab compared to neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy alone 

- Lower costs associated with reduced disease progression and subsequent therapy and terminal care costs from improved event-free and metastasis-free survival for durvalumab. 

The modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER are: 

- Model selection for the extrapolation of OS in the comparator arm 

- The starting age of the modelled cohort 

- Increased risk of non-cancer-related death.

## _**1.5 Company’s modelling errors identified by the EAG**_ 

The EAG reviewed the company’s model in detail and applied the TECHnical VERification (TECHVER) checklist (see Appendix 3)[1] . The EAG corrected the following modelling errors: 

1. The extrapolated MFS curve picked up the extrapolated EFS curve at the point of crossing, while the CS states that ‘ _EFS is constrained to values that are less than or equal to MFS’_ . The EAG corrected this error such that the EFS curve picked up the MFS curve at the point of crossing. 

2. Calculation formulae in the model workbook, with details provided in Section 5.2.1. 

## _**1.6 Summary of EAG’s preferred assumptions and resulting ICER**_ 

As discussed in key issue 1, the EAG considers the relevant comparator to be neoadjuvant chemotherapy and RC, followed by no treatment or adjuvant nivolumab in eligible patients. The comparator with adjuvant nivolumab was excluded from the company’s base case but included as a separate scenario. Therefore, the EAG presents two base cases: 

- (i) EAG base case 1 with the same comparator as the company’s base case (i.e., without adjuvant nivolumab); and 

- (ii) EAG base case 2 with comparator consisting of neoadjuvant chemotherapy and RC, followed by no treatment or adjuvant nivolumab in eligible patients.

## **2 BACKGROUND** 

This report critiques the company submission for durvalumab with gemcitabine and cisplatin before surgery (neoadjuvant) then alone after radical cystectomy (adjuvant) for treating patients with resectable muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). This regimen is also referred to as ‘perioperative durvalumab’. 

The company received marketing authorisation for perioperative durvalumab for this indication from the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (UK MHRA) in August 2025 after approval by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in February 2025 and the US Food & Drug Administration (FDA) in March 2025.[2, 3] 

## _**2.1 Critique of the company’s description of underlying health problem**_ 

The company provides a clear description of bladder cancer, including the clinical presentation and the diagnosis and staging of MIBC. The company submission Document B (CS) briefly describes the epidemiology and burden of disease, mostly relating to bladder cancer generally. It highlights the burden of disease for patients, which is marked by pain, psychological distress, and limitations on daily life and routines. One of the EAG’s clinical advisers similarly stressed that MIBC is a type of cancer which presents with symptoms which significantly affect quality of life before, during, and after treatments. 

## **2.1.1 Muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC)** 

The company estimate that MIBC, which are primarily urothelial carcinomas, account for approximately 25% of bladder cancer cases. The most recent NHS data freely available online, recorded between 2013 and 2019, showed 20.4% of bladder cancer patients to have MIBC.[4] 

Clinical staging of MIBC is based on the Tumour-Node-Metastasis (TNM) classification, which is summarised in Table 4 (based on CS pp. 19-20). Stages relevant to this appraisal are T2-T4a in combination with N0 (no lymph node involvement) or N1 (metastasis in one lymph node) and M0 (no distant metastasis).[5] 

**Table 4 Tumour-Node-Metastasis (TNM) classification[5]** 

|**Stage**|**Explanation**|**Categories**|
|---|---|---|
|T (tumour)|Depth of invasion of the primary tumour|1 invasion of subepithelial connective tissue<br>2 muscle invasion<br>3 invasion of perivesical tissue<br>4 invasion of adjacent tissues|

<!-- page 403 -->

|**Stage**|**Explanation**|**Categories**|
|---|---|---|
|N (node)|Number and location of infected lymph nodes|0 no lymph node involvement<br>1 metastasis in one lymph node<br>2 metastases in multiple regional lymph nodes<br>3 metastases in iliac lymph node(s)|
|M (metastasis)|Presence of distant metastasis|0 no distant metastasis<br>1 distant metastasis|



In a clarification question to the company (A2), the EAG asked for further information on the demography of patients with MIBC eligible for radical cystectomy (RC) in the UK. The company provided some additional comments on the data collected in the 2022 British Association of Urological Surgeons (BAUS) audit of Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer at Transurethral Resection of Bladder (MITRE),[6] but no further data on the characteristics of patients with MIBC eligible for RC in the UK. 

Data from the 2022 BAUS MITRE audit[6] includes a total of 641 complete data records across 98 UK hospitals submitted in the first quarter of 2019. Most of the population (81.2%) had no distant metastasis and no or limited nodal involvement (stage N0/M0 or N1/M0). The mean age of patients with MIBC was 76 (range 35-104). The company commented in the response to clarification question A2 that the MITRE data set concerns a broader population than the population in scope for this appraisal, and that the broader population of patients with MIBC is generally older and less fit than those eligible for neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Only 46 out of 641 patients (7.2%) in the MITRE dataset received neoadjuvant chemotherapy prior to cystectomy.[6] 

A study by John et al. (2021) reported on NHS data from 2016 on non-metastatic MIBC.[7] Of all patients with stage T2-4 non-metastatic MIBC, 8.7% received neoadjuvant chemotherapy and cystectomy. The median age of patients was 76, but this varied by type of treatment. Patients who received neoadjuvant chemotherapy and RC had a median age of 67 (9% of patients), compared to a median age of 80 for patients who had radiotherapy without neoadjuvant treatment (15%). However, no age data were available specifically for the population in the NICE scope (resectable MIBC, cisplatin eligible). 

The EAG requested information from NHS England on the characteristics of UK patients with resectable MIBC who receive neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy, as these patients would be eligible for perioperative durvalumab. NHS England shared that, in the Northeast of England, patients are on average 66 years old. The period of data collection is unknown, and it is not certain that the mean age of patients in the Northeast is representative of the national population. 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 404 -->

In conclusion, the group of patients with MIBC in scope for this appraisal have resectable MIBC and are eligible to receive gemcitabine and cisplatin (T2N0/1M0 to T4aN0/1M0) (Section 2.3). This is a subset of all MIBC patients, and this subset is younger and fitter than the broader population of patients with MIBC. There is a lack of published evidence on the characteristics of the population in the scope, and it is therefore difficult to provide an accurate and detailed overview of the demographics of this population in the NHS. 

_2.1.1.1 Survival rates of patients with MIBC_ 

Survival rates of patients with MIBC are not explicitly discussed in the background section of the CS, but an overview of evidence from various trials and other sources is provided by the company in Table 40, p. 128. These data are difficult to interpret, given the range of data sources, countries and period of data collection. The oldest included trials with data collection completed before the year 2000, predating the introduction of neoadjuvant chemotherapy for MIBC.[8] The EAG has supplemented these data with additional sources of information, prioritising more recent and UK/European real-world evidence identified through a pragmatic search of the literature (Table 5). 

One of the EAG’s clinical advisers indicated that survival rates observed in clinical practice are significantly lower than in clinical trials, regardless of the type of treatment. Using NHS data, Catto et al (2023) estimated a five-year survival rate of 24.1% for patients with urothelial MIBC between the years of 2013 and 2019, although they did not provide estimates for the population in the NICE scope (resectable MIBC, cisplatin eligible).[4] 

The National Disease Registration Service (NDRS) dataset from 2013 recorded an overall 5-year survival rate of 34.3%, based on 3290 patients with local (T2, N0, M0) or locally advanced (T3/T4a or N1-N3) urothelial MIBC (Table 5).[9] There were marked differences in 5-year survival between men (48.0%) and women (36.9%).

## _**2.2 Critique of the company’s overview of current service provision**_ 

The CS shows the current clinical pathway for resectable MIBC in the UK in Figure 1 (p. 24). Clinical advice to the EAG confirmed that the diagram is an accurate illustration of NHS practice and is aligned with the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Clinical Practice Guideline for diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up, and European Association of Urology (EAU) Guidelines on Muscle-Invasive and Metastatic Bladder Cancer. The pathway illustrated in the diagram (CS Figure 1, p. 24) is split between the neoadjuvant treatment phase, prior to RC, and the adjuvant phase after RC. The current standard of care for patients eligible to receive neoadjuvant chemotherapy is gemcitabine plus cisplatin. Clinical advice to the EAG was that radiotherapy is also a treatment option for this patient population, which is omitted from the company’s representation of the treatment pathway. Radiotherapy can be offered to patients for whom treatment with neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) is unsuitable, or as an alternative to RC for patients for whom NAC is suitable. It is therefore not a comparator for perioperative durvalumab, and not relevant to the decision problem for this appraisal. 

## **2.2.1 Current neoadjuvant treatment** 

As shown in Figure 1 (CS p. 24), patients who are fit enough will be offered neoadjuvant gemcitabine plus cisplatin, which is referred to as NAC in this report. Clinical advice to the EAG is that, after 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 407 -->

assessment of fitness, comorbidities, performance status, and renal function, around 70% of patients will be eligible to receive NAC. Most patients will then undergo a RC; a surgical procedure in which the bladder and any surrounding tissue affected by the tumour are removed. A small proportion of patients may not initially be eligible to proceed to RC but may become eligible after receiving cisplatin-based therapy. 

The BAUS MITRE audit found that cystectomy was performed in 20.9% of patients with MIBC, and 38.7% of this group received NAC. Catto et al. reported treatment choices for 23,373 patients with urothelial MIBC from 2013 to 2019 and found that 23.7% of patients received RC.[4] 

## **2.2.2 Current adjuvant treatment** 

The current clinical pathway (CS Figure 1, p. 24) has multiple options for adjuvant treatment, depending on whether patients are at high or low risk of recurrence, and whether they are suitable to receive adjuvant chemotherapy therapy if at high risk of recurrence. 

Post-surgery, MIBC is considered at high risk of recurrence if classed as pathological stage T3 (invasion into perivesical tissues), T4a (invasion into adjacent structures), or N+ (lymph node involvement) (see also Section 2.1.1).[15] Patients considered at low risk of recurrence after RC will receive ‘best supportive care’ (BSC) (CS Figure 1, p. 24). Clinical advisers to the EAG clarified that BSC after a RC includes stoma care follow-up, clinical review and testing of renal function, and scans at 6, 12, and 24 months as a minimum, and annually thereafter for five years. 

Patients considered at high risk of recurrence may receive BSC, or adjuvant chemotherapy (gemcitabine plus cisplatin) if they did not receive NAC. In addition, nivolumab was recommended by NICE in 2022[15] for adjuvant treatment of muscle-invasive urothelial cancer in adults if 

- Programmed Cell Death Ligand 1 (PD-L1) is expressed at a level of 1% or above, also described as ‘PD-L1 positive’, and 

- Adjuvant treatment with platinum-based chemotherapy is unsuitable, and 

- The cancer is at high risk of recurrence. 

If patients considered high risk in a post-surgery assessment, PD-L1 testing is undertaken to determine suitability for adjuvant nivolumab. 

## _**2.3 Critique of company’s definition of decision problem**_ 

The company’s decision problem is largely in line with the NICE scope. Deviations from the NICE scope are justified and considered acceptable by the EAG, see Table 6 for details.

## **3 CLINICAL EFFECTIVENESS** 

This section presents a summary and critique of the clinical-effectiveness evidence included in the company’s submission. Section 3.1 focuses on the company’s review of clinical and safety evidence. Sections 3.2 to 3.3 provide a critique of the included studies and clinical-effectiveness analyses. Sections 3.4 to 3.5 critique any indirect comparisons presented by the company. 

## _**3.1 Critique of the methods of review**_ 

The company conducted a systematic literature review (SLR) to identify clinical evidence on treating MIBC in adults. Overall, an adequate range of relevant databases were searched alongside a good range of conference proceedings, grey literature sources and trials registries. The reporting of the searches was mainly clear and the structure of the search, its limits and filters were appropriate. The search terms could have been more comprehensive. The EAG is not aware that relevant evidence was missed, although it is unable to verify this systematically due to time constraints. 

The original company submission included searches to identify clinical evidence for treating MIBC in adults. A description of the searches and the search strategies were included in Appendix B (pp. 1-41). In response to the EAG’s clarification questions C1-C7, the company provided additional information. 

The EAG’s appraisal of evidence identification can be found in Table 32, Appendix 1. 

## **3.1.1 Inclusion criteria** 

The eligibility criteria for identifying relevant clinical evidence in the SLR were presented in CS Appendix B Table 1. These criteria were broadly appropriate to address the decision problem. Adults with untreated (first-line, 1L) muscle-invasive urothelial cancer (MIUC) or MIBC (≥ 75% bladder cancer), including those receiving adjuvant therapy after prior neoadjuvant therapy, were eligible for inclusion. A wide range of intervention treatments were considered eligible as monotherapy or in combination, including various chemotherapy regimens, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and combination therapies, administered in either the neoadjuvant or adjuvant setting. There was no requirement to limit treatments to a specific perioperative phase, and receipt of RC was also not required for study inclusion. Comparators included any treatment or placebo and only Phase II–IV RCTs published in English were included. 

## **3.1.2 Critique of study selection and data extraction** 

Study selection was performed independently by two reviewers against pre-specified eligibility criteria at both the title/abstract and full-text stages. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or by a third reviewer. Data extraction was done by one reviewer and checked by another. 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 413 -->

The EAG believes that the study selection process was methodologically sound and well-documented. The exclusions were appropriate based on study design, intervention, population, and relevance of outcomes to the PICOS (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes, Study design) criteria. 

## **3.1.3 Quality assessment** 

RCTs included for data extraction were assessed using the RoB 2 tool.[16] One reviewer used the checklist to independently assess the quality of the included studies, and a second reviewer checked their assessment. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or by involving a third reviewer. Risk of bias was assessed by outcome as per Cochrane guidance, mainly for overall survival (OS), event-free survival (EFS), and pathological complete response (pCR). In a few cases, risk of bias varied across different outcomes within the same study. The EAG’s assessment of the NIAGARA trial is reported in Section 3.2.2. 

## **3.1.4 Evidence synthesis** 

Because only one relevant trial (NIAGARA) evaluating perioperative durvalumab for the treatment of patients with resectable MIBC was identified, a meta-analysis of effectiveness outcomes was not conducted. Instead, a narrative synthesis of effectiveness and safety outcomes was provided (CS Appendix B, Section B.1.8.3) for 58 studies, including two perioperative studies, 27 neoadjuvant studies, 14 adjuvant studies, and 15 studies that evaluated other treatment settings. 

A standard indirect comparison of perioperative durvalumab with adjuvant nivolumab was not feasible due to differences in the control arms, timing of randomisation, and the inclusion criteria. Therefore, an alternative ‘survival time-adjusted ITC’ was conducted, which is discussed in sections 3.4 and 3.5. 

## _**3.2 Critique of the methods of the trials of the technology of interest**_ 

## **3.2.1 Study design** 

The NIAGARA trial (NCT03732677) is an ongoing phase 3, randomised, open label, multicentre study to examine the efficacy and safety of perioperative durvalumab in patients with MIBC. The trial evaluated neoadjuvant durvalumab in combination with gemcitabine and cisplatin, followed by adjuvant durvalumab monotherapy (intervention arm), compared neoadjuvant gemcitabine and cisplatin with no adjuvant therapy (control arm). A total of 1,063 patients were randomised in a 1:1 ratio and included in the intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis. The dual primary endpoints of the trial were EFS and pCR, both assessed by blinded independent central review (BICR). ## **3.2.2 Critical appraisal** 

The company presented two quality assessments of the NIAGARA trial. One assessment focused on NIAGARA alone using a tool adapted from CRD’s guidance, presented in section 2.5 of the CS. The second was conducted using the RoB 2 tool and included NIAGARA alongside the other 57 studies identified from the SLR in CS Appendix B. The company concluded that NIAGARA was at low risk of bias. 

The EAG performed its own assessment of NIAGARA based on CRD guidance as shown in Table 9. The EAG agrees that the methodology of NIAGARA appears generally robust and to have minimised the risk of most biases. However, NIAGARA is an open-label study, which may introduce bias, particularly through patient expectations or differential drop-out. Clinical advisers acknowledged that patients are likely to prefer durvalumab plus NAC over NAC alone. However, they consider it unlikely this will bias results. In response to clarification question A1, the company stated that potential bias was mitigated through BICR of primary endpoints (pCR, EFS) and a sponsor-blinded data management process. Completion of neoadjuvant therapy was similar between arms (78.7% for the durvalumab arm vs 74.0% for the control arm), as were rates of proceeding to cystectomy and discontinuation for patient decision, suggesting the open-label design did not materially affect treatment uptake, surgical intervention, or retention. Overall, the EAG agrees that the risk that the risk 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 418 -->

of bias from the open-label design of NIAGARA is low. However, the lack of participant blinding means that HRQoL, which relies on self-reported information, is at high risk of bias.

## **3.2.3 Baseline characteristics of NIAGARA participants** 

Baseline characteristics of participants included in NIAGARA are presented in CS Table 7 (pp. 4041). Characteristics were broadly comparable between the perioperative durvalumab (durvalumab + gemcitabine + cisplatin, D+G+C) and control (G+C) arms. The median age was 65 years, 82% were male, 67% were White, and 73% had high PD-L1 expression. Most patients had ECOG PS 0 (78%), adequate renal function (81%), and tumour stage > T2N0 (60%). The trial population had numerically higher proportion of smokers in the control arm, but clinical advisers did not consider this to affect prognosis or treatment efficacy.

## **3.2.4 Applicability of the NIAGARA results to the NHS setting** 

The NIAGARA trial included four UK centres out of 168 global sites. The countries with the most sites were Japan (20), America (14), Brazil (12), Germany (12) and Poland (10). 

A limitation to the applicability of the NIAGARA trial results to the NHS setting is the control arm, which does not capture the potential use of adjuvant nivolumab after NAC and RC in PD-L1 positive patients at high-risk of recurrence after RC. In addition, there is uncertainty about the applicability of the demographics of the NIAGARA trial participants to the NHS population eligible for treatment with perioperative durvalumab. 

Firstly, in NHS practice, a subset of patients who undergo RC and are at high risk of recurrence with PD-L1 positive tumours are offered adjuvant nivolumab, in line with current NICE guidance. This option was not available in the NIAGARA control arm, where patients received no adjuvant therapy. Nivolumab for adjuvant treatment of invasive urothelial cancer at high risk of recurrence and PD-L1 positive was recommended by NICE in August 2022, and recruitment for NIAGARA finished in July 2021.[18] In response to a clarification request from the EAG (question A8), the company reported that just xxxx patients in the control arm received nivolumab as subsequent therapy following trial therapy discontinuation. Consequently, the control arm of the NIAGARA trial does not reflect current NHS practice, in which a proportion of patients at high risk of recurrence are eligible for nivolumab after RC. However, in response to an EAG request, communication from NHS England indicated that only 5-10% of post-RC patients in the NHS would be eligible for adjuvant nivolumab with only 7-8 patients per month starting this regimen in England. 

Secondly, as discussed in Section 2.1.1, there is a lack of published evidence on the characteristics of patients with MIBC who are eligible for NAC and RC. The average age of participants in the NIAGARA trial was 64.4 years (SD 8.94), and 81.8% were male (18.2% female), which was comparable across arms. One clinical adviser to the EAG noted that although the trial population was considered broadly representative of patients undergoing RC, patients treated in UK clinical practice tend to be slightly older. One of the company’s clinical advisers similarly stated that the median baseline age in the trial was younger than the typical UK patient, estimated to be 70 years old.[19] 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 420 -->

Based on information from the Systemic Anti-Cancer Therapy (SACT) data set and BAUS MITRE audit[6] one of the EAG’s clinical advisers suggested a median age closer to 70–76 years for MIBC patients. The EAG agrees with the company that the BAUS MITRE audit reports on a broader MIBC population than the population in scope, and that this general population can be expected to be older and less fit than patients eligible for NAC and RC (see clarification response A2). 

The EAG notes that the target population of patients eligible for perioperative durvalumab represents a very small proportion of the overall UK MIBC population. In response to an EAG request, communication from NHS England indicated that, patients with resectable MIBC receiving neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy have a mean age of 66 years with 75% being male. These figures are broadly consistent with the NIAGARA trial population (mean age 64.4 years; 81.8% male). However, the NHS England estimates were from data in the Northeast of England only, with the reporting period and patient numbers not specified, which raises uncertainty about applicability to the wider NHS setting. 

The extent to which the NIAGARA trial population reflects the NHS population is therefore uncertain. This uncertainty is also relevant to the company’s economic model (Section 4.2.5.2), because the modelled baseline age has an impact on the cost-effectiveness results. Given the potential implications for cost-effectiveness estimates, the EAG considers this a key issue. 

## **3.2.5 Patient disposition** 

Patient disposition in the NIAGARA trial is summarised in Table 6 and Figure 3 in CS appendix B. A total of 1,063 patients were randomised in the NIAGARA trial between 16 November 2018 and 23 August 2021, with 533 assigned to the perioperative durvalumab arm and 530 to the control arm. Nearly all patients (99%) received the allocated study treatment. Of these, 78.7% in the durvalumab arm and 74.0% in the control arm completed neoadjuvant treatment. 

Neoadjuvant treatment was discontinued for 21.3% of patients in the durvalumab arm and 26% in the control arm. The most common reason in both arms was adverse events (15.5% in the durvalumab arm and 15.2% in the control arm). In response to clarification question A4a, the company stated discontinuation of neoadjuvant therapy did not necessarily preclude patients from undergoing RC. In the durvalumab arm, 88% underwent RC compared with 83.2% in the control arm. 

Of those in the durvalumab arm who had surgery, 72.3% initiated adjuvant durvalumab with 53.8% completing all eight cycles. Nineteen percent of patients who had surgery did not start adjuvant treatment. The company identified reasons in a subset of these patients: permanent discontinuation of durvalumab during the neoadjuvant phase without reinitiation (n=19), post-surgical death due to 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 421 -->

adverse events (n=14), or post-surgical disease progression (n=9). No specific reason was recorded for the remainder. 

A small number of participants in the durvalumab arm (n=6; 1.1%) entered a non-cystectomy extension phase during which they received durvalumab 1500 mg as monotherapy every 28 days for a maximum of eight doses. Participants could enter the non-cystectomy extension phase if they refused RC at the specified time after achieving a complete clinical response and without additional interventions. Participants in this group were included in the ITT population for survival outcomes, HRQoL, and safety analyses. 

Clinical advisers to the EAG considered the rates of treatment completion, discontinuation, and surgical uptake to be consistent with clinical expectations in the NHS. They noted that three to four cycles of NAC are standard in practice, with early discontinuation in patients experiencing renal decline, neuropathy, or bladder-related complications. Clinical advisers also noted that such patients often remain operable and may still be eligible for adjuvant immunotherapy such as nivolumab. Overall, patient flow and retention were broadly comparable between arms, with no major imbalances that would limit the interpretation of trial results. 

## _**3.3 Critique of the results of the trials of the technology of interest**_ 

## **3.3.1 Efficacy** 

## _3.3.1.1 Overview of NIAGARA efficacy endpoints_ 

The company report results for the ITT population for the primary outcomes EFS evaluated by blinded independent central review (BICR) and pCR evaluated by blinded central pathology review (BCPR), and a range of secondary and exploratory outcomes (Table 7). 

The latest data cut-off (DCO) was 29[th] of April 2024. At this time, 433 EFS events and 305 OS events had been recorded. Data on pCR from the first DCO (14 January 2022) was re-analysed following the discovery of a mistake in the earlier calculations. Post-hoc analyses were conducted for EORTC QLQ-C30 and EQ-5D-5L to correct for a programming error leading to missing data. 

Further analyses are planned when the EFS data have reached 451 events (43% maturity), and when the OS data have reached 428 events (41% maturity) across arms (CS Table 11, pp. 44-45).

## _**Proportion of patients undergoing RC**_ 

A numerically greater proportion of patients in the durvalumab arm underwent RC (Table 10), although the difference was not statistically significant. The EAG’s clinical advisers judged the proportion of patients not receiving RC (12% in durvalumab arm, 16.8% in the control arm) to be representative of clinical practice. See Section 3.2.5 for details on the trial participant flowchart. 

## _**EFS**_ 

EFS is longer for participants in the durvalumab arm compared to participants in the control arm (Table 10), with median EFS reached in the control arm but not in the durvalumab arm. 

Kaplan Meier (KM) curves for the two trial arms separate prior to the RC, from two months after randomisation in the neoadjuvant treatment phase (CS Figure 5, p. 51). The company argue this implies a noticeable benefit of durvalumab in the neoadjuvant period (CS p. 50). However, as shown in Table 7, EFS events include time to recurrence, progression or death, and time to expected surgery for patients who do not proceed to RC. Information provided in the CSR and shown in Table 11 

shows xxxxxxxxx in progression prior to RC, but a xxxxxxxxxx of patients with residual disease not proceeding to RC in the control arm (CSR Table 23, p. 106). Reasons for not proceeding with surgery include patient decision, unfit for surgery, death, and study discontinuation (CS Table 6, p. 38). It is not clear that the difference in refusal or failure to undergo RC in patients with residual disease can be explained by differential efficacy of the study treatments.

Median MFS was also not reached at the April 2024 DCO. The hazard ratio showed a benefit of durvalumab compared to neoadjuvant gemcitabine plus cisplatin (Table 10). The KM plot shows a sustained difference in the probability of MFS from around 6 months onwards (CS Figure 9, p. 59). ## _**OS**_ 

Median OS was not reached for either trial arm, with 71.1% of participants in the durvalumab arm and 62.8% of patients in the control arm still alive and in follow-up at the time of the April 2024 DCO (Table 10). KM curves diverge from approximately 6 months after randomisation (CS Figure 7, p. 55), showing a greater survival rate for durvalumab compared to the control arm. Five-year OS was a prespecified endpoint and is reported separately in the CS (p.55). However, the immaturity of the OS data, and high rates of censoring from approximately 32 weeks follow-up and limited numbers of patients at risk mean that these results are relatively uninformative. 

The EAG requested that the company provide information on the potential confounding effect of subsequent therapies following discontinuation on OS estimates, using trial evidence as appropriate. The information provided showed that very few patients received nivolumab in the comparator arm and that several subsequent therapies received in NIAGARA are not commonly used in the NHS (response to clarification question A8, Table 3). 

An analysis of data on PFS-2 (progression or recurrence after the first EFS event) (NIAGARA CSR Section 11.1.3.7) added limited additional information. Because most PFS-2 events were deaths 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 425 -->

(durvalumab arm xxxx, control arm xxxx of PFS-2 events) (CSR Table 32, p. 126) and rates of censoring were high, the results largely align with the OS results. 

The impact of subsequent treatments on OS therefore remains uncertain. Further follow-up data would help to explore the extent to which subsequent therapies may impact on longer-term OS. 

## _3.3.1.3 Results for additional outcomes_ 

Other efficacy outcomes reported include a higher pCR rate for durvalumab versus the control group upon re-analysis of the data at DCO April 2024 (CS section 2.6.1.2, pp. 52-53), improved DSS (CS section 2.6.2.5, pp. 59-60), longer DFS (CS Section 2.6.2.6, pp. 61-62), and greater PFS-2 (CS Section 2.6.2.7, pp. 62-63). 

## _**Quality of life**_ 

Quality of life was measured using the EORTC QLQ-C30 and EQ-5D-5L questionnaires. A substantial proportion of the data was missing at baseline and later timepoints (compliance 73.1% and 71.7% in the durvalumab and control arms, respectively, for the EORTC QLQ-C30, and 78.2% and 81.1%, respectively, for the EQ-5D-5L) (CS pp.64-65). It is unclear whether data were missing at random, which affects the certainty of the results. 

Using the prioritised EORTC QLQ-C30 subscales (Table 7), the company found that mean scores measured at week 25 and week 29 were similar between the study groups, and concluded that perioperative durvalumab does not negatively affect quality of life compared to the control arm. The EQ-5D-5L results similarly showed little difference in mean scores between the study arms at the different follow-up times over the duration of the study. 

## _3.3.1.4 Subgroup analyses_ 

Prespecified subgroup analyses are presented in the CS section 2.7, pp.67-69, including Figure 13 for EFS (p. 68) and Figure 14 for OS (p. 69). Although these analyses are generally underpowered, with low numbers of patients in some subgroups, the EAG is satisfied that the analyses do not show a difference in the efficacy of perioperative durvalumab with neoadjuvant cisplatin-based therapy compared to neoadjuvant cisplatin-based therapy for any of the subgroups. 

The NICE scope included PD-L1 status as a possible subgroup analysis (CS Table 1, p. 14), because nivolumab is recommended in the UK for the subgroup of patients with high risk of post-surgery recurrence and PD-L1 ≥ 1%. In subgroup analyses, hazard ratios for EFS (CS Figure 13, p. 68) and OS (CS Figure 14, p. 69) were similar for high versus low or no PD-L1 expression at baseline. The company advised caution regarding the emphasis on PD-L1 expression when considering evidence of durvalumab efficacy, arguing that it is not considered relevant in clinical decision-making as the value 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 426 -->

of PD-L1 expression as a prognostic marker is unclear and evaluation of PD-L1 status is not required for perioperative durvalumab or NAC. The EAG’s clinical advisers agreed.
