## _3.3.2.1 Summary of adverse events_ 

AEs were common in both treatment arms, with nearly all patients experiencing at least one AE of any grade (99.4% in the perioperative durvalumab arm vs 99.8% in the control arm). The most frequently reported AEs (≥ 15% of patients in either arm) included nausea, anaemia, constipation, fatigue, and urinary tract infection. Grade 3 or 4 AEs occurred in a similar proportion of patients across arms (69.4% in the durvalumab arm vs 67.5% in the control arm). The pattern and severity of these events were broadly consistent with the known toxicity profiles of the individual agents. 

## _3.3.2.2 Discontinuation due to adverse events_ 

More patients in the perioperative durvalumab arm experienced AEs leading to permanent discontinuation of any study treatment than in the control arm (21.1% vs 15.2%). Notably, 16.2% discontinued durvalumab, with 7.9% of patients discontinuing due to AEs considered possibly related to durvalumab. In the neoadjuvant period, xxxx of patients in the durvalumab arm discontinued any study treatment due to AEs, whereas xxxx discontinued durvalumab during the adjuvant period. This may be clinically relevant given the intention for prolonged adjuvant use. AE-related dose 

interruptions or reductions were also more common with perioperative durvalumab (57.5% vs 47.0%). These findings suggest a higher overall treatment burden in the durvalumab group. 

## _3.3.2.3 Immune-mediated adverse events (imAEs)_ 

Immune-related toxicities were more frequent in the perioperative durvalumab arm (20.9%) compared to control (3.0%). Most events were low grade, but some, including pneumonitis, hepatitis, renal events, and hypothyroidism, required systemic corticosteroids or led to discontinuation. 

Hypothyroidism affected over 10% of patients in the durvalumab arm, with most cases unresolved by DCO. The need for endocrine therapy was also considerably higher (12.3% in the durvalumab arm vs 1.7% in the control arm). 

## _3.3.2.4 Serious adverse events (SAEs) and deaths_ 

SAEs were reported in 61.5% of patients in the durvalumab arm and 54.6% in the control arm. The most common SAEs were infections, urinary tract disorders, and incidental prostate cancer detected post-surgery. The proportion of deaths attributed to AEs was similar across groups (5.1% in the 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 428 -->

durvalumab arm vs 5.5% in the control arm), with only one AE-related death considered possibly related to durvalumab (cardiorespiratory arrest). 

## _**3.4 Critique of studies identified and included in the indirect treatment comparison or multiple treatment comparison**_ 

The final scope issued by NICE included NAC followed by RC and adjuvant nivolumab as a comparator. However, the NIAGARA trial did not allow adjuvant nivolumab to be given in the G+C arm (control arm), for patients that would be eligible for adjuvant nivolumab in NHS practice (PD-L1 positive tumours at high risk of recurrence, see Table 6). Therefore, a direct comparison of perioperative durvalumab with NAC (D+G+C) to NAC followed by no additional adjuvant treatment or adjuvant nivolumab for eligible patients (G+C+N) is not available. 

The comparison between perioperative durvalumab (D+G+C) and adjuvant nivolumab (G+C+N) is complicated by, among other factors, the difference in the decision point for treatment in NHS clinical practice, and consequent differences in the populations. In NHS clinical practice, eligibility for adjuvant nivolumab is decided only after RC, based on PD-L1 status and risk of recurrence. Thus, patients are only eligible for nivolumab if they have successfully undergone NAC, RC and have PDL1 positive tumours at high risk of recurrence. Eligibility for perioperative durvalumab is decided prior to RC, based on eligibility for NAC, thus some patients eligible for perioperative durvalumab will end up not completing the course of neoadjuvant treatment, or not having surgery. In addition, PD-L1 status will not necessarily be know at the point of eligibility for perioperative durvalumab, nor will it be known if the cancer will be at high risk of recurrence post-surgery (since eligibility for perioperative durvalumab is determined pre-surgery). 

Whilst the company acknowledged that adjuvant nivolumab is a relevant treatment option in NHS clinical practice, due to the differences in decision time points the company claimed that the overlap between patients eligible for perioperative durvalumab and adjuvant nivolumab is minimal. Therefore, a comparison of perioperative durvalumab with the use of adjuvant nivolumab in high-risk PD-L1 positive patients following NAC and RC was only considered as a scenario in the company’s costeffectiveness analysis and not included in the company’s base case (Section 4.2.4.2). 

As no direct evidence for the comparison between perioperative durvalumab and NAC followed by no treatment or adjuvant nivolumab was identified, the company conducted an indirect treatment comparison (ITC) (CS Section 2.9). The systematic literature review (Section 3.1) identified the CheckMate-274 RCT as the only trial aligned with the NICE final scope of this appraisal and relevant to the UK clinical setting that considered adjuvant nivolumab after NAC.[20] 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 429 -->

## **3.4.1 Trial design and participants** 

CheckMate-274 was a phase III, parallel double-blind RCT. A total of 709 patients with muscleinvasive urothelial carcinoma were randomised to adjuvant nivolumab or placebo after RC.[20] 

Patients with urothelial carcinoma were eligible to enrol in CheckMate-274 if they had received prior radical surgery within 120 days from randomisation, with or without neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy, and were at high risk of recurrence (pathological stage of pT3, pT4a, or pN+ and not eligible for or declined adjuvant cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy for patients who had not received neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy and pathological stage of ypT2 to ypT4a or ypN+ for patients who received neoadjuvant cisplatin). See Section 2.1.1 for an explanation of disease stages. 

Participants received adjuvant nivolumab (240 mg intravenously) or placebo every two weeks for up to a year after surgery. In the ITT population, 43% of participants had received neoadjuvant cisplatin (308 out of 709).[21] 

In order to match nivolumab patients to the TA817[15] indication, which focused on a narrower population of high-risk patients with PD-L1 ≥ 1%, only subgroup data from CheckMate-274 were included in the indirect treatment comparison. However, data for the subgroup matching the decision problem were not available. This is further discussed in Section 3.5.1. 

## _3.4.1.1 Study population_ 

The NIAGARA and CheckMate-274 participants start the trial at different points in their treatment pathway. NIAGARA participants were randomised to receive neoadjuvant durvalumab plus chemotherapy (gemcitabine and cisplatin) or chemotherapy alone (gemcitabine and cisplatin), prior to RC, followed by adjuvant durvalumab or no treatment regardless of the success of RC, whereas CheckMate-274 participants were only randomised to receive nivolumab after RC if they were deemed at high-risk of recurrence (post-RC). Thus, all participants in CheckMate-274 had surgery and were considered to be at high-risk of recurrence, whilst NIAGARA participants were allocated to trial therapies prior to RC. A proportion of patients in NIAGARA did not receive RC (ITT population: 11.8% durvalumab arm and 15.8% control arm) including some who did not receive RC due to progression or death (ITT population: 2.6% durvalumab arm, 3.2% control arm – see Section 3.2.5). 

During TA817, the EAG commented that CheckMate-274 participants were young compared to the patient population expected to be treated in the NHS.[15] Compared to NIAGARA, CheckMate-274 participants were of a similar age, but more likely to be female. In terms of disease characteristics, CheckMate-274 participants were worse affected in their daily activity (NIAGARA 78.4% ECOG 0, 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 430 -->

CheckMate-274 60.2% ECOG 0) and their disease had progressed further (NIAGARA 94.5% N0, CheckMate-274 45.9% N0). 

No baseline characteristics were available for the subset of patients from CheckMate-274 with MIBC, prior NAC, PD-L1 ≥ 1% and high risk of recurrence. Therefore, the applicability of CheckMate-274 to the NHS, and the comparability of the CheckMate-274 and NIAGARA relevant subpopulations are uncertain. This is further discussed in Section 3.5.1.1. 

_3.4.1.2 Study endpoints and analyses_ 

A summary of differences in endpoints and analyses between the NIAGARA (EFS, OS) and CheckMate-274 results (DFS, OS) is presented in CS Table 24. In response to a clarification request from the EAG (question A19), the company provided results for DMFS, which, like DFS, were informed by an extended three-year follow-up analysis from CheckMate-274.[21] There was uncertainty regarding the source of OS results, which is discussed in Section 3.5.1.1. 

In NIAGARA, EFS included events in both the neoadjuvant and adjuvant phases (see Table 7). In CheckMate-274 DFS was defined as the time between randomisation (start of adjuvant phase) and first recurrence (local or distant) or death. The EAG agrees with the company that EFS as defined in NIAGARA covers different phases of treatment compared to DFS, so EFS and DFS cannot be directly compared across studies. However, in the context of the ITC, the EAG considers that the company’s pragmatic decision to use DFS from CheckMate-274 to inform EFS in the adjuvant phase of the control arm with adjuvant nivolumab is acceptable. 

DFS endpoints in the adjuvant phase are broadly equivalent between the two trials, as they were both measured at a similar timepoint, although the EAG agrees with the company that differences in inclusion criteria between NIAGARA and CheckMate-274 limit direct comparability between the trials for this outcome. 

DMFS was defined in CheckMate-274 as the time between randomisation and any non-local recurrence (i.e. outside the urothelial tract, pelvic soft tissue or pelvic nodes below the aortic bifurcation) or death, whichever occurred first. For subjects who remained alive and distant recurrence-free, DMFS was censored on the date of last disease assessment. The definition of DFMS in CheckMate-274 and MFS in NIAGARA both include distant metastases and exclude local metastases (see Table 7). However, the time from randomisation between the two trials differs, as CheckMate-274 only included participants in the adjuvant phase following RC. For the sake of simplicity, DMFS will be referred to as MFS throughout. 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 431 -->

OS in NIAGARA captures death in the neoadjuvant and adjuvant phases and for patients who did not undergo RC, whereas CheckMate-274 only measured death after surgery. The EAG agrees with the company that direct comparisons of OS between the trials are of limited relevance. 

## **3.4.2 Critical appraisal** 

The company reported a critical appraisal of CheckMate-274 as part of the literature review (CS, Appendix B). The Risk of Bias 2 tool was used, and overall ratings per domain are reported.[16] Each domain was found to be at low risk of bias. The EAG broadly agrees with this assessment. Although results for outcome-specific domains (missing outcome data, outcome measurement, reporting) were not reported by outcome, the EAG agrees these domains are at low risk of bias for EFS, MFS, and OS. 

As part of the nivolumab appraisal (TA817), the EAG noted that discontinuation due to drug toxicity was substantially higher in the nivolumab arm (14%) than the placebo arm (2.3%).[15] Pneumonitis, rash, colitis, and increased alanine aminotransferase level were among the reasons for discontinuation relating to treatment with nivolumab.[20] Clinical advice to the EAG suggests that side effects of nivolumab are normally infrequent, and well-tolerated. 

## _**3.5 Critique of the indirect comparison or multiple treatment comparison**_ 

The EAG agrees with the company that due to differences in trial design and patient populations at randomisation between NIAGARA and CheckMate-274, standard ITC methods are not suitable for a comparison between perioperative durvalumab with NAC, versus NAC followed by no treatment or adjuvant nivolumab in high-risk PD-L1 positive patients. The EAG agrees with the company that an unadjusted comparison of only the adjuvant phases of both trials would be at high risk of bias. 

The company proposed an ITC using a survival time-adjusted approach where survival times for the control arm of the NIAGARA trial are adjusted to simulate a scenario where eligible (high-risk PD-L1 positive) patients received nivolumab instead of no treatment after NAC and RC. The analysis is presented for EFS and OS in the CS (CS, Table 24), and for MFS in response to EAG clarification question A19. An adjusted comparison of safety or tolerability outcomes was not conducted. 

The company’s survival time-adjusted analysis is based on existing recommendations to adjust for treatment switching[22] (where in this case eligible patients who did not have adjuvant treatment are “adjusted” to have nivolumab), which appear to have been appropriately applied and well described in the CS and accompanying appendices, supplemented by additional information provided in response to the clarification questions. However, as far as the EAG is aware, this methodology has not previously been used in the context of the adjustments required in this appraisal and therefore its 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 432 -->

performance in this context has not been externally validated. We provide an overview and critique of the proposed method below. 

## **3.5.1 Methods** 

To simulate the scenario where eligible patients in the control arm of NIAGARA receive adjuvant nivolumab, the company used counterfactual survival time methods where the estimated counterfactual survival time represents the survival time that would have been observed for an individual under a different treatment than the one experienced. A counterfactual control arm was estimated to represent the outcomes of NAC followed by no treatment or adjuvant nivolumab in highrisk, PD-L1 positive patients (G+C+N), for the outcomes of EFS, MFS and OS, which are then used to compare perioperative durvalumab with NAC (D+G+C), to NAC followed by no treatment (G+C). The simulated counterfactual arm G+C+N aligns with the current treatment pathway in the NHS. 

The full ITT population of the NIAGARA trial and subgroup data from CheckMate-274 were used for the ITC. Pseudo-IPD were reconstructed from published KM curves from CheckMate-274 post-hoc subgroups and used to conduct the analysis (for further details see Section 3.5.1.1). 

For each outcome, the analysis consisted of 3 steps: 1) estimate an acceleration factor (AF) expressing the survival increase associated with adjuvant nivolumab; 2) create the counterfactual survival estimates for survival outcomes; and 3) conduct the ITC to provide relative estimates of EFS, MFS and OS. Following guidance, analyses were conducted with and without re-censoring.[22, 23] Recensoring was used to reduce the risk of informative censoring bias (i.e. censoring that is related to prognostic characteristics) in the counterfactual data set which may occur through the adjustment of survival times of eligible ‘high-risk’ patients but not of ineligible patients in the NIAGARA trial. The methods are briefly described below, with further details provided in CS Section 2.9.2. 

First, an AF for the effect of nivolumab compared to placebo was estimated by fitting different acceleration failure time (AFT) models to the pseudo-IPD from both arms of CheckMate-274 subgroup data (Table 12), with a covariate representing treatment. Where standard AFT models were considered to not fit well, models with time-varying effects were also considered for EFS and OS. In response to EAG clarification question A19, the company provided analyses for MFS, although timevarying effects were not considered due to time limitations. The calculation and application of timevarying AFs for EFS and OS is detailed in Section 2.9.2 of the CS with further details provided in response to clarification question A11.

The final step of the ITC compared the survival times of the perioperative durvalumab arm to the counterfactual control arm in the NIAGARA trial where the xx eligible patients are assumed to have had NAC followed by adjuvant nivolumab, and the remaining patients had NAC followed by no treatment. Because all patients were included in the NIAGARA trial, the company was able to use a stratified Cox-regression analysis as all baseline participant characteristics are known (see CS Section 2.9.2, Step 3, for details). Confidence intervals were obtained by bootstrapping to capture uncertainty in the estimated HRs. 

Additional piecewise analyses were conducted to obtain HRs comparing the NAC followed by adjuvant nivolumab arm (G+C+N) with the NAC-only arm (G+C) over the first 6 months and post-6months to use in the company’s scenario that presents cost-effectiveness results with adjuvant nivolumab.

It is also unclear to the EAG whether the CheckMate-274 subgroup characteristics in this table are those of the subgroup whose survival curves informed the ITC. 

## **3.5.2 Results** 

Flexible parametric survival models were fitted to the EFS (DFS in CheckMate-274), MFS and OS KM curves generated from reconstructed IPD from CheckMate-274. For EFS, although the generalised gamma curve provided the best fit it appeared to underestimate survival for the nivolumab arm, so the log-logistic AFT was selected as the most conservative (it provided more optimistic results for nivolumab) and used in the base case ITC. Spline models with time-varying effects were also fitted and the 3-knot spline was used to estimate the AF in a sensitivity analysis (results are presented in Appendix B of the CS, which are similar to those obtained using the log-logistic – see also response to clarification question A13). For MFS all parametric models displayed poor fit to the data (see Figure 2 in the Appendix to the company’s response to clarifications). Although the generalised gamma had the best fit, it again appeared to underestimate survival on nivolumab, predicting the lowest AFT for nivolumab compared to placebo so the log-logistic was chosen as the most conservative (spline models were not considered due to limited time). For OS all standard parametric models fitted well and yielded similar AFs so time-varying models were not considered. The log-normal was selected as the best fitting model. The AFs used for EFS and OS are given in Table 27 of the CS, and the AF for MFS is given in page 5 of the Appendix to the company’s response to clarification questions. The AF is largest for EFS, slightly reduced for MFS and lowest for OS although all indicate improved outcomes on adjuvant nivolumab compared to placebo.

The ITC was carried out using the adjusted survival times for EFS, MFS and OS with and without the application of re-censoring. Because the effect of nivolumab is to extend survival times, without recensoring survival times for the G+C+N arm extend far beyond the observed period. Application of re-censoring leads to similar follow-up times across all arms and is the company’s preferred analysis. The EAG agrees that results using re-censoring are preferred. The use of the “adjusted” survival times for the nivolumab eligible patients in NIAGARA led to a separation in the EFS, MFS and OS curves favouring G+C+N versus G+C. Because this separation only applied to the adjuvant period (all patients receive the same treatment up to RC) there is a delay in the separation of survival curves, thus the treatment effect for G+C+N versus the G+C varies over 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 437 -->

time. To account for this in the cost-effectiveness model, the company estimated the survival-time adjusted hazard ratios for G+C+N versus G+C for 0 up to 6 months and beyond 6 months, in a piecewise Cox regression analysis. The 6-month cut point was selected to coincide with the start of adjuvant treatment in the economic model, and it also matches the time point at which the G+C and G+C+N curves start to separate and the expected timing of adjuvant therapy in practice. In response to clarification question A22, the company provided Schoenfeld residual plots for G+C+N versus G+C for EFS, MFS and OS after 6 months which support the assumption of an approximately constant and proportional effect in the post-6 months period. Whilst it is generally good practice to explore the impact of alternative cut‑points in piecewise models, the EAG considers the 6‑month cut‑point to be clinically appropriate, reflecting the expected timeframe for starting adjuvant therapy. The EAG also considers that small variations around the 6‑month cut‑point would have minimal impact on cost-effectiveness results. In response to EAG clarification question A22b, the company provided an updated model enabling independent extrapolation for EFS using a spline‑based model with a 3‑knot hazard. However, as the proportional hazards assumption does not appear to be violated for any survival outcome, the company’s piecewise approach is appropriate for use in the economic model. 

As explained by the company in the response to clarification question A20, the ITC focused on efficacy rather than safety outcomes. The company therefore described the safety profile of CheckMate-274 without a formal comparison with NIAGARA. Patients in the adjuvant nivolumab arm were more likely to experience any grade or grade 3 or above treatment-related adverse events compared to placebo. Immuno-mediated adverse events were observed in 34.5% of the nivolumab arm and 6.9% of the placebo arm. The company state that the higher rates of adverse events and grade 3+ adverse events in the NIAGARA trial are explained by the side effects of chemotherapy, which is not given in the adjuvant phase. 

## **3.5.3 EAG comments** 

The lack of a randomised comparison between perioperative durvalumab and current NHS practice (that is, NAC followed by RC and no adjuvant treatment or adjuvant nivolumab for high-risk PD-L1 positive patients) is a significant limitation of existing evidence. The CheckMate-274 RCT compared adjuvant nivolumab in the high-risk PD-L1 positive population but the limited comparability in designs and populations between NIAGARA and CheckMate-27 precludes standard comparisons. An ITC was conducted using an adjusted survival time approach based on post-hoc subgroup data from CheckMate-274 that included patients with and without prior NAC. The ITC relies on AFs calculated from CheckMate-274 which requires the assumption that the effect of adjuvant nivolumab is exchangeable across the CheckMate-274 and NIAGARA trials, i.e. that the effect of nivolumab compared to placebo observed in CheckMate-274 also applies to the patients in the adjuvant phase of 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 438 -->

NIAGARA. However, the subgroup data available from CheckMate-274 does not fully match the population of high-risk PD-L1 positive, MIBC patients who received NAC (only a minority of patients in CheckMate-274 received NAC). It is unclear whether previous NAC is a treatment effect modifier for adjuvant nivolumab but if it is, the estimated AFs may not be transferrable to the NIAGARA population, leading to possible bias in the adjusted survival times. 

The ITC also relies on adjusting survival times in the adjuvant phase for NIAGARA patients who would have been eligible for adjuvant nivolumab in NHS practice (xxx% of all randomised patients or xxx% of patients who underwent surgery). The proportion of patients assumed to have received nivolumab in the ITC is therefore higher than NHS England’s estimate of 5-10% of patients who had NAC followed by RC eligible for adjuvant nivolumab. However, the ITC method can only be used to create counterfactual survival times for patients in NIAGARA who fulfilled criteria for adjuvant nivolumab. If a lower proportion of patients are eligible for adjuvant nivolumab in clinical practice, the adjustment may overestimate the additional benefit of nivolumab in the NHS population. 

The company compared the HRs of adjuvant nivolumab compared to no adjuvant treatment obtained from the adjusted analysis in eligible NIAGARA patients to the original HRs in CheckMate-274 (Table 13). All HRs from the adjusted analyses were more favourable to nivolumab than the HRs estimated in CheckMate-274, suggesting that the company’s analyses may be conservative, i.e. they may overestimate the benefit of adjuvant nivolumab. This may somewhat mitigate the concerns regarding comparability of the populations in NIAGARA and CheckMate-274. 

Due to the separation of the adjusted survival curves in the adjuvant period, the company carried out additional piecewise ITC over the first 6 month and post-6 months. The EAG believes it is inconsistent to present results for the whole period as the main results from the ITC, but then use the piecewise results in the economic model. However, the EAG agrees that the piecewise results better reflect the effect of adjuvant nivolumab as the proportional hazards assumption appears to hold beyond 6 months for all survival outcomes and the cut-off point at 6 months is justified. Therefore, the EAG agrees that the HRs from the piecewise analyses should be used in the economic model. 

Overall, the EAG believes that the methods used by the company to adjust the survival times are appropriate. The lack of consideration of spline models for the ITC of MFS despite the poor fit of parametric models is a limitation, although it is unclear whether this would have meaningfully impacted the results. The ITC results are also associated with uncertainty due to the non-randomised nature of the comparison and required assumptions. 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 439 -->

The lack of an ITC for safety outcomes was justified by the company and a narrative summary provided in response to a clarification request, although this is still a limitation. The relative safety of perioperative durvalumab compared to adjuvant nivolumab in eligible patients is uncertain. 

## _**3.6 Additional work on clinical effectiveness done by the EAG**_ 

## None. 

## _**3.7 Conclusions of the clinical-effectiveness section**_ 

The clinical evidence submitted by the company was generally clearly presented. The evidence on the efficacy and safety of perioperative durvalumab in combination with neoadjuvant cisplatin-based therapy for MIBC comes from NIAGARA, an ongoing multicentre, open-label RCT. There is some uncertainty about the comparability of the trial participants to the NHS population. The EAG found NIAGARA to be at low risk of bias for EFS, MFS and OS; however, participants and care providers were not blinded for treatment allocation, which means that HRQoL results are at high risk of bias. At the 29 April 2024 data cut-off, median OS and MFS were not reached in either trial arm, and median EFS was only reached in the control arm. The NIAGARA trial provided statistically significant evidence that perioperative durvalumab improved EFS, MFS and OS compared to the control arm. Quality of life was similar between the two study arms. Participants in the durvalumab arm were more likely to experience immune-related adverse events and SAEs, which the EAG’s clinical advisers judged to be consistent with the known safety profile of the treatments. 

No direct evidence was available for the comparison between perioperative durvalumab and adjuvant nivolumab. It was not possible to indirectly compare evidence from NIAGARA and the CheckMate274 trial of nivolumab using conventional methods, due to the differences in trial populations and designs so the company adapted methods commonly used to adjust for treatment-switching to perform the analyses. The EAG considers the company’s approach for the ITC justified. Overall, this showed an improvement in outcomes in the control arm of NIAGARA where eligible patients were given adjuvant nivolumab (counterfactual control arm) but HRs for perioperative durvalumab compared to NAC alone or with adjuvant nivolumab for eligible patients suggested greater benefit for perioperative durvalumab for EFS, MFS and OS. However, the results of the ITCs are uncertain as they rely on the assumption that the effect of adjuvant nivolumab is exchangeable between CheckMate-274 and NIAGARA trials, although there is insufficient evidence to support this. In addition, the applicability of CheckMate-274 participants and results (EFS, MFS, OS) to the NHS population is uncertain. Finally, the relative safety of perioperative durvalumab versus NAC alone or followed by adjuvant nivolumab for eligible patients in uncertain as safety outcomes were not included in the ITC. 

29/08/2025

## **4 COST-EFFECTIVENESS** 

This section presents a summary and critique of the cost-effectiveness evidence included in the company’s submission. Section 4.1 focuses on the company’s review of the cost-effectiveness evidence from previous studies and section 4.2 covers the company’s economic evaluation. 

## _**4.1 Critique of the review of cost-effectiveness evidence**_ 

## **4.1.1 Summary of company’s submission** 

The company’s systematic literature review did not identify any economic evaluations of durvalumab for the treatment of adults with MIBC (see Appendix E of the CS for a detailed description of the searches and results of the review). Three UK-based studies were identified that evaluated adjuvant nivolumab in MIBC, including NICE Technology Appraisal 817 (TA817) of nivolumab for adjuvant treatment of invasive urothelial cancer at high risk of recurrence, published in 2022.[15, 25, 26] In all three studies identified, the models reported were structurally identical and based on the same underlying evidence. 

In addition, the company undertook a targeted search of previous appraisals published by NICE, the Australian Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee (PBAC) and Canada’s Drug Agency (CDAAMC) to compare modelling approaches in cost effectiveness analyses conducted for therapies in MIBC and oncology therapies in the perioperative setting outside of MIBC. From the targeted search for therapies in MIBC, two further appraisals for adjuvant nivolumab by PBAC and CDA-AMC (PC0272-000) were identified,[27, 28] while in the perioperative setting outside MIBC, two appraisals were considered – pembrolizumab for triple-negative breast cancer (TA851)[29] and durvalumab for non-small cell lung cancer (TA1030).[30] The company provides a description of the studies identified in Section 3.1.2 of CS. 

## **4.1.2 Points for critique** 

The literature searching for the company’s review of cost-effectiveness evidence appears to have been conducted to a high standard and is well reported – See Appendix 2 for details. The EAG considers that all relevant publications are likely to have been identified. 

The company’s review of identified studies, reported in Section 3.1.2 of the CS, indicates that all previous studies used semi-Markov or Markov models to assess the cost effectiveness of the intervention under consideration, which differs from the company’s _de-novo_ approach using partitioned survival modelling (see Section 4.2.2 below). The company states that the use of semiMarkov state transition modelling in previous appraisals was motivated by the lack of OS data available at the time of the submissions for nivolumab (TA817) and pembrolizumab (TA851), while 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 441 -->

OS data are available from the NIAGARA trial to allow a partitioned survival modelling approach (PSM) for durvalumab. However, the EAG notes that the use of semi-Markov state transition modelling versus PSM did not form part of the committee discussions in TA817 and TA851 and, therefore, the appropriateness of PSM for modelling therapies in MIBC has not been considered to date. Instead, previous committee discussions have centred on the assumptions used for the modelled health states and treatment lines, and the assumptions required to translate improvements in diseasefree survival to OS when modelling long-term effects of treatment. 

The company highlights that in the PBAC and CDA assessments of nivolumab, concerns were expressed about the use of a single health state for disease recurrence. Therefore, for durvalumab, the company splits disease recurrence into locoregional and distant metastasis health states to better reflect differences in outcomes post-recurrence in these health states. The EAG also notes that in TA817 for adjuvant nivolumab, the committee expressed concern that post-recurrence outcomes were not robustly modelled because the model did not allow for the consideration of survival outcomes from further treatment lines. The use of a standard PSM (progression-free and first occurrence of progressed disease) for durvalumab means that the model cannot explicitly consider the impact of subsequent treatments on survival outcomes, which the EAG considers to be a limitation from previous studies that the company’s _de-novo_ model for durvalumab has not addressed (see Section 4.2.2.2). 

Previous studies for nivolumab have assumed a cure point at 5 years, with no disease recurrence after 5 years in the DFS state, which was supported by evidence from the CheckMate-274 trial (adjuvant nivolumab compared to placebo) in MIBC, showing that the risk of death approaches that of the general population at 5 years. However, the committee for TA817 also considered external evidence demonstrating an increased mortality risk for people with resected urothelial cancer compared with the general population, even after 5 years in a disease-free state. The committee concluded that there is evidence that disease recurrence may take place after 5 years and mortality risks remain elevated; therefore, it remains uncertain at what time point it is reasonable to assume that people are cured from cancer.[15] In the company’s _de-novo_ model for durvalumab, the model does not include an explicit cure assumption, but it implicitly captures ‘cure’ through the selection of extrapolation curves to survival outcomes that imply decreasing hazards of events as observed in the follow-up period of the NIAGARA trial (see Section 4.2.5). 

The review of previous appraisals also highlights the need to carefully consider the current standard of care as a relevant comparator in the economic analysis, even if the trials only include a placebo comparator arm. In TA817, the committee considered that adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy was likely to be a suitable treatment option for people with urothelial carcinomas of the upper urinary tract and concluded that, when suitable, it is a relevant comparator. However, because the committee 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 442 -->

had not been presented with any cost-effectiveness results comparing nivolumab with platinum-based chemotherapy, and the indirect comparison results showed no statistically significant difference in treatment effect between nivolumab and platinum-based chemotherapy, the NICE recommendation for adjuvant nivolumab was restricted to when adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy is unsuitable. The population eligible for adjuvant nivolumab is also restricted to those at high risk of recurrence after radical resection in adults whose tumours express PD-L1 at a level of 1% or more, in line with its marketing authorisation in MIBC. The EAG considers that while adjuvant nivolumab and perioperative durvalumab occupy distinct points in the treatment pathway for MIBC and target different populations, the relevance of including adjuvant nivolumab for patients at high risk of recurrence and PD-L1 ≥ 1% (when adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy is unsuitable) as part of the treatment pathway for the neoadjuvant comparator to durvalumab (i.e., neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy) needs to be carefully considered in the assessment of the cost-effectiveness of durvalumab in a perioperative setting (see Sections 2.2.2, 3.2.4). 

## _**4.2 Critique of the submitted economic evaluation**_ 

The company submitted a _de-novo_ model to assess the cost-effectiveness of durvalumab in combination with gemcitabine and cisplatin as neoadjuvant treatment in adults with resectable MIBC, followed by durvalumab as monotherapy adjuvant treatment after RC (referred to as perioperative durvalumab), compared with neoadjuvant gemcitabine and cisplatin (also termed NAC) followed by RC and either (i) no treatment (company’s base case analysis) or (ii) adjuvant nivolumab for patients whose tumours express PD-L1 ≥ 1% and present high-risk of recurrence (company’s scenario analysis). 

A PSM is used to estimate the long-term health outcomes and costs associated with progression and the clinical care pathway of resectable MIBC in the UK for patients eligible for neoadjuvant cisplatinbased chemotherapy prior to RC. In the PSM, the time-dependent risk of disease progression and death is modelled by extrapolating clinical trial endpoints from the NIAGARA trial to directly determine the proportion of patients alive, event-free (defined as no recurrence after RC, no documented progression or residual disease in patients precluded from RC, or death) and metastasisfree (i.e., free of distant metastases) over a lifetime horizon for both perioperative durvalumab and neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy. The effects of subsequent anticancer therapies for disease recurrence on post-progression survival are implicitly accounted for in the extrapolated OS curve. 

Perioperative durvalumab is modelled to affect QALYs by increasing the proportion of patients who are alive (improvement in OS) and event-free and metastasis-free (associated with improved healthrelated quality of life) over time relative to neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy alone. 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 443 -->

Perioperative durvalumab is modelled to affect costs primarily due to the additional drug acquisition and administration costs of durvalumab compared to neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy alone. However, this cost is partially offset by lower costs associated with reduced disease progression and subsequent therapy and terminal care costs from improved event-free and metastasis-free survival for durvalumab.

## **4.2.2 Model structure** 

## _4.2.2.1 Summary of company’s submission_ 

The model structure is a four-state PSM comprising health states for event-free (EF), locoregional recurrence (LR), distant metastatic disease (DM) and death (see Figure 21 of CS). The cohort enters the model in the EF health state to begin NAC, with or without perioperative durvalumab, followed by RC, if suitable. The EF state represents the pre-recurrence phase and includes patients who progress before surgery, decline surgery, or are deemed unfit for surgery. From the EF state, patients may transition to LR, DM or death states. LR includes recurrence in MIBC patients who are free of distant metastases, including those who did not undergo surgery, while DM includes patients with distant metastases. The recurrence phase is split into LR and DM to reflect the different prognosis of each state, where DM is associated with poorer survival and lower HRQoL compared to LR. The death state captures all-cause mortality. 

The transitions from the EF state to LR, DM or death states are defined by the time-dependent EFS, MFS and OS curves from the NIAGARA trial and extrapolated beyond the available data using parametric models over a lifetime horizon (Section 4.2.5). The proportion of patients alive over time is estimated directly from the OS curve, with the hazard of death constrained to be at or above the corresponding age- and gender-matched all-cause general population risk of death by age. OS is partitioned into the proportion of patients who are alive with DM (OS minus MFS) and the proportion of patients who are alive without DM (MFS). The EFS curve partitions MFS into the proportion of patients who are EF, based on the cumulative survival probabilities of EFS, and those with a nonmetastatic recurrence who occupy the LR state (MFS minus EFS). The EFS curve is constrained to values less than or equal to MFS, while the MFS curve is constrained to values less than or equal to OS. The hazard of EFS and MFS is also constrained to be at or above the age- and gender-adjusted all-cause general population risk of death by age. Figure 22 of the CS illustrates the PSM simulation for the four health states in the model. 

## _4.2.2.2 Points for critique_ 

The EAG considers the company’s PSM structure to be broadly appropriate because it allows direct modelling of the key NIAGARA trial outcomes of EFS, MFS, and OS. PSM is widely accepted as an appropriate approach for economic evaluations in oncology and has been employed in 73% of NICE oncology submissions reviewed between May 2013-February 2016 in NICE Technical Support Document (TSD) 19.[31] However, it is important to consider the suitability of PSM in the context of the decision problem and compared to the common alternative of state transition modelling (STM) because PSM and STM can produce substantively different survival extrapolations.[32] Previous studies of adjuvant nivolumab for MIBC, along with the two NICE appraisals in the perioperative setting outside MIBC (identified in Section 4.1.1), used STM rather than PSM. The company justified its 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 445 -->

approach by citing the availability of mature OS data from NIAGARA, which contrasted with previous NICE appraisals where limited OS data restricted the use of PSM. 

The EAG considers the appropriateness of the company’s PSM to be largely dependent on the maturity of the observed data informing survival outcomes, particularly OS. The extrapolation of outcomes over a lifetime horizon (see Section 4.2.5) is critical as uncertainty in long-term OS directly leads to uncertainty in the cost-effectiveness estimates. Despite the company’s statement of mature OS data from NIAGARA, with a median follow-up of 42.3 months in the perioperative durvalumab arm and 39.6 months in the control arm, the EAG notes that only 305 death events had occurred corresponding to 28.7% maturity for OS overall (Table 17 of CS, OS IA-1 data-cut), and median OS has not yet been reached. Therefore, although the OS data from NIAGARA is relatively mature compared to data available in previous appraisals, it is still not fully mature with fewer than 50% of trial participants experiencing a death event. 

One of the main limitations of PSM is that OS is determined independently of other clinical outcomes, including EFS and MFS, i.e., the survival curves that inform the estimates of health state membership are modelled completely independently. Therefore, when the OS data in the company’s model is extrapolated over the long-term it is done completely independent of the other endpoints. This structural independence within a PSM makes it very difficult to judge the clinical and biological plausibility of the extrapolations of each endpoint in relation to one another, which is a fundamental difference from STMs where clinical events underlying the extrapolations can be structurally and explicitly related. Although the OS extrapolations in the company’s model were validated against external data and expert clinical opinion (Section 4.2.5), the company did not present separate survival curves for pre-progression and post-progression deaths to allow exploration of the treatment effect pre- and post-progression (recurrence) on OS. Furthermore, due to the modelled independence between trial outcomes (lack of structural relationship between endpoints), the extrapolated intermediate outcomes of EFS and MFS may lie above the OS curve (e.g., a higher proportion of patients predicted to be in the EF, LR and DM health states than alive), or the extrapolated EFS curve may be greater than the extrapolated MFS curve. To avoid these logical inconsistencies in the model, the company imposed ad-hoc restrictions to the extrapolated survival outcomes. Specifically, the EFS curve is constrained to values less than or equal to MFS, and the MFS curve is constrained to values less than or equal to OS. While this approach overcomes the limitations of the PSM and is not, in principle, unreasonable, the restrictions do not reflect empirical data or inherent structural links between endpoints. Therefore, it is important to assess the appropriateness of the extrapolated survival curve fits (EFS, MFS and OS) relative to one another to ensure logical consistency across outcomes (Section 4.2.5). 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 446 -->

Importantly, the company’s model does not account for survival outcomes related to separate clinical events within the post-progression health state, beyond the distinction between LR and DM. This includes outcomes for patients in the post-recurrence period (e.g., post-recurrence events and deaths), which are likely to be affected by subsequent therapy use after recurrence. This means that the extrapolated survival outcomes only reflect subsequent anticancer therapies used in NIAGARA, and the PSM does not allow adjustment to the survival outcomes for the use of different types of postprogression therapies, such as those used in the NHS. Furthermore, the use of external data from metastatic trials cannot be incorporated into the PSM to more accurately reflect outcomes in the DM state. While the separation of the LR and DM states is important in MIBC, the modelled costs of subsequent therapies are expressed as a proportion of all progressed patients (Section 4.2.7). This means that any differences in costs (or benefits) of subsequent therapies cannot be attributed to the individual LR and DM health states, although the EAG’s clinical advisor indicated that subsequent therapy costs are expected to be similar between these states. 

Additionally, the PSM approach is only valid if patients move progressively through health states to a worse health state. This is a potential limitation if post-recurrence therapies can return a proportion of patients to an event-free state where their health-related quality of life and risk of future events is similar to patients in the pre-recurrence EF health state. 

The EAG notes that the NIAGARA trial included a PFS-2 outcome, defined as the time from randomisation to subsequent progression or recurrence post-EFS event, or progression-free survival after second-line therapy. The EAG considers this endpoint important in the perioperative setting because it reflects the durability of treatment benefit beyond the first treatment and could offer greater granularity in modelling of events over time. At the clarification stage, the EAG requested that the company consider amending the existing model structure to incorporate PFS-2 data and, if this was not feasible, to provide qualitative commentary on the potential implications of excluding these data from the existing model structure (EAG clarifications, question B4). In their response, the company states that the exclusion of PFS-2 data from the model was an intentional structural decision, informed by both clinical and modelling considerations, for the following reasons: (i) the model based on the primary EFS and secondary OS and MFS endpoints fully capture the clinical and economic outcomes in the MIBC setting; (ii) the approach is aligned with previous NICE appraisals (TA871,[15] TA683[33] and TA816[34] ) that utilised similar primary and secondary endpoints; (iii) the model structure and selected endpoints have been validated and supported by HTA experts in an advisory board meeting; and (iv) the model structure would require potentially non-standard health state definitions and transition pathways, introducing extra complexity and uncertainty into the model for questionable analytic gain. Whilst the EAG acknowledges these points, the EAG believes that PFS-2 data could provide additional granularity in the area between the EFS and MFS curves by providing information 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 447 -->

on the timing and sequence of subsequent events, as well as the impact of subsequent treatments on long-term survival outcomes. This may be particularly important in the perioperative setting, where multiple phases of treatment are considered and long-term outcomes are influenced by both initial and subsequent therapies. PFS-2 data is also gaining increasing interest because it often correlates more strongly with OS than PFS alone,[35] especially when subsequent lines of therapy can confound OS. Nonetheless, the EAG notes that xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx in the NIAGARA trial (Figure 12 and Section 2.6.2.7 of the CS), indicating xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx 

xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx 

xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx. Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that additional modelling of PFS-2 data from NIAGARA would offer limited further insight. 

In summary, while the EAG considers the company’s model structure to be appropriate, the EAG considers it important to acknowledge the limitations of the PSM compared to alternative STMs. 

## **4.2.3 Population** 

## _4.2.3.1 Summary of company’s submission_ 

The target population consists of adults with resectable MIBC who are eligible to receive gemcitabine and cisplatin, in line with the anticipated marketing authorisation for perioperative durvalumab and the population included in the NIAGARA trial. The trial included adults with histologically or cytologically documented resectable MIBC (T2N0/1M0-T4aN0/1M0) who were cisplatin-eligible, candidates for RC, and had not received prior systemic chemotherapy or immunotherapy for MIBC. 

The modelled population is based on the baseline characteristics of participants in the ITT population of the NIAGARA trial, with a mean age of 64.4 years, proportion of males 81.8%, and a mean weight of 77.1 kg (see Table 7 of CS). 

No subgroups are considered in the model. 

## _4.2.3.2 Points for critique_ 

The EAG is satisfied that the modelled population aligns with the final scope issued by NICE and the anticipated marketing authorisation for perioperative durvalumab. However, as discussed in Section 3.2.1, the EAG has some concerns about the generalisability of the NIAGARA trial population to NHS patients. Specifically, the trial excluded patients with advanced lymph node N2 and N3 disease, and the EAG’s clinical advisor considered the NIAGARA population may be younger than patients with MIBC who are eligible for RC in UK clinical practice. Although data provided by NHS England for the North East suggests that patients with resectable MIBC who receive neoadjuvant cisplatinbased chemotherapy have a mean age of 66 years and 75% male, which is not dissimilar to the 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 448 -->

average age and percentage of males used in the model. However, it remains uncertain whether this regional data is representative of the whole of England and Wales. 

In response to EAG clarifications (questions A2 and A3), the company states that the generalisability of the NIAGARA trial population was discussed with UK-based clinicians who unanimously confirmed that it was reflective of NHS patients eligible for cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy. The company was unable to provide a comparison to SACT data and indicated that the BAUS MITRE audit only includes a small subset of patients (8.08% of the overall audit) representative of the target population. 

The EAG specifically notes age as important because the cost-effectiveness of perioperative durvalumab is sensitive to the baseline starting age used in the model, where the modelled long-term extrapolation survival curves are adjusted for the corresponding age- and gender-matched general population hazard rates of all-cause mortality (Section 4.2.5). 

The EAG considers it reasonable to not consider subgroups in the economic analysis because subgroup analyses from the NIAGARA trial (reported in Section 2.7 of CS) showed consistency in efficacy between the ITT population and the prespecified subgroups, including stratification by tumour PD-L1 expression level, clinical tumour stage, and renal function. 

## **4.2.4 Interventions and comparators** 

## _4.2.4.1 Summary of company’s submission_ 

The intervention is neoadjuvant durvalumab (1500 mg IV) in combination with gemcitabine (Day 1 and Day 8 at dose 1000 mg/m2) and cisplatin (Day 1 at dose 70 mg/m2) for four cycles every three weeks prior to RC, followed by durvalumab as monotherapy adjuvant treatment after RC for up to eight cycles every four weeks post-surgery. Perioperative durvalumab represents a fixed-duration regimen. In the model, time on treatment for the neoadjuvant and adjuvant phases is based on the observed proportions of participants who received each scheduled cycle in each arm of the NIAGARA trial (Section 4.2.7). 

The comparator in the company’s base case analysis aligns with the single treatment decision point for perioperative durvalumab, which is made before surgery and determines both pre- and post-RC treatment. For the neoadjuvant period, the comparator treatment is gemcitabine (Day 1 and Day 8 at dose 1000 mg/m2) and cisplatin (Day 1 at dose 70 mg/m2) for four cycles every three weeks prior to RC, i.e., the same as the intervention arm but without durvalumab. For the adjuvant period following NAC and RC, the comparator includes no treatment, which aligns with the control arm of NIAGARA. 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 449 -->

The company acknowledges that adjuvant treatment with nivolumab for people at high risk of recurrence after surgery and whose tumours express PD-L1 at a level of 1% or more was included in the NICE scope for this appraisal. In line with NICE TA817, nivolumab is recommended as an option for the adjuvant treatment of muscle-invasive urothelial cancer that is at high risk of recurrence after radical resection in adults whose tumours express PD-L1 ≥ 1%, only when adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy is unsuitable. Accordingly, for cisplatin-eligible patients, adjuvant nivolumab is appropriate if the patient has already received NAC. 

The company included adjuvant nivolumab (for the subset of patients meeting the treatment criteria) as part of the comparator arm in a scenario analysis only. The company’s justification for excluding adjuvant nivolumab from its base case analysis follows: 

- Adjuvant nivolumab and perioperative durvalumab occupy distinct points in the treatment pathway, where the decision on nivolumab treatment is only made after surgery: adjuvant nivolumab represents a reactive intervention based on post-surgical assessment and PD-L1 expression status, whereas the perioperative approach is a proactive strategy made pre-RC for all eligible patients. 

- The introduction of perioperative durvalumab is expected to displace the use of NAC alone, which in turn will reduce the use of subsequent treatments such as adjuvant nivolumab. 

- The control arm of NIAGARA did not include adjuvant nivolumab and the company acknowledges the challenges with conducting comparisons between adjuvant and perioperative settings. 

In response to the NICE scope that included adjuvant nivolumab in the comparator, the company conducted a scenario analysis where eligible high-risk PD-L1 ≥ 1% patients received adjuvant nivolumab instead of no treatment after neoadjuvant chemotherapy and RC. For this scenario, counterfactual survival times were estimated for the control arm of NIAGARA using a novel survival time-adjusted ITC approach (Section 3.5). 

## _4.2.4.2 Points for critique_ 

The primary issue with the comparator in the model is whether to include or exclude adjuvant nivolumab for the subset of patients eligible for this treatment. Adjuvant nivolumab is part of the current treatment pathway in the NHS for NAC patients at high-risk of recurrence post-surgery and with PD-L1 ≥ 1%. Thus, the appropriate comparator in the model to reflect established standard of care in the NHS should include a proportion of the population who meet the eligibility criteria receiving adjuvant nivolumab. 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 450 -->

The NIAGARA trial was not designed to include adjuvant nivolumab in the control arm for the highrisk, PD-L1 ≥ 1% population. Consequently, the control arm does not fully reflect the established standard of care in the NHS. To address this, the company conducted a scenario analysis that includes a proportion of the population receiving adjuvant nivolumab, based on NICE recommendations in TA817. This approach, however, required the company to estimate counterfactual survival times for the control arm of NIAGARA for the proportion of patients eligible for adjuvant nivolumab. As discussed in Section 3.5.3, the EAG acknowledges the limitations of the proposed survival timeadjusted ITC approach but, overall, considers the methods and approach used to include adjuvant nivolumab to be reasonable. Therefore, the EAG considers that the comparator arm should include a proportion of the population receiving adjuvant nivolumab to reflect the current treatment pathway in the NHS. 

## **4.2.5 Treatment effectiveness and extrapolation** 

## _4.2.5.1 Summary of company’s submission_ 

The model includes three elements relating to the treatment effectiveness and extrapolation of effects from the NIAGARA trial over a patient’s lifetime, separated by treatment arm: 

- (i) EFS, i.e., the time from initiation of intervention until the first occurrence of one of the following events: recurrence of disease after RC, disease progression in patients precluded from RC, residual disease in patients who refuse or fail to undergo RC, or death due to any cause. 

- (ii) MFS, i.e., the time from initiation of intervention until the first recognition of distant metastases or death due to any cause, whichever occurs first. 

- (iii) OS, i.e., the time from initiation of intervention until death due to any cause. 

The Kaplan-Meier (KM) time-to-event data from the NIAGARA trial (29 April 2024 data cut-off) for EFS, MFS, and OS is extrapolated over the long-term. This extrapolation uses parametric fitting to independent curves for each separate arm to determine health state membership (EF, LR, DM, or death) over time. Table 35 of the CS and section 3.2.1 (Table 5) summarises the endpoints included in the model. 

The survival modelling for EFS, MFS and OS included an assessment of the proportional hazards and accelerated failure time assumption, statistical goodness-of-fit measures (Akaike Information Criteria [AIC] and Bayesian Information Criteria [BIC]), visual inspection of model fit to KM data, and an assessment of the clinical plausibility of the extrapolations. Standard parametric models (exponential, Gompertz, Weibull, log-normal, log-logistic, generalised gamma, and gamma) and flexible spline models (Royston-Parmar spline models with 1–3 knots, link functions including hazard, normal, or 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 451 -->

odds) were considered. The company examined the hazard trend over time of the survival data to determine the candidate parametric or flexible models for each outcome independently. 

For EFS, the hazard profiles for each arm of NIAGARA exhibits a different non-monotonic hazard pattern; therefore, the company considered flexible models to be well suited for this outcome. From the spline-based models, all models showed a good visual fit to the data and the company’s clinical experts agreed that all curves presented could be plausible. The company selected the best-fitting spline model for each arm: for perioperative durvalumab this was 1-knot spline odds and for the control arm this was 2-knot spline normal. Figure 26 of CS shows the base case curve selection and fit to KM data for EFS. 

For MFS, the hazard profiles were broadly similar across arms with rates initially increasing to a peak before declining towards zero over the remaining follow-up. Standard parametric curves were excluded from consideration due to poor visual fit to the KM data. From the spline-based models, all models showed a good visual fit to the data and the company’s clinical experts agreed that all curves presented could be plausible. The company selected the best-fitting spline model for each arm: for both arms this was the 1-knot spline hazard. Figure 30 of CS shows the base case curve selection and fit to KM data for MFS. 

For OS, the company considered the hazard profiles to be well-captured by standard parametric models and therefore flexible models were not considered. In response to EAG clarifications question B6, the company provided spline-based models for OS; however, the company holds the view that standard parametric models are sufficient for OS extrapolation. For the perioperative durvalumab arm, the company selected the Gompertz distribution because it was preferred by two out of four clinical experts, even though it was not the best-fitting model according to goodness-of-fit statistics. For the control arm, the company excluded the best-fitting generalised gamma model from consideration because one clinical expert did not consider it plausible; although the reasons for this clinical opinion were not provided and no data presented to support it. In addition to assessing visual fit and clinical expert validation, the company compared the next three best-fitting distributions for the control arm (log-normal, Gompertz and log-logistic) with external literature for 5- and 10-year OS estimates (Table 40 of CS). The company selected the log-logistic distribution for the control arm because two out of the four clinical experts considered its long-term extrapolation more plausible and the 10-year estimate aligns more closely with external literature, even though it was the fourth best-fitting distribution and provided the lowest estimates of long-term OS. Figure 33 of CS shows the base case curve selection and fit to KM data for OS. 

Tables 41 and 42 of CS summarise the model selection for EFS, MFS and OS by treatment arm in the base case and scenario analyses where these curves are varied, respectively. 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 452 -->

The model uses UK life table data from the Office for National Statistics to constrain age- and genderadjusted mortality.[36] This ensures that the risk of death remains at or above background levels by age, i.e., the model is prevented from predicting that a patient’s risk of death is lower than the general population's risk by age. The hazards of EFS and MFS are also constrained to be at or above the ageand gender-adjusted all-cause general population risk of death by age. In addition, the EFS curve is constrained to values less than or equal to MFS, while the MFS curve is constrained to values less than or equal to OS. 

Figure 2 shows the survival curves used in the company’s base case analysis for the perioperative durvalumab and control arms. The time points indicated on the figure represent the points at which the curves pick up the all-cause general population risk of death. For perioperative durvalumab, the EFS picks this up at xx years, the MFS curve at xxxx years, and the OS curve at xxxx years. For the control arm, the EFS curve picks up the all-cause general population risk at xxxx years, the MFS curve at xxxx years, and the OS curve at xxxx years.

## _4.2.5.2 Points for critique_ 

The EAG has three primary concerns relating to the treatment effectiveness evidence and assumptions used in the model: 

- Immaturity of the OS data; 

- Model selection for the extrapolation of OS; and 

- Impact of starting age on survival outcomes. 

Before discussing these concerns in detail, the EAG critiques the company's approach to modelling survival outcomes using independent curve fits and the implementation of model constraints. This is necessary to evaluate the survival extrapolations, including the implicit cure assumption in the longterm projections. The EAG also considers the risk of non-cancer-related death from comorbidities in the target population. 

## _**Model selection based on independent curve fit**_ 

When modelling the survival outcomes of EFS, MFS, and OS, the curves fitted to the KM data to allow for long-term extrapolations are selected independently for each outcome, i.e., for each separate outcome, the most appropriate model (standard parametric or flexible spline) is fitted to the trial data. The approach used by the company for model selection appropriately follows guidance in NICE Decision Support Unit Technical Support Document (TSD) 14[37] and TSD 21[38] , which involves selecting a model with good statistical fit and clinical plausibility for each endpoint and with the extrapolated survival probabilities validated against clinical expert opinion and external literature. 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 454 -->

However, when the endpoints are considered independently, the extrapolated outcomes may create clinically implausible scenarios, e.g., the intermediate outcomes of EFS and MFS may predict better survival than OS, or the extrapolated EFS curve may cross the MFS curve. To address these inconsistencies, the company added ad-hoc restrictions to the extrapolated survival outcomes in the model. While the EAG considers the added restrictions to be a reasonable approach, the EAG believes it is important to assess the appropriateness of the extrapolated survival curve fits (EFS, MFS and OS) relative to one another rather than examine the best fitting distribution to each outcome independently. This can be done by identifying a consistent set of extrapolation functions across all three outcomes that satisfy the requirement for EFS ≤ MFS ≤ OS ≤ general population mortality, thereby removing the need for ad-hoc constraints within the model. 

In response to EAG clarifications (question B5a), the company states that for most parametric distributions, it is not feasible to identify alternative survival functions that logically align EFS, MFS and OS without the need for such constraints. Within the company's model, the EAG explored different combinations of alternative survival functions in an attempt to logically align the three outcomes; however, the EAG noted that a trade-off is required between the model's fit to the trial data and logical consistency across the outcomes, i.e., the set of extrapolation curves that logically align are not among the best-fitting models to the KM data, either statistically or visually. The EAG also notes that models with excellent fit to the observed data may perform poorly in extrapolation.[39] Therefore, the EAG accepts that the company’s approach is reasonable, but consideration must be given to the time points at which the logical constraints are imposed in order to assess the robustness of the extrapolations. 

## _**Implementation of constraints within the model**_ 

To overcome the logical inconsistencies in the model between the extrapolated curves for EFS, MFS, OS and background all-cause general population risk of death, constraints are implemented in the model using a two-step approach. In step 1, the hazard rates for EFS, MFS, and OS are constrained to be at or above the corresponding age- and gender-matched all-cause risk of death for the general population. For each treatment arm, Figure 4 shows the time points at which the hazard rate for each survival endpoint matches this background mortality rate, at which point the background hazard rate is applied. The hazard rate for OS in the perioperative durvalumab arm matches the background mortality hazard at xxx years, while in the control arm, this happens much later at xxxx years. In the perioperative durvalumab arm, the hazard rates for EFS and MFS match the background mortality hazard at xxx and xxxx years, respectively, while in the control arm the corresponding time points are xxxx for EFS and xxxx years for MFS. 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 455 -->

These time points, at which the risk of an event approaches the background mortality of the general population, are important for interpreting the implied ‘cure’ from cancer arising from the model selection, and the impact of starting age in the model, both of which are discussed further below. 

## **Figure 4 Independent hazard rate plots for EFS, MFS and OS compared to general population mortality hazards by treatment arm** 

**==> picture [451 x 127] intentionally omitted <==**

In step 2, the survival probabilities for OS are constrained to be the maximum of EFS and MFS, while the EFS curve is constrained to values less than or equal to MFS. The EAG noted that the latter constraint was implemented within the electronic version of the model such that the MFS curve picked up the values of the EFS curve at the point of crossing rather than an adjustment to the EFS curve to match MFS (i.e., EFS=MFS at the point of crossing) as implied in the CS by the statement that _“EFS is constrained to values that are less than or equal to MFS”_ . The EAG updated the company’s electronic model to reflect this logical constraint on EFS (see Section 5). 

The adjustment to OS was implemented in the model by specifying a dominant curve for extrapolation, with two options available in the electronic version of the model: (i) OS set equal to EFS at the point of crossing; or (ii) EFS set equal to OS at the point of crossing. In the base case analysis, the company chose option (i). When the EAG requested justification for this (clarifications question B5b), the company explained that patients who achieve long-term remission in the EFS state are likely to be cured of their disease and would only experience background all-cause mortality. The company argued against the alternative of setting EFS equal to OS at the crossing point because it could potentially lead to an abrupt decline in EFS, implying a rapid increase in mortality from the crossing point forward. However, the EAG notes that if the EFS curve is constrained to values less than or equal to MFS, and the MFS curve is constrained to values less than or equal to OS, then the EFS curve would never dominate the OS curve. Thus, the adjustment to OS is not required in the model when the adjustment to the EFS curve is made such that EFS is less than or equal to MFS. 

## _**Immaturity of the OS data used in the extrapolations**_ 

The OS data used in the company’s base case analysis from NIAGARA, as of the 29 April 2024 data cut-off, is immature (28.7% maturity overall with 305 death events). Median OS has not yet been 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 456 -->

reached. The median duration of follow-up for OS was 42.3 months in the perioperative durvalumab arm and 39.6 months in the control arm. The date at which the final data cut for OS (IA-2) will become available is not indicated in the CS. 

Different parametric extrapolations of the immature OS data lead to different projections of long-term survival. Figure 5 shows the extrapolated OS curves based on the four best-fitting parametric models (ranked by AIC/BIC, Table 38 of the CS), with constraints implemented. The 10-year survival probabilities for the perioperative durvalumab arm range from xxxx using the log-logistic model (least optimistic parametric model for both arms) to xxxxx using the Gompertz model (most optimistic parametric model for both arms), while the corresponding probabilities for the control arm range from xxxx to xxxx for the log-logistic and Gompertz models, respectively. The implications of the different parametric OS extrapolations on the company’s cost-effectiveness results are explored in Section 5.2.2, where the EAG explores the impact of selecting the most optimistic OS in both arms (Gompertz model) and the least optimistic OS in both arms (log-logistic model). 

Importantly, the EAG notes that uncertainty in the OS projections not only impacts the survival benefit for perioperative durvalumab relative to the control arm, but it also has implications for the implied time point of ‘cure’ from cancer, where the risk of death becomes equal to that of the general population. Consequently, the starting age in the model is a key input as it directly determines the allcause mortality risk in the general population.

## _**Model selection for extrapolation of survival outcomes**_ 

The EAG has no major concerns regarding model selection for the extrapolation of KM data for EFS and MFS. The approach used by the company aligns with guidance from the NICE DSU TSD 14 and TSD 21, and the EAG agrees with the company that the hazard profiles for both outcomes suggest flexible models may be more appropriate than standard parametric models. However, the EAG is unclear why the generalised gamma model was not considered suitable by the company for the extrapolation of EFS in the control arm. This model was ranked first by statistical AIC and BIC criterion across both the parametric and flexible models (Table 36 of the CS) and shows a good visual fit to the KM data. Whilst the company states that this model offers poor fit to the observed hazards, the EAG considers the fit comparable to that of the spline-based models (Figure 9 for generalised gamma model compared to Figures 6, 7 and 8 for spline-based models in Appendix L of the CS). In Section 5.2.2, the EAG explores the impact on the cost-effectiveness results of selecting the generalised gamma model for EFS in the control arm. 

In contrast, the EAG has two major concerns regarding model selection for the extrapolation of OS. Firstly, the EAG considers the justification for selecting standard parametric models over flexible models for OS extrapolation to be inconsistent with the approach taken for MFS. The hazard profile for OS is not dissimilar to that for MFS; for both outcomes, the hazard rates initially increase to a peak before declining towards zero over the remaining follow-up - although the control arm MFS hazard appears to flatten slightly from 36 months onwards (see Figures 10 and 19 in Appendix L of the CS for MFS and OS, respectively). However, flexible models were not considered for the extrapolation of OS. Moreover, the presence of two turning points in the OS hazard plot for the control arm suggests that a flexible model may be appropriate. In response to EAG clarification question B6b, the company supplied an updated electronic version of the model that allows for flexible models (Royston-Parmar spline models with 1–3 knots, link functions including hazard, normal, or odds) to be implemented for OS extrapolation. 

The EAG considers that the flexible models provide sufficient statistical and visual fit to OS for both arms of NIAGARA. The flexible models have lower AIC and BIC values than standard parametric models, suggesting better statistical fit (Table 18 of the company’s response to EAG clarifications for flexible model and Table 38 of the CS for standard parametric models). The EAG also considers the visual fit of the alternative flexible models to be sufficient (Figures 11-13 of the company’s response to EAG clarifications). The impact of using flexible models on the long-term OS projections when compared with the company’s base case parametric model selections (Gompertz for the perioperative durvalumab arm and log-logistic for the control arm) differs by treatment arm. For the perioperative durvalumab arm, the company’s base case selection closely aligns with the best‑fitting flexible model of 1‑knot odds (see Figure 6). In contrast, for the control arm, there is a substantial difference in the 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 458 -->

OS projections between the best‑fitting flexible model of 1‑knot hazard and the company’s base case selection of log-logistic (see Figure 6). Figure 6 also shows that the generalised gamma and Gompertz models are the standard parametric models that most closely align with the projections from the best fitting flexible model. Therefore, the EAG is satisfied that the model selection for OS in the perioperative durvalumab arm in the company’s base case is reasonable, but the selection of the loglogistic model for the control arm may not be reasonable as it produces the least favourable OS compared to alternative better fitting models.

Secondly, the EAG is concerned that the trend in OS hazard rates between the perioperative durvalumab and control arms in the company’s base case analysis is inconsistent with the observed hazard rates over time from NIAGARA. Figure 32 of the CS shows that the OS hazard rates in both the perioperative durvalumab and control arms reach a peak at around 10 months post-randomisation. After this point, the observed differences between arms start to converge, moving towards near‑zero rates by the end of the follow‑up period. The EAG believes the model selection for the extrapolation of OS should reflect this convergence between arms of the trial (i.e., the hazard ratio for the difference between arms should approach the value of one beyond the trial follow-up period to reflect the convergence in the observed hazards in NIAGARA). Therefore, the EAG considers the company’s base case model selection for OS extrapolation in the control arm to be overestimating mortality in this arm, because the difference between the treatment arms over the long-term is implying that the hazard ratio is increasing over a longer period, but there is no empirical evidence to suggest that the hazard is increasing over time. 

In response to EAG clarifications (question B7), the company argues that the observed convergence in the OS hazard rates between arms (Figure 32 of the CS) may be unduly influenced by a low number of participants at risk at the end of the trial follow-up period. Thus, the company did not explicitly consider this convergence when selecting the independent OS extrapolations for each arm. In addition, the company states that the application of the general population mortality constraint means 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 459 -->

that hazards between arms eventually converge in the model. Whilst the EAG acknowledges this eventual convergence, the EAG considers that the convergence trend starts much earlier in the observed hazards for OS (i.e., not just in the tails of the KM data), where a reasonable number of participants are still at risk. The hazards for both arms eventually converge due to the general population mortality constraint, but this only occurs at the time point of xxx years, when the OS hazard rate in the control arm matches the general population mortality hazard rate. Therefore, the EAG considers the company’s base case model selection for OS (Gompertz, which is the most optimistic model selection for the perioperative durvalumab arm, and log‑logistic, which is the most pessimistic model selection for the control arm) to be inconsistent with the observed hazards from NIAGARA. Figure 7 shows that the hazard rates for OS in the perioperative durvalumab and control arms of the company’s base case analysis increases over time until the general population mortality constraint is applied at xxxx years.
