In the company’s base case, the log‑logistic model was selected for OS in the control arm because it provided 10-year projections that closely align with external registry data and because two out of the four clinical experts consulted by the company considered it the most plausible long‑term extrapolation (Tables 39 and 40 of the CS). Whilst the EAG agrees that long-term OS estimates should be externally validated, the relative effect between treatment arms must also be appropriately assessed. The company’s approach of independently fitting models separately to each arm means that the relative effectiveness between arms has not been sufficiently validated. The EAG also notes that the population in the NIAGARA control arm and the external registry studies considered by the company for validation differ (see Table 5). In particular, none of the registry studies are UK-based; the median ages reported in Mahoney 2025 (72 years) and Faraj 2021 (69 years) are higher than in NIAGARA (64.4 years), Mak 2014 includes data collected between 1988 and 2007 and Vlaming 2020 is a single-institution study conducted in the Netherlands, with data collection from 1998 to 2016. 

In summary, the EAG considers the best fitting flexible models (1-knot odds model for the perioperative durvalumab arm and the 1-knot hazard model for the control arm) to be the most appropriate model selection for OS extrapolation because they best reflect the observed hazard profile of OS in the NIAGARA trial. These models inform the EAG’s preferred base case assumptions (Section 5.2.3) 

## _**Implicit cure assumption**_ 

In NICE technology appraisal (TA817) for adjuvant nivolumab, a cure assumption was explicitly modelled. This was based on evidence from CheckMate-274 which showed that the risk of death approaches that of the general population at 5 years. In TA817, the company’s base case assumed a cure point of 5 years, while the EAG’s exploratory analysis considered a 10-year cure point. However, the committee concluded that it remains uncertain at which time point it is reasonable to assume that people are cured of cancer. The committee noted that there is evidence that disease recurrence may take place after 5 years and mortality risks remain elevated.[15] 

For perioperative durvalumab, the company’s model does not include an explicit cure assumption. Instead, a time point for cure from cancer is implicitly modelled via the decreasing hazards of survival over time, particularly for the perioperative durvalumab EFS curve, where a large proportion of patients are implicitly treated as ‘cured’. For a patient to be considered ‘cured’ of MIBC, two conditions must be met: (i) the risk of events (recurrence or progression) defined by the EFS curve must not be greater than the risk of all-cause death, and (ii) there must be no risk of cancer-related deaths. In the company’s base case analysis, these conditions are met after xxx years in the perioperative durvalumab arm and after xxxx years in the control arm (see Figure 2). At these time points, xxxxx of patients in the perioperative durvalumab arm and xxxxx of patients in the control arm 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 462 -->

remain in the EF health state. These patients have no risk of recurrence, progression or cancer-related death, and their only risk is all-cause mortality. Therefore, a large proportion of patients are considered ‘cured’ in the company’s base case analysis after xxx years in the perioperative durvalumab arm and xxxx years in the control arm. 

The clinical advisor to the EAG suggested that it is clinically plausible that a proportion of patients with MIBC can be considered cured if they have no disease recurrence after a significant period. However, this proportion is uncertain. The EAG notes that a comparison with TA817 cannot be made because the population (high-risk of recurrence) and timepoint of treatment (adjuvant following RC) is different from the perioperative setting. The EAG considers the proportion of patients implicitly assumed to be cured to be an uncertainty in the company’s cost-effectiveness results. The time point of cure implied by the long-term projections of survival should be assessed in relation to the plausibility of the company’s survival extrapolations, which are also impacted by the starting age of the modelled cohort. 

## _**Impact of baseline age on modelled survival outcomes**_ 

The starting age of the modelled cohort has a large impact on the extrapolated OS probabilities (see Figure 10). This is because the hazard rate of OS is constrained to be at or above the age- and gendermatched all-cause general population risk of death. Therefore, the time point at which the risk of death approaches that of the general population depends on the starting age used in the model. The impact of age is more pronounced in the perioperative durvalumab arm than in the control arm for two main reasons: (i) the OS hazard rates in the perioperative durvalumab arm approach the general population mortality earlier than in the control arm (xxx years vs xxxx years, respectively); and (ii) a greater proportion of patients are still alive in the perioperative durvalumab arm compared to the control arm when the OS hazard rate is equal to the general population hazard of death (xxxxx vs xxxxx respectively). Consequently, when the modelled cohort starts perioperative treatment at an older age (e.g., age 70 years in Figure 10 compared to the base case starting age of 64.4 years), where general population mortality rates are higher, the difference in survival between the two arms diminishes more rapidly after the point at which the hazards meet. This reduces the estimated life year gains for the perioperative durvalumab arm compared to the control arm from xxx years in the company’s base case analysis to xxx years with a starting age of 70 years. The opposite is true for a younger starting age (e.g., age 60 years in Figure 10), where general population mortality rates are lower, the relative difference in survival between treatment arms is permitted to last longer, resulting in an increase in life year gains to xxx years. 

One of the EAG’s clinical advisors suggested that patients eligible for neoadjuvant chemotherapy for MIBC in the NHS are typically older than those in the NIAGARA trial, with many patients between 70 and 79 years of age. However, data provided by NHS England to the EAG suggests that NHS 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 463 -->

patients in the North East with resectable MIBC who receive neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy have a mean age of 66 years and 75% are male, which is not dissimilar to the company’s base case starting age and gender distribution, but it is uncertain whether this data is representative of the whole of England and Wales. In Section 5.2.2, the EAG explores the impact on the cost-effectiveness results of using a starting age of 70 years in the model.

## _**Increased risk of non-cancer-related death due to comorbidities in population with MIBC**_ 

The EAG is concerned that people with MIBC in the NIAGARA trial are likely to have a higher risk of non-cancer-related death compared with the general population. This is because participants have mortality risk factors including smoking (23.7% current smokers and 49.3% ex‑smokers; see Table 7 of the CS) and other comorbidities (section 3.2.3). The EAG clinical advisors confirmed that an increased mortality risk (cancer non-related) for this population is clinically plausible. This means that even after removing the risk of cancer‑related death, the overall risk of death for this population is likely to be higher than the general population mortality risk. 

An excess risk has not been considered in the company’s base case analysis. The EAG notes that data from NIAGARA can provide some information about the increased risk due to comorbidities in the target population. In NIAGARA, there were 305 deaths in total across the two arms (see Table 17 of the CS); of these deaths, 199 were attributed to bladder cancer (see Table 20 of the CS). This indicates that at least 106 deaths were due to non-cancer-related causes over a 5-year follow-up period (longest follow up = 64.7 months) (it is “at least” because some deaths among withdrawals [n=53 across two arms – see Table 6 of the CS] may not have been recorded). The 5-year probability of non-cancerrelated death in NIAGARA is therefore estimated to be 9.97%. The corresponding 5-year age- and gender-adjusted mortality probability for the general population is 7.11%.[36] Assuming an exponential model for simplicity, the hazard ratio (increased death risk) would be 1.42 for people in NIAGARA 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 464 -->

versus the general population (details on how this risk is calculated are provided in the electronic version of the model). The EAG considers that this increased risk may provide a plausible scenario to reflect the mortality risk attributed to non-cancer causes in the target population. In Section 5.2.2, the EAG explores the impact on the cost-effectiveness results of using an increased death risk (hazard ratio of 1.42) in the target population compared to the general population risk. 

## **4.2.6 Health related quality of life** 

## _4.2.6.1 Summary of company’s submission_ 

The company conducted a systematic literature review to identify studies reporting HRQoL data in patient with MIBC (see Appendix F of CS). Of the 24 studies identified, only one study[40] reported EQ-5D-5L UK data but did not provide utility values mapped to the EQ-5D-5L UK value set. Furthermore, another study[41] provided relevant EQ-5D-3L utilities for the health states (as described in Section 4.2.2) used in the cost-effectiveness model. However, the utility values were based on the United States based value set. The company identified NICE appraisal TA817[15] that used utility values relevant to the UK setting but the actual scores used in TA817 were redacted in the final reports. Therefore, the company considered the health state utilities identified in the SLR unsuitable for use in the cost-effectiveness analysis. 

The NIAGARA trial collected individual patient-level HRQoL data using the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire. The health state utilities used in the cost-effectiveness analysis were derived from the analysis of the NIAGARA trial EQ-5D-5L data using Hernandez-Alava et al.'s 5L to 3L mapping algorithm[42] and using a mixed effects repeated measures (MMRM) model. The utilities were modelled as treatment-independent estimates, assuming that a patient's HRQoL in a given health state is the same regardless of whether they receive perioperative durvalumab or the control arm. 

The company used the prospective bladder cancer infrastructure (ProBCI) registry[43] to validate the utilities derived from the analysis of the NIAGARA trial. Health state utilities were capped by ageand sex-matched UK general population utility. The age-adjustment was modelled using the health state utilities by age equations from Ara and Brazier (2010)[44] and applied to each cycle for the duration of the time horizon. 

HRQoL decrements (disutilities) are applied to the proportion of patients who underwent cystectomy and to patients experiencing AEs while on treatment. The one-off QALY adjustment was accrued at the start of the time horizon in the model as the model assumes that both cystectomy and treatmentrelated AEs are expected to have a temporary impact on HRQoL. 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 465 -->

## _4.2.6.2 Health state utilities_ 

To derive the health state utilities, the company performed four MMRM analyses with covariates for ‘randomised group only’, ‘disease state only’, and two models combining disease state and randomisation group, with and without interaction terms. The relative performance of each model was assessed using statistical goodness-of-fit based on AIC (see Table 43 of CS). The best-fitting model was the MMRM with covariates for ‘disease state only’. The analysis estimated utilities using the event times for EFS and MFS from the NIAGARA study. 

The company used ProBCI registry,[43] which collects clinical and HRQoL (including EQ-5D-5L) data from patients with MIBC, non-muscle invasive and metastatic bladder cancer in the Netherlands, to validate the findings of the NIAGARA study. The changes in the health state utilities comparing preversus post-recurrence in ProBCI (xxxx) was considered consistent by the company with the NIAGARA results for DM MIBC (xxxx), while mean utilities for the pre-event state (xxxx) in ProBCI were also considered similar to the mean utility for EF in NIAGARA (0.847). The company notes that the analysis of ProBCI registry data does not yield different results based on LR or DM, and hence it is only used to validate the NIAGARA findings. The CS did not provide details about the patient characteristics from the ProBCI sample. However, in response to EAG clarifications (question B20) the company indicated that the difference in health state utilities between pre- and postrecurrence states was for a subpopulation of ProBCI that best matched the key inclusion criteria of the NIAGARA trial and valued using the UK 5L value set[45] (Table 29 of company’s response to EAG clarifications).

## _**Points for critique**_ 

The EAG considers the company’s approach for estimating health state utilities to be appropriate. The approach used is consistent with that used in NICE TA817 for adjuvant nivolumab, and the justification for selecting the best-fitted model is appropriate. However, the EAG notes that the utility values derived from the NIAGARA study are xxxxxxxx. In fact, the utility value for the EF health state is higher than the corresponding age- and gender-matched general population utility value of 0.816 based on Ara and Brazier (2010). This suggests that HRQoL for patients with MIBC in an EF 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 466 -->

state in the NIAGARA study is greater than HRQoL of the UK general population without cancer, which may suggest that the population of the NIAGARA trial had better quality of life than patients who receive NAC in the NHS 

The difference between the mean health state utilities for LR and DM is relatively small (xxxxx). Clinical advice to the EAG stated that MIBC has a substantial impact on patients’ HRQoL, with LR potentially having worse HRQoL than metastasis due to pain. The company states that the small difference in utility values between DM and EF from the NIAGARA study ( xxxxx) represents a conservative estimate for cost-effectiveness. This is because the perioperative durvalumab arm has a greater proportion of the cohort in the EF health state than in the DM state, relative to the control arm. The EAG agrees that the small difference for DM is potentially conservative as a larger decrement in HRQoL would be expected for DM, given its poorer prognosis and survival. 

_4.2.6.3 Disutility associated with AEs and cystectomy_ 

The company’s model considers HRQoL loss associated with treatment-related AEs and cystectomy. At the start of the model’s time horizon, a one-off QALY decrement is applied to the proportion of patients who underwent cystectomy and to the proportion of patients who experienced treatmentrelated AEs. The utility decrements for these events were primarily sourced from published literature, mainly previous NICE TAs (see Table 45 of CS). The EAG notes that the company did not justify whether it was possible to derive utility decrements for these events from the analysis of EQ-5D-5L data collected in the NIAGARA study. 

## _**Cystectomy**_ 

The utility decrement for cystectomy was sourced from the Life After Bladder Cancer (LABC) study,[46] a prospective UK study in patients with a new bladder cancer diagnosis. The EAG’s clinical advisor indicated that undergoing RC has a drastic impact on patient’s HRQoL; while some patients adapt successfully to live well without their bladder, others experience severe leakage issues causing profound distress, embarrassment and diminished HRQoL. Many patients in this demographic have multiple age-related health complications, further complicating recovery. 

The model applies a temporary impact on HRQoL in the early phases of treatment, with a disutility (- 0.06) during the first 6 months after surgery. Advice from the EAG’s clinical experts and published evidence[47] indicates that patients with a history of cystectomy have a detrimental effect on HRQoL compared with an average person of the same age and sex without MIBC. 

## _**Adverse events**_ 

Utility decrements associated with AEs (Table 16) were not treatment-specific and sourced from published literature. The included AEs are Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) of grade 3 or 4 with an incidence of ≥ 5% in either treatment arm of NIAGARA. The 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 467 -->

impact of AEs was calculated as the sum of the product of disutility, frequency, and duration of the AE. 

A similar assumption was applied in the company’s scenario with adjuvant nivolumab to estimate the QALY loss associated with AEs. In this scenario, AEs of CTCAE grade 3 or higher was sourced from the CheckMate-274 trial.[20]

For the utility decrement for cystectomy, the EAG’s clinical advisors considered a timeframe of 6 months for the impact on patients’ HRQoL to be short. The utility decrement duration had minimal impact on the costeffectiveness results (see Tables 32 and 33 of company’s response to EAG clarifications). 

The selection of AEs for the perioperative durvalumab and control arms are described clearly in the CS. The EAG notes that the duration of AEs in the model is shorter than the model cycle length and the frequency of AEs is less than 20%. Therefore, AEs have minimal impact on the cost-effectiveness estimates. 

## **4.2.7 Resources and costs** 

## _4.2.7.1 Summary of company’s submission_ 

The company conducted a systematic literature review to identify relevant cost and healthcare resource use (HCRU) data in patients with MIBC (see Appendix G of CS for details). Of the studies identified, only two studies provided resource use and cost data for a UK setting;[52, 53] however, these studies did not provide sufficient detail and were not considered relevant for the model by the company. 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 468 -->

The CS includes costs related to: (i) drug acquisition and administration; (ii) cystectomy; (iii) health state resource use; (iv) AE management; (v) subsequent treatments post-recurrence; and (vi) end of life care. Unit costs were informed by national published sources, including the National schedule of NHS costs, BNF, PSSRU costs and eMIT, inflated to 2023/24 prices where appropriate and discounted at an annual rate of 3.5%. The dosing regimen for each drug was based on their respective SmPCs. Table 17 summarises the costs included in the company’s base case analysis. 

The time on treatment for neoadjuvant and adjuvant components of both the perioperative durvalumab and control arms was modelled using the observed proportions of patients who received each scheduled cycle in each arm of the NIAGARA trial (see Table 24 of company’s response to EAG clarifications). The proportions of patients receiving treatments from the NIAGARA study could be used directly in the model, without the need for extrapolation beyond the observed trial period, because no patients remained on neoadjuvant or adjuvant treatment at the data cut-off. 

The administration form for all drugs considered was intravenous (IV), except for the subsequent treatment of erdafitinib, which takes oral form. The same administration costs (£394.17) were applied for all IV therapies in the model. If several drugs were given together, it was assumed they incurred a single administration cost. 

The costs associated with cystectomy were based on the proportion of patients undergoing cystectomy in the NIAGARA trial. The company considered only patients who underwent RC (88% in the perioperative durvalumab arm and 83.2% in the control arm). The unit cost of RC was sourced from NHS reference costs 2023-24[54] and calculated as a weighted average of service codes associated with cystectomy, urinary diversion and reconstruction using NHS activity as weights (Table 52 of CS). The six patients in the NIAGARA trial (1.1% of participants included in the study) who refused cystectomy but achieved a complete clinical response and entered the non-cystectomy extension phase received durvalumab for up to eight additional cycles, following their initial four cycles of neoadjuvant durvalumab plus chemotherapy. The cost of cycles administered during the noncystectomy extension phase were excluded from the treatment cost calculations used in the model. 

HCRU associated with disease management was incorporated to capture costs of medical resource use by patients in each health state. The same disease management costs were applied to both treatment arms (Table 50 of CS). 

The company included costs associated with AEs by estimating the sum product of the unit cost, duration and frequency, and applying it as a one-off cost at the start of the model time horizon. Unit costs for AE management were sourced from NHS reference costs 2023-24.[54] The company did not 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 469 -->

include any AE costs for subsequent therapies post-recurrence because the company expected it to have minimal influence on incremental cost-effectiveness results. 

The company included subsequent treatments post-recurrence by assuming that a different proportion of patients received subsequent cancer treatment in the perioperative durvalumab and the control arms. In the NIAGARA trial, the proportion of patients who received a subsequent anticancer therapy was xxxxx; however, a lower proportion of patients received at least one anticancer therapy poststudy treatment discontinuation in the perioperative arm (xxxxx) as compared to the control arm (xxxxx). The company states that some of the treatments received in the NIAGARA trial are not reflective of UK clinical practice. Therefore, in order to align with UK clinical practice, the subsequent treatments used in the model are based on UK clinical expert opinion (see Table 17). The subsequent treatment use by treatment arm was derived as an average across the four clinical experts interviewed by the company, which was xxxxx for the perioperative durvalumab arm and xxxxx for the control arm. These estimates were applied in the model to all patients who experienced progression (i.e., upon leaving the EF health state). In response to EAG clarifications (question B12b), the company provided an additional scenario analysis using the proportions of subsequent treatments based on the NIAGARA trial (see Table 25 of company response to EAG clarifications). 

The cost of end of life or terminal care was applied as a one-off cost upon entering the death state (Table 55 of CS).

## _4.2.7.2 Points for critique_ 

In general, the EAG considers the approach used by the company to derive resource use and costs to be appropriate. The drug acquisition and administration costs were informed with appropriate sources. The approach to estimate time on treatment based on the observed proportion of patients who received each scheduled treatment cycle in each arm of NIAGARA is appropriate as there is no reason to expect it to differ if administered in the NHS and no patient remained on neoadjuvant or adjuvant treatment in NIAGARA at the data cut-off. One limitation is that the costs of treatment cycles administered during the non-cystectomy extension phase were excluded from the treatment cost calculations. However, given that these patients represented only 1.1% of the trial population, this limitation is expected to have minimal impact on the results. In addition, these patients are expected to fall outside the licensed indication. 

For the costs of cystectomy, the EAG notes that the company assumed different proportions of patients in each arm undergoing surgery based on the NIAGARA trial. The EAG assesses the assumption that durvalumab leads to a lower proportion of patients undergoing cystectomy as uncertain in NHS practice. However, the EAG’s clinical advisor considered it a reasonable assumption in the absence of an alternative source. 

The EAG notes that the company included costs associated with AEs for the intervention and comparator but did not include costs associated with AEs for subsequent treatments post-recurrence because any AE costs for subsequent therapies are expected to impact both arms of the model. However, the EAG notes that the company assumed different proportions of patients receiving subsequent treatments post-recurrence for the perioperative durvalumab and control arms; therefore, total costs associated with AEs would be expected to differ between the two arms. Nonetheless, the EAG notes that the company’s assumption is potentially conservative given that the proportion of patients who received subsequent cancer treatment was higher in the control arm than the perioperative durvalumab arm. Therefore, the EAG does not expect the exclusion of AE costs associated with subsequent therapies to have a material impact on the cost-effectiveness results. 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 472 -->

The EAG has some concerns about the assumptions used for subsequent treatments in the model. The EAG notes that the subsequent treatment use was based on the opinion of four UK clinicians rather than the subsequent treatments used in the NIAGARA trial. The company justifies this approach because the NIAGARA trial was a global, multinational study where post-progression clinical practice varied between centres and different treatments may be available in each country. In principle, the EAG agrees with the company’s approach because the treatments used post-recurrence should reflect those available and most frequently used in NHS practice for MIBC. However, the extrapolated survival outcomes used in the model only reflect subsequent anticancer therapies used in NIAGARA. The model does not allow for adjustment to these survival outcomes to account for the different types of post-progression therapies, such as those used in the NHS. The EAG’s clinical advisors reviewed the treatments included in the company’s base case analysis and determined that most of them reflect UK clinical practice. However, they noted that nivolumab is not licensed as a treatment for recurrent/metastatic MIBC, i.e., not included as part of the subsequent treatments postrecurrence. Nivolumab is recommended as an adjuvant treatment for invasive urothelial cancer at high risk of recurrence. For this reason, in the EAG’s base case, the EAG has excluded nivolumab from the subsequent treatments post-recurrence (Section 5.2.3). Adjuvant nivolumab is considered as part of the treatment pathway for the comparator arm for patients eligible to receive it. 

The EAG's clinical advisor was uncertain about the proportion of patients receiving subsequent postrecurrence treatments in the NHS but agreed that the estimates in Table 54 of the CS are reasonable. The average cost of subsequent therapies was applied as a one-off cost to the proportion of all progressed patients, independent of the LR and DM health states. This means that any differences in costs of subsequent therapies cannot be attributed to the individual LR and DM health states. The EAG’s clinical advisor considered this to be a reasonable assumption because treatment regimens are similar across local and distant recurrences for MIBC. The EAG does not expect differences in subsequent treatments for LR and DM to have a material impact on cost-effectiveness results. 

The company has assumed that nivolumab and atezolizumab are used in IV form only. However, the EAG notes that both these drugs are also available in subcutaneous (SC) form. The EAG’s clinical advisors were unable to provide an estimate of the proportion of SC use verses IV use in NHS practice but noted that the availability of subcutaneous administration was a factor when choosing a treatment because it has time and resource savings compared with intravenous administration. In the absence of an estimate of the proportion of SC use, the EAG has considered a scenario in Section 5.2.2 that assumes that 25% of patients receive these treatments subcutaneously in NHS practice (i.e., 25% SC use and 75% IV use) based on recommendations in NICE Technology Appraisal ID6346[60] for SC use. In this scenario, the cost of SC administration is based on NHS reference cost code N10AF (£110.64 from NHS national tariff 2022/23 for SC[60] ). 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 473 -->

## _4.2.7.3 Summary of the costs included in the company’s scenario with nivolumab_ 

In Appendix K of the CS, the company provides information on HCRU and costs for the scenario that includes adjuvant nivolumab for PD-L1 expression ≥ 1% and high-risk MIBC patients. The drug acquisition cost for nivolumab was sourced from the BNF (2025) and its dosing regimen was derived from the SmPC for nivolumab and the CheckMate-274 trial (Table 5 of Appendix K to CS). Drug acquisition costs for the other treatments that form part of the control arm remain unchanged from the company’s base case. 

Time on treatment data was not available from the CheckMate-274 trial; therefore, time on treatment for adjuvant nivolumab was estimated using the adjusted EFS curve from the ITC to determine the proportion of patients receiving treatment in each model cycle. It was assumed that 15% of patients would discontinue adjuvant nivolumab after a single dose due to adverse events, based on CheckMate-274 data, while the remaining 85% would continue treatment until recurrence (according to the survival-time-adjusted EFS data from the ITC) or until completion of 12 months of therapy. The proportion of patients receiving each cycle of treatment is provided in Table 7, Appendix K, of the CS. 

The model used cost and healthcare resource use data for the health states from NICE TA817, which did not differ by treatment arm. The cost of cystectomy and AE management costs were based on assumptions made in the base-case analysis and assumed equal across arms (see AE frequencies provided in Table 3, Appendix K of CS). Subsequent treatment profiles for nivolumab were assumed to be the same as in the base-case analysis without nivolumab, but excluding the use of nivolumab as a subsequent treatment post-recurrence (see Table 8, Appendix K of CS). End-of-life costs were the same as the company’s base-case analysis. 

## _4.2.7.4 Points for critique_ 

For the resource use and costs assumed in the scenario that includes nivolumab, the EAG considers the assumptions associated with drug acquisition and administration costs to be reasonable, except that SC nivolumab may be used for a proportion of patients in NHS practice. 

The EAG notes that the company did not account for the cost of testing patients for the presence of PD-L1 expression ≥ 1%. In the perioperative durvalumab arm, all patients receive adjuvant durvalumab regardless of their PD-L1 expression level but, in the control arm, for patients to be eligible to receive adjuvant nivolumab they need to be at high risk of recurrence after radical resection and have tumours expressing PD-L1 at a level of 1% or more. Therefore, testing for PD-L1 expression is required for patients at high-risk of recurrence in the control arm. Consequently, the EAG has included the costs for PD-L1 testing in the scenario with nivolumab (Section 5.2.3). The unit cost for a PD-L1 test (£121.08) is based on NICE TA639.[61] This cost is applied as a one-off cost to 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 474 -->

the proportion of patients in the G+C+N arm (xxxxx the same as the proportion of patients who were at high risk of recurrence without residual disease after surgery in the NIAGARA control arm - see Table 7 of the company’s response to EAG clarifications). 

The company assumed the same subsequent treatments post-recurrence for the scenario with nivolumab as the base-case analysis, except with the exclusion of nivolumab as a post-recurrence treatment. The EAG notes that the use of adjuvant nivolumab could impact on the choice of subsequent therapies post-recurrence and, therefore, some differences may be expected in subsequent treatment use, with and without adjuvant nivolumab. Nonetheless, the EAG expects the impact of any differences on the cost-effectiveness results to be minor.

## _**5.2 EAG’s additional analyses**_ 

## **5.2.1 Model validation and face validity check** 

The EAG reviewed the company’s model in detail and applied the TECHnical VERification (TECHVER) checklist (see Appendix 3).[1] The EAG identified several errors in the electronic version of the model, which were corrected by the EAG: 

1. The extrapolated MFS curve picked up the extrapolated EFS curve at the point of crossing, while the CS states that ‘ _EFS is constrained to values that are less than or equal to MFS’_ . The EAG corrected this error such that the EFS curve picked up the MFS curve at the point of crossing, in line with the statements in the CS. This correction also meant that an adjustment to the OS curve was not required in the model when the extrapolated EFS curve crossed the OS curve because when the EFS curve is constrained to values less than or equal to MFS, and the MFS curve is constrained to values less than or equal to OS, then the EFS curve would never implausibly dominate the OS curve. 

2. The calculation formulae in worksheet ‘Model’, columns ER and HQ, rows 376-461 was not consistent with previous cells. For example, for cell ER376 the formulae =IF(Settings!$G$13="OS",MAX(EK376,EL376),EL376) was corrected to =MAX(EQ376,EL376). 

3. The calculation formulae relating to the hazards for the company’s scenario in response to EAG clarifications that sets the HR=1 after 5 years. However, this scenario does not form part of the company’s base case or EAG analyses; therefore, the error has no impact on the costeffectiveness results. 

4. In the probabilistic setting for the Cholesky decomposition for OS (calculation errors when selecting flexible models for OS extrapolation). This error involved corrections to multiple cells in the ‘parameters’ worksheet. 

Table 22 presents the results of the EAG corrected company base case, while Table 23 presents the results of the EAG corrected company scenario with adjuvant nivolumab.

## **5.2.3 EAG’s preferred assumptions** 

The EAG’s preferred assumptions include the following changes to the company’s base case: 

- The EAG considers the relevant comparator to be neoadjuvant chemotherapy and radical cystectomy (RC), followed by no treatment or adjuvant nivolumab in eligible patients. 

- The OS extrapolations are informed by the best fitting flexible spline models for each arm: for perioperative durvalumab this is the 1-knot spline odds and for the control arm this is the 1- knot spline hazard. This contrasts with the company’s standard parametric models, with the Gompertz distribution selected for the perioperative durvalumab arm and the log-logistic distribution for the control arm. 

- Subsequent treatments post-recurrence excludes nivolumab (nivolumab is not licensed as a treatment for recurrent/metastatic MIBC), which is included in the company’s base case. 

- The EAG includes the cost of PD-L1 testing for the comparator with adjuvant nivolumab. 

The comparator with adjuvant nivolumab was excluded from the company’s base case but included as a separate scenario by the company. Therefore, the EAG presents two base cases: 

- (i) EAG base case 1 with the same comparator as the company’s base case (i.e., without adjuvant nivolumab); and 

- (ii) EAG base case 2 with comparator consisting of neoadjuvant chemotherapy and RC, followed by no treatment or adjuvant nivolumab in eligible patients. 

Table 27 shows the cumulative impact of the EAG’s preferred assumptions on the company’s base case ICER – EAG base case 1, while Table 28 shows the cumulative impact of the EAG’s preferred assumptions on the company’s scenario with adjuvant nivolumab – EAG base case 2. 

Table 29 shows the corresponding probabilistic results for EAG base case 1 and EAG base case 2. The EAG notes that the probabilistic ICERs are sensitive to greater uncertainty in the flexible spline models for OS.

## **5.2.4 Scenario analyses using EAG’s preferred assumptions** 

Two important uncertainties remain that have a substantial impact on the cost-effectiveness results: 

- The starting age used in the model. 

- The increased death risk due to comorbidities. 

The company’s base case and scenario analyses are based on a starting age of 64.4 years from the NIAGARA trial. The starting age of the modelled cohort has a large impact on the extrapolated OS probabilities because the hazard rate of OS is constrained to be at or above the age- and gendermatched all-cause general population risk of death. The time point at which the risk of death approaches that of the general population depends on the starting age used in the model. Similarly, an increased death risk (1.42) relative to the general population risk due to comorbidities in the target population has a large effect on the extrapolated OS in the model due to mortality risk constraints. 

Table 30 summarises the EAG’s scenario analyses that use a starting age of 70 years and an increased death risk of 1.42 in the model to illustrate the impact on the cost-effectiveness results.

## _**5.3 Decision modifiers**_ 

## **5.3.1 QALY weighting for severity** 

The company has not presented a case for a QALY weighting for severity. After checking eligibility for a severity modifier using QALYs estimated from the control arm of the company’s and EAG’s base case and the additional scenario with adjuvant nivolumab, the EAG agrees with the company that the intervention does not meet the thresholds for a QALY weight of 1.2 or 1.7 under absolute or proportional QALY shortfall calculations. 

## **5.3.2 Uncaptured benefits** 

In section 3.13 of the CS, the company highlights several benefits not captured in the QALY calculations: the value of hope associated with a new treatment, option value, early treatment planning, costs of informal care and impact on caregivers and family members, society benefits, longterm care costs from a Personal Social Services perspective, addressing inequalities, and addressing an unmet need in MIBC. 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 484 -->

The EAG considers the value of hope and option value to be subjective and difficult to quantify, whilst outside the NICE reference case. The benefits of early treatment planning are also outside the NICE reference case. The costs of informal care and impact on caregivers and family members could be a significant benefit that is not captured in the QALY calculations; however, the company have not presented any quantitative evidence to show that MIBC is associated with a substantial effect on carer's health-related quality of life and how the availability of perioperative durvalumab benefits carers. Similarly, the company have not provided comprehensive information on the costs of longterm care that are expected to be significantly different between perioperative durvalumab and the comparator. The EAG considers the extent of unmet need is reflected within the severity definition, but a disease severity modifier does not apply in this appraisal. 

The EAG has identified a potential uncaptured benefit in the company's model, which is the impact of post-recurrence therapies. The model's long-term survival projections are based only on the subsequent cancer treatments used in the NIAGARA trial. However, a limitation is that some postrecurrence therapies might be so effective that they return a proportion of patients to a state of eventfree survival. In this scenario, their quality of life and risk of future events may be similar to those of patients who never had a recurrence. If this is the case, the model may not be fully capturing the true, long-term benefits of these later-line treatments, which remains an uncertainty. 

## **5.3.3 Health inequalities** 

The company has not presented any quantitative evidence to show that perioperative durvalumab substantially affects health inequalities, but the company states that the intervention addresses inequalities, especially for women and people with a lower socioeconomic status (Section 3.13 of CS). 

## _**5.4 Confidential comparator and subsequent treatment prices**_ 

The confidential appendix to this EAR includes analyses using confidential prices for atezolizumab, avelumab, nivolumab, and erdafitinib. The confidential appendix presents the results of the company base-case analysis, sensitivity and scenario analyses and the results of exploratory analyses conducted by the EAG, with results reflecting the application of confidential discounts. 

## _**5.5 Conclusions of the cost-effectiveness section**_ 

The company submitted a partitioned survival model to estimate the cost-effectiveness of perioperative durvalumab compared with neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by RC and either (i) no treatment (company’s base case analysis) or (ii) adjuvant nivolumab for patients whose tumours express PD-L1 ≥ 1% and present high-risk of recurrence (company’s scenario analysis). The EAG considers the relevant comparator to be neoadjuvant chemotherapy and RC, followed by no treatment 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 485 -->

or adjuvant nivolumab in eligible patients (i.e., the company’s scenario analysis) because this reflects established standard of care in the NHS. However, the NIAGARA trial was not designed to include adjuvant nivolumab in the control arm for the high-risk, PD-L1 ≥ 1% population. Consequently, counterfactual survival times for the control arm of NIAGARA for the proportion of patients eligible for adjuvant nivolumab had to be estimated (Section 3.5). The EAG considers the approach used may overestimate the effectiveness of nivolumab; however, a control without adjuvant nivolumab as used in the company’s base case analysis is likely to underestimate the effectiveness of the comparator. Consequently, the EAG presents two base case analyses, with and without adjuvant nivolumab. 

The EAG considers the company’s partitioned survival model to be appropriate, but its validity largely depends on the maturity of the survival data, particularly OS. Because the model projects survival outcomes over a patient's lifetime, any uncertainty in the long-term OS projections directly impacts the cost-effectiveness of perioperative durvalumab relative to the comparator. The EAG also notes that uncertainty in the OS projections not only impacts the survival benefit, but it also has implications for the implied time point of ‘cure’ from cancer, where the risk of death becomes equal to that of the general population. Consequently, the starting age in the model is a key input as it directly determines the all-cause mortality risk in the general population. 

The EAG has a number of concerns in relation to the treatment effectiveness evidence and assumptions used in the model. The first concern is the extrapolation of immature data. The company’s analysis relies on the NIAGARA interim results (April 2024 cut off), in which median EFS was reached only in the control arm, while median MFS and OS were not reached in either arm. Extrapolating the immature data beyond the trial follow-up introduces uncertainty in the long-term projections. The second concern is model selection for OS extrapolation. In the NIAGARA trial, OS hazard rates in both arms peak at around 10 months post-randomisation and then converge, approaching near-zero by the end of follow-up. In contrast, the company’s base-case OS extrapolation produces diverging hazards, with the hazard ratio increasing over time before eventually converging due to the constraint of general population mortality. The EAG considers that there is no empirical evidence to support an increasing hazard ratio over time. The third concern is the effect of model starting age. The starting age of the modelled cohort strongly influences extrapolated OS probabilities because the hazard rate is constrained to be at or above the age- and sex-matched general population risk of death. Consequently, the time at which the predicted mortality approaches the general population depends on the cohort’s starting age. 

Another key concern for the EAG is that people with MIBC in the NIAGARA trial are likely to have a higher risk of cancer-non-related mortality than the general population. Many NIAGARA participants had risk factors such as smoking (23.7% current smokers and 49.3% ex-smokers) and 

29/08/2025 




<!-- page 486 -->

other comorbidities. As a result, even if cancer-related deaths are removed, the overall mortality risk in this population is likely to exceed that of the general population. 

The EAG also has three minor concerns: (i) the inclusion of nivolumab in the basket of subsequent treatments post-recurrence, despite it not being licensed for recurrent or metastatic MIBC; (ii) the assumption that nivolumab and atezolizumab are administered intravenously, whereas subcutaneous formulations are recently available for both treatments; and (iii) the omission of costs for PD-L1 testing in the adjuvant nivolumab scenario. 

The model assumptions with the greatest influence on the ICER are: 

- The choice of extrapolation model for OS in the comparator arm 

- The starting age of the modelled cohort 

- Increased risk of non-cancer-related death.

## **APPENDIX 2. COST-EFFECTIVENESS, HEALTH-RELATED QUALITY OF LIFE, COST AND HEALTHCARE RESOURCE IDENTIFICATION, MEASUREMENT, AND VALUATION SEARCHES** 

## **Summary** 

Overall, an appropriate adequate range of relevant databases were searched alongside conference proceedings and health technology assessment agency websites. The reporting of the searches was mainly clear, and the structure of the search and the limits applied were appropriate. The search terms could have been more comprehensive, but the company confirmed that no relevant evidence was missed. 

## **Search strategy** 

The original company submission included searches to identify cost-effectiveness studies for muscleinvasive bladder cancer in adults. A description of the searches and the search strategies were included in Appendix E (pp. 1-36). The health-related quality of life searches referred to in Appendix F and the cost and healthcare resource identification, measurement, and valuation searches referred to in Appendix G were also described and documented in Appendix E (pp. 1-36). In response to the EAG’s points for clarification, the company provided additional information and corrections to errors.

old), the primary evidence base for this appraisal. Baseline characteristics used in the economic model must ensure consistency with the most relevant source of evidence, i.e., the NIAGARA trial, on which other key parameters are based (e.g., efficacy data, treatment duration and utilities) and adopting external sources will lead to internal inconsistency in the economic analysis and bias interpretation of the outcomes. In conclusion, the scenario adopting a starting age of 70 years for patients in the economic model should be removed. It is not supported by clinical trial data, national and international registry evidence, or expert consensus. The population under appraisal—resectable MIBC patients eligible for cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy—is consistently shown to be substantially younger than the broader MIBC population, with robust data demonstrating a mean age closer to 64 years. Including a scenario based on a starting age of 70 is methodologically unjustified, internally inconsistent with key efficacy and utility parameters, and risks distorting the appraisal’s results and conclusions. For decision-making to be rigorous and clinically relevant, the age assumptions must accurately reflect the population in scope; therefore, the 70year starting age scenario should not be considered.

## **ID6168: Durvalumab with gemcitabine and cisplatin before surgery (neoadjuvant) then alone after surgery (adjuvant) for treating muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC)** 

## **Summary** 

AstraZeneca appreciates the opportunity to comment and provide additional evidence regarding the preferred assumptions selected by the Committee as part of the streamlined decision process for appraisal ID6168. We are disappointed that the Committee was unable to issue a positive recommendation and remain concerned that the Committee’s preferred assumptions, including an increased risk of non-cancer-related death (hereafter referred to as the standardised mortality ratio (SMR) for consistency with previous appraisals), age, and overall survival extrapolations, are overly pessimistic and lack validity. Moreover, the preferred assumptions adopted in ID6168 are inconsistent with previous appraisals, the available evidence base, and the outcome of clinical validation exercises. 

MIBC poses a significant clinical challenge as it is associated with rapid progression, aggressive tumours, high recurrence rates, and limited effective therapeutic options. Despite standard treatments such as neoadjuvant chemotherapy and radical cystectomy, patients face high recurrence and progression rates, with less than 60% five-year overall survival (OS) and a substantial quality of life (QoL) impact. 

The NIAGARA clinical trial is the first immuno - oncology trial to demonstrate superiority over standard of care in resectable, cis-eligible MIBC, with statistically significant improvements in event free survival (EFS) and OS. Perioperative durvalumab demonstrated a 32% reduction in the risk of recurrence or death (HR 0.68; 95% CI 0.59, 0.82) and a 25% reduction in the risk of death (HR: 0.75; 95% CI 0.59, 0.93) versus neoadjuvant gemcitabine and cisplatin (G+C), and is considered by clinical experts to be the next standard of care in this disease setting. 

Given the unmet need and the recognition as the future standard of care, it is critical that the Committee can reach timely, pragmatic guidance for perioperative durvalumab. To address Committee’s feedback and facilitate a streamlined decision for patient access, we have provided additional evidence on the following key areas: 

- **Application of age in the model:** the Committee’s preferred age assumption is not generalisable to the whole of England and Wales. Furthermore, deviating from the mean age in the NIAGARA trial, introduces internal inconsistency and bias in the economic analysis (Section A). 

- **Application of SMR in the model:** applying a 42% uplift in mortality across the fulltime horizon of the model imposes a disproportionate and unvalidated penalty, neither justified by the available evidence or clinical expert opinion, and is inconsistent with all precedents established in prior relevant NICE appraisals (Section B). 

- **Overall Survival extrapolations:** because perioperative durvalumab achieves earlier EFS stabilization than G+C (as accepted by EAG and NICE), an earlier decline in excess mortality should be expected. Enforcing the cure times (as described by the 



<!-- page 526 -->

EAG) to align between arms through the selection of a 1-knot spline for the control arm inflates post-progression survival for control arms without clinical justification, disconnects OS from EFS/MFS, and undermines clinical plausibility. (Section C). 

The following sections present further scenario analyses to explore the impact of starting age and SMR on the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER), and present further supportive evidence, including alternative approaches to address Committee’s feedback and facilitate a streamlined decision. The scenario results confirm that, when correctly applied, these parameters do not materially influence decision-making, with perioperative durvalumab - remaining cost effective with ICERs ranging from £13,983 to £14,316 per QALY gained depending on the scenario. 

Additionally, reflecting the Committee’s preference for earlier convergence of OS hazards than in the Company’s base case, we present an alternative OS scenario retaining the Committee’s preferred 1-knot spline odds distribution for perioperative durvalumab arm and applying a log-normal curve to the control arm. 

Furthermore, we tested the alternative SMR scenarios (Scenarios 1–2 in combination with the log-normal curve for OS for the control arm) and found perioperative durvalumab remains cost-effective across all scenarios with ICERs ranging from £14,759 to £16,821 per QALY gained. 

## **Section A: Application of age in the model** 

AstraZeneca considers that the Committee should retain the mean age of 64.4 years from the NIAGARA clinical trial as the model starting age instead of the North-East data provided by NHSE during the development of the EAG report. 

The North-East dataset has an unknown period of data collection and, as noted by the EAG, it is uncertain whether the mean age observed in that region is representative of the whole of England and Wales. Population statistics from the Office for National Statistics confirm that North-East England population is older than the national average (median age 41.7 years versus 40.2 years for England, mid-2020 estimates). A higher mean age in North-East data therefore likely reflects regional population ageing rather than characteristics of patients eligible for perioperative durvalumab. Without transparent metadata for the North-East dataset (period of collection, sample size, inclusion criteria) and evidence of national representativeness, it should not supersede the trial as the basis for a preferred assumption. 

Furthermore, UK clinical experts indicated that NIAGARA trial baseline characteristics are broadly representative of clinical practice. Within NIAGARA trial, 19 patients were enrolled across four UK sites (Weston Park Hospital, Barts Health NHS Trust, Clatterbridge Cancer Centre NHS Foundation Trust, and Edinburgh Cancer Centre). The UK subset’s mean age was 64.3 years, with a median of 64 years and a range of 51 to 77 years, which aligns closely with the overall trial mean of 64.4 years and supports transferability to the national setting. 

Baseline characteristics used in the economic model should remain aligned with the trial to preserve internal consistency across key parameters such as efficacy (EFS, MFS and OS), treatment duration, and utilities. Substituting the starting age in the model with a regional 



<!-- page 527 -->

demographic while leaving the NIAGARA data inputs anchored to the trial cohort introduces internal inconsistency, particularly in a model where OS is constrained to be at or above ageand sex-matched general population mortality. Increasing the starting age mechanically brings forward the point at which modelled mortality approaches the general population rate, and thereby artificially reduces extrapolated survival for both arms in a way not driven by the NIAGARA trial data. Changing only the model starting age therefore risks biasing cost - effectiveness results and decision - making. 

## **Section B: Application of SMR in the model** 

AstraZeneca maintains that adopting the Company’s assumption would be more appropriate, given substantive methodological limitations implemented by the EAG, absence of clinical expert validation and the exploratory nature of the EAG scenario. The EAG’s rationale to explore this issue relied on the hypothesis that the target population has an increased risk of non - cancer mortality due to comorbidities including smoking, hypertension, diabetes, and renal or urinary disorders. While clinical advisors discussed the plausibility of these comorbidities impacting survival, the technical approach is flawed and the hazard ratio used - to quantify excess non cancer mortality was not validated with clinical experts by the EAG. In contrast, the Company validated the plausibility of the OS curves, which incorporated non-cancer mortality, with clinical experts. 

Given the lack of clinical plausibility in the Committee preferred assumptions on the SMR, relevant precedent in the same disease setting should not be dismissed. For example, in TA817, a time-limited excess mortality of 10% (i.e., HR of 1.1) was applied in the DFS health state beyond five years and removed after ten years, with patients thereafter reverting to age- and sex-matched general population mortality, acknowledging that excess non-cancer risk is modest and diminishes over time. In contrast to the current appraisal, TA817 comprised both cisplatin eligible and cisplatin ineligible patients. Because cisplatin ineligible patients have a greater comorbidity burden (e.g, renal impairment), they consequently exhibit higher baseline non-cancer mortality than cisplatin eligible populations alone. Accordingly, applying TA817 precedent would still overestimate risk and represent a conservative scenario for perioperative durvalumab in MIBC. 

The Company also performed a targeted review of appraisals in other disease settings that applied an excess risk of death above the general population (see Appendix A Table 5). More broadly, other appraisals commonly adopt modest SMRs in the approximate range of 1.09 to 1.2, often beyond a cure point and sometimes time bounded. Large, permanent uplifts similar to 1.42 have only been applied in disease settings with markedly greater comorbidity burdens - or persistent treatment related risks than perioperative MIBC. This is explained in detail in Appendix A _._ 

In the current appraisal, the EAG estimated an excess risk of death above the general population by comparing the probability of non-cancer-related deaths across the NIAGARA trial follow-up period (~ 5 years, 64.7 months) with the corresponding 5-year age- and sexadjusted mortality probability for the general population using the Company base case age (64.4 years). Assuming an exponential model, the EAG translated this into a constant hazard ratio of 1.42 and applied it across the full-time horizon in the model. As previously mentioned, this contrasts with relevant precedent, where excess non-cancer risk is assumed to diminish over time. 



<!-- page 528 -->

A lifetime application of a constant excess non-cancer mortality (HR 1.42) is clinically - implausible and overly simplistic. Excess non cancer risk is typically concentrated in the early - post-treatment period, reflecting complications and therapy related comorbidities, and diminishes as survivors remain disease free, with mortality risk converging towards age and sex matched population levels over time. The EAG also acknowledged that further evidence is required before applying an SMR and did not include this in their preferred assumptions; different starting age and increased mortality risk were exploratory analysis, with no scenario implementing both concurrently. 

Furthermore, the Committee’s preference for a higher starting age and excess mortality risk of 1.42 is inconsistent. The excess risk calculated by the EAG was based on a model starting age of 64.4. If model starting age were to increase, background mortality would also increase. As demonstrated in Table 1, the ~5-year mortality probability for the general population is 7.11% when starting at age 64.4 vs. 8.16% when starting at age 66. When the excess mortality risk is recalculated, this drops to 1.23 with the higher starting age. We recognise that the excess mortality risk in NIAGARA trial may also change with age, but the general population is expected to increase more rapidly as age becomes the primary driver of mortality for both populations. Our example has illustrated that increasing the starting age of the model is highly likely to reduce the estimated excess risk. Moreover, applying a fixed excess-mortality rate across the lifetime horizon implies an effectively increasing risk of mortality over time. This is inconsistent with the accepted view that excess risk declines over time .

## **Alternative SMR and age scenarios** 

Following the methodological and clinical basis outlined above, it can be concluded that the EAG’s exploratory assumptions are inappropriate and should not be adopted by the Committee as part of the base case for decision making. To address the interest expressed by the Committee in exploring an increased mortality risk, even where this is not aligned with feedback from consulted clinicians, we present two scenarios that build on the above rationale and more closely reflect the available evidence, relevant precedent, and clinical plausibility. Both scenarios are conservative: 1) age aligned with NIAGARA trial and SMR of 1.1 applied for entire modelled time horizon and 2) age aligned with NIAGARA trial and using the EAG’s calculated SMR 1.42 for the first five years, followed by a downward trend towards 1, frontloaded to reflect the post - treatment complications or therapy - related comorbidities.

The scenario results are provided to confirm that these parameters do not materially influence decision-making, as perioperative durvalumab remaining cost - effective in both cases. Nonetheless, consistent with clinical input, precedent, and model coherence, the base case - should use an SMR of 1, with these higher SMR scenarios serving only as sensitivity checks. 

## **Section C: Overall survival extrapolation** 

## _**OS curve selection**_ 

The NIAGARA trial provides the longest follow-up in this disease setting extending beyond five years (64.7 months). However, median OS was not reached, and 71.1% of participants in the durvalumab arm and 62.8% of patients in the control arm were still alive and in follow-up at the time of the April 2024 DCO, indicating high rates of right-censored observations. 

Based on this, the company disagrees with the overly pessimistic OS curve selection in the EAG base case, as part of the Committee preferred assumptions. The EAG considered the 1- knot spline odds model for the perioperative durvalumab arm and a 1-knot spline hazard model for the control arm to be the best-fitting models for the extrapolation of OS. This judgement was made on the goodness-of-fit compared to the observed trial data, primarily on patterns observed in the hazard profiles, without integrating external registry evidence or clinical expert opinion. Prioritising best visual fit to the observed early data, and not considering the clinical - validity of extrapolations, risks over fitting to the immature tails, forcing premature - convergence of arm hazards, and generating long term survival patterns (e.g., in - post progression survival) that are inconsistent with external evidence, expert expectations, and the observed separation in EFS and MFS Kaplan Meier curves. 

Extrapolation should place greater weight on external evidence on long-term survival, clinical expert expectations, and internal consistency across EFS, MFS, DSS, and OS endpoints. The Company selected the extrapolation for the control arm based on clinical plausibility and concordance with external long-term evidence. The OS log-logistic model was chosen as the base-case for the control arm because it aligned with external literature for long-term OS in MIBC (see CS document section 3.3.2, Table 40), and it was the clinician-preferred option, with two of four experts judging it most plausible. 



<!-- page 530 -->

## _**Cure assumption**_ 

The EAG notes that the Company’s model does not include an explicit cure assumption, and instead, the EAG considers the timepoints from which implicit cure is achieved. According to the EAG report, for a patient to be considered ‘cured’ of MIBC, two conditions must be met: (i) the risk of events (recurrence or progression) defined by the EFS curve must not be greater than the risk of all-cause death, and (ii) there must be no risk of cancer-related deaths. In the Company’s base case analysis, these conditions are met after xxxx years in the perioperative durvalumab arm and after xxxxx years in the control arm. Whilst it is important to consider the timepoints from which patients are ‘cured’, if perioperative durvalumab achieves earlier EFS stabilisation compared to G+C (e.g., the risk of recurrence or progression defined by the EFS curve is equal to the risk of all-cause death), which has been accepted by the EAG and the NICE committee, excess disease-related mortality should plausibly decline earlier in the perioperative durvalumab arm, and thus a difference in cure timepoint (as defined by the EAG) should be expected. A recent systematic review by Sternberg et al. (2025) found evidence of a strong association between EFS and OS treatment effects in neoadjuvant/perioperative MIBC trials, supporting the idea that earlier EFS stabilisation should translate into earlier cure, according to the definition by the EAG. In the NICE preferred based case analysis, the two conditions for patients to be cured are met after xxxx years in the perioperative durvalumab arm and xxxx years in the control arm, meaning that the early modelling of converging hazards resulting in closely matched cure times across arms has overlooked an expected EFS-driven difference. 

The alignment of the cure timepoint (as defined by EAG) between arms through the selection - of the 1-knot spline hazard model for G+C arm implicitly lengthens post progression survival for G+C and G+C+N relative to perioperative durvalumab, and produces a disproportionately longer post progression survival for G+C and G+C+N versus perioperative durvalumab, that - is not supported by clinical evidence (see Table 3). Mechanistically, longer post progression survival could be justified if there were durable effects after treatment cessation typical of immunotherapy, or if patients in the G+C arm systematically accessed effective therapies at recurrence. However, neither of these explanations holds here. In the perioperative - durvalumab versus G+C+N comparison, both regimens are immunotherapy containing, and any immunologic persistence should be comparable. The model also assumes the same distribution of subsequent therapies across these arms, removing differential post-progression efficacy driven by treatments as an explanation. In the perioperative durvalumab versus G+C comparison, there is likewise no clinical basis for control patients to experience substantially - longer survival after progression than those initially receiving an IO based perioperative regimen, especially given the consistent improvements in EFS, MFS, DSS and PFS - 2 with durvalumab. In contrast, the company base case using loglogistic for G+C provides a comparable distribution of pre- and post-progression LYs across arms, with the distribution of life - years remaining primarily in the event - free state and a smaller share accruing in - post progression, consistent with the observed EFS/MFS separation and the modelled - similarity (G+C) or equivalence (G+C+N) in subsequent therapy use.

## _**Alternative curve selection**_ 

It is acknowledged that the Committee may prefer a scenario in which OS hazards converge earlier than in the company’s base case, and the difference in time points between arms where ‘cure’ conditions are met is less. This could be represented by the log-normal curve for the control arm, which was considered a plausible alternative by clinicians in the interviews conducted by the Company. In this scenario, the committee’s preference for the 1-knot spline odds distribution for durvalumab’s arm has been retained. As with the Gompertz model, the 1-knot spline odds model yields comparable distributions of pre and post-progression life-years across arms with most life-years in the event-free state and fewer post-progression consistent with the observed EFS/MFS separation and the modelled similarity (G+C) or equivalence (G+C+N) in subsequent therapy use (see Table 3). The EAG’s conditions for implicit ‘cure’ are met after xxxx and xxxxx years for the control and perioperative durvalumab arms, respectively, converging earlier than company base case, yet preserving the EFS-driven difference.

## _**Conclusion**_ 

The company maintains the preference for the OS curves as per the base case in the submission, as it is plausible, internally consistent, and grounded in external evidence and clinical validation. By anchoring OS extrapolation to standard parametric models (loglogistic/lognormal) that reflect a transparent, monotone decline in hazards consistent with perioperative bladder cancer data, the base case preserves coherence across EFS, MFS, - DSS, and OS and avoids over fitting immature NIAGARA tails with splines. This yields a credible “implicit cure” dynamic aligned with earlier EFS stabilization on perioperative - - - durvalumab and produces balanced pre and post progression life year distributions consistent with observed clinical trial data and subsequent therapy use. 

If residual concerns remain that OS hazards should converge earlier than in the Company’s - base case, the only clinically plausible and evidence based option for the control arm is the - - log normal curve, paired with the Committee preferred 1 knot spline odds for durvalumab. This - alternative maintains methodological rigor (hazard profile assessment and clinical validation), preserves internal consistency across endpoints, and continues to demonstrate perioperative durvalumab as cost - effective across tested age and SMR scenarios.
